name: CCAR-P Core Bank
description: 210 blueprint-weighted items for Claude Certified Architect - Professional, written against the official Exam Guide v1.0, the Partner Academy prep-course objectives and current Anthropic documentation. Every item is tagged to a verbatim guide objective and set in one of the six industries the guide names.

items.objective: 1.1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
items.stem: A commercial bank monitors loan covenants by hand. Each quarter borrowers send financial statements as PDFs in dozens of layouts, and analysts key the figures into the loan system. The loan system already stores each covenant's formula, such as debt service coverage, and computes ratios and breach flags once figures are entered. Credit officers then decide whether a breach gets a waiver or a formal notice, which has legal effect. The sponsor asks for 'Claude to read the statements, compute the ratios and send the breach notices.' Which division of work should the architect propose?

options.text: Claude extracts figures from the varied statements into a schema with page citations, the loan system computes ratios and flags breaches, and officers decide.
Claude extracts the figures, calculates every covenant ratio with step-by-step reasoning, re-checks its own arithmetic, and officers spot-check one notice in ten.
Analysts keep keying figures from the statements by hand, and Claude drafts the breach notices from the loan system's breach flags for officer sign-off.
Claude runs end to end as an agent with loan-system access, and any notice it scores below 0.9 self-reported confidence goes to an officer first.

items.explanation: The first move in translating a business request is to split it into what Claude does, what existing systems do and what humans do, using the four properties of generative AI as the lens. Reading statements in dozens of inconsistent layouts is unstructured-language work that plays to Claude's strengths. Applying fixed covenant formulas is deterministic arithmetic that the loan system already does exactly and auditably once figures are entered, so handing it to the model adds error risk for no gain. A waiver or a formal notice has legal effect, so the decision stays with an accountable credit officer. Page citations on the extraction, which the Citations feature returns as page ranges when the source is a PDF, let the officer verify the inputs behind every flagged breach.

rationales.B: This hands deterministic formula work to a probabilistic model and then compensates with self-review and a 10% sample; a legal-effect notice that escapes the sample is sent unreviewed, and the loan system would have computed the ratio exactly.
rationales.C: This leaves the hard, high-volume part (reading statements in dozens of layouts) manual and uses Claude only for templated drafting, so it misplaces Claude on the work where it adds least value.
rationales.D: A self-reported confidence score is a weak compensating control for a decision with legal effect, and giving an autonomous agent end-to-end authority removes the officer from most decisions the bank must own.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 1.1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
items.stem: A hospital pilots a Claude assistant that answers clinicians' questions about the hospital's own drug formulary, which the pharmacy committee revises every week. In testing, the assistant answers fluently but names drugs that were removed months ago and misses newly added restrictions. Using the four properties of generative AI as the lens, what is the limitation and the matching design response?

options.text: Steerability: the instructions are too weak, so add a firm system-prompt rule that the assistant may answer only from the current hospital formulary list.
Working memory: the sessions run too long for the assistant to track, so cap each clinician session at five turns and then start a fresh one.
Next token prediction: the assistant writes plausible text, so turn on extended thinking and require it to state a confidence level with each answer.
Knowledge: the weekly formulary cannot be in the model's training data, so ground each answer in the current formulary via retrieval or a lookup tool.

items.explanation: Anthropic Academy's four properties (next token prediction, knowledge, working memory, steerability) are the feasibility lens the prep course names for scoping. Anthropic publishes a reliable knowledge cutoff for every model, the date through which its knowledge is most reliable, and facts that are private to the organisation and change weekly cannot be in any model's training data, so this is a knowledge gap. The design response is to supply the knowledge at request time from the system that owns it, through retrieval over the current formulary or a lookup tool, rather than to ask the model to try harder. Recognising which property is the binding limit tells the architect which component to add.

rationales.A: Instructing the model to answer only from the formulary does not give it the formulary; a prompt-only fix cannot supply data the model never had, so it would still answer from stale training-era knowledge or refuse.
rationales.B: The failure is about facts the model never had, not about losing track within long sessions; shorter sessions change nothing about removed or newly restricted drugs.
rationales.C: Extended thinking lets the model reason longer over what it already has, and a self-stated confidence level is not grounded in the current formulary, so neither change supplies the missing knowledge.

items.objective: 1.1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
items.stem: A grocery chain has budget for one Claude project this quarter. Candidate one is assigning tax codes to about 4 million catalogue updates a month from a 40-code taxonomy unchanged for three years; an incumbent model trained on 2 million labelled examples scores 98.7% and nobody needs explanations. Candidate two is routing supplier dispute emails, free text in five languages, whose categories are revised every quarter and for which only about 300 labelled examples exist. Which recommendation is best supported?

options.text: Start with tax codes, since 4 million updates a month gives the largest absolute saving once Claude matches the incumbent's 98.7% accuracy.
Take on both at once, sending tax codes to the fastest tier and disputes to the most capable tier so that spend across the two stays balanced.
Leave tax codes on the incumbent model and apply Claude to the dispute inbox, where scarce labels, shifting categories and five languages all favour an LLM.
Use Claude to relabel the tax-code training data so the incumbent improves, and revisit disputes once several thousand labels have accumulated.

items.explanation: Anthropic's classification guidance lists when an LLM beats traditional machine learning: limited labelled data (a few dozen examples can be enough), categories that change over time, unstructured text, semantic rules, a need for explanations, and multilingual input without separate models. The dispute inbox has nearly all of these properties. The tax-code task has none: a stable taxonomy, abundant labels, an incumbent at 98.7% and no need for explanations. Translating a business problem into a Claude solution includes deciding where Claude should NOT go, and replacing a well-performing deterministic or classical system is a scoping failure rather than a win.

rationales.A: Volume is not fit. Matching 98.7% only reproduces what the incumbent already delivers, so the saving is speculative while the migration risk is real, and the problem that actually needs an LLM stays manual.
rationales.B: The sponsor funded one project, and splitting the effort still spends it re-solving a task the incumbent already does well; balancing spend across tiers does not make the tax-code work worth doing.
rationales.D: The incumbent is not short of labels or accuracy, and the dispute inbox does not need thousands of labels before an LLM can handle it, so this delays the right project for a reason that does not apply.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 1.1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
items.stem: A security-analytics software company is adding a Claude-powered alert-summary feature to the edition it hosts for a US federal agency. The agency contract requires FedRAMP High authorization with AWS as the sole data processor. The team also wants to reuse Agent Skills it built for its commercial edition. Which TWO statements reflect a correct reading of these constraints? (Select TWO)

options.text: Claude in Amazon Bedrock is the route Anthropic documents for FedRAMP High workloads that need AWS as the sole data processor.
Claude Platform on AWS satisfies the contract, because it is billed through AWS Marketplace and authenticated with AWS IAM credentials.
The first-party Claude API with inference_geo set to 'us' satisfies the contract, because inference then stays in United States regions.
Claude on Google Cloud (formerly Vertex AI) in a US region satisfies the contract, because it runs on FedRAMP-authorized infrastructure.
Agent Skills are not available on the Bedrock route, so the federal edition must deliver those capabilities another way, such as prompts or tools.

items.explanation: The prep course asks the architect to separate user entry points, build-time interfaces and the delivery routes an enterprise procures, and to rule out the routes that governance excludes before any other trade-off. Anthropic's Claude Platform on AWS documentation states that organisations that require FedRAMP High, or that need AWS to be the sole data processor, should use Claude in Amazon Bedrock, which runs on AWS-managed infrastructure with zero operator access for Anthropic personnel. A FedRAMP certification attaches to a specific cloud service offering and supports the agency's own authorization decision, so what matters is which service processes the data, not whose infrastructure sits underneath. The Bedrock documentation lists Agent Skills among the features it does not support, so the compliance decision has a feature consequence the design must absorb. Choosing the route first and then re-planning features is the correct order.

rationales.B: AWS billing and IAM authentication do not change who operates the service: on Claude Platform on AWS, Anthropic operates the stack and is the inference data processor, so AWS is not the sole processor.
rationales.C: inference_geo controls where inference runs, which is a residency setting; it does not make the first-party API a FedRAMP High service with AWS as sole processor.
rationales.D: Whatever Google Cloud's own authorizations, the contract names AWS as the sole data processor, so Claude on Google Cloud fails that clause in any region; governance constraints eliminate routes before other trade-offs.

items.objective: 1.1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
items.stem: A university wants 'an AI advisor for students'. Discovery on a term of advisor email shows that 70% are degree-requirement questions answered in the published catalogue, 20% need the student's own record (credits earned, registration holds) and 10% involve wellbeing, academic misconduct or visa status. Which initial solution scope should the architect propose?

options.text: Claude answers catalogue questions by retrieval, reads the student's record via an authenticated read-only tool, and routes sensitive cases to advisors.
Claude handles every category, with a system prompt telling it to take care on wellbeing, misconduct and visa topics and to add a disclaimer to those replies.
Claude uses retrieval and a read-only record tool, and on wellbeing, misconduct and visa cases gives general guidance, then offers to book an advisor.
A model is fine-tuned on five years of advisor email threads so that it learns how advisors answer every category, including all of the most sensitive cases.

items.explanation: The prep course expects a vague request to become a scoped architecture with explicit boundary conditions. Each slice of demand gets the mechanism that fits it: published catalogue content is static knowledge suited to retrieval; a student's credits and holds are live, per-person state that a scoped, authenticated tool call to the system of record should own; and wellbeing, misconduct and visa cases sit outside the solution boundary and go to a human advisor. Writing that boundary into the architecture, rather than into a prompt, is what makes it enforceable and defensible to the sponsor.

rationales.B: A prompt instruction plus a disclaimer is not a boundary condition; the assistant would still give substantive answers on visa status or misconduct, which are high-stakes cases a human must own.
rationales.C: The catalogue and record mechanisms are right, but the sensitive cases are still answered: a boundary condition means wellbeing, misconduct and visa cases are routed to a human, not answered first with an optional offer of an advisor afterwards.
rationales.D: Fine-tuning on historical email does not supply current records, does not create any boundary for sensitive cases, and puts years of personal data into training material without need.

items.objective: 1.1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
items.stem: A state benefits agency wants Claude to summarise appeal letters for caseworkers. Volume is 60,000 letters a month; each call sends about 6,000 input tokens (letter plus instructions) and returns about 500 output tokens. For the estimate use 3 USD per million input tokens and 15 USD per million output tokens. The program office approved 2,000 USD a month. A deputy director wants a second call on every letter that re-reads the letter and the summary to check for omissions, at about 6,500 input and 200 output tokens. A pilot eval on 3,000 letters found omissions only in letters over 20 pages, which are 10% of volume; on those, the check call is about 13,000 input and 200 output tokens. Which assessment should the architect present?

options.text: One pass costs about $1,530 a month and fits; checking every letter would reach about $2,880, so run a fresh omission eval before adding any check.
One pass costs about $15,300 a month, nearly eight times the budget; move to the fastest tier before doing any further design work.
One pass costs about $1,530 a month and fits; checking only the long letters adds about $250, so propose that, not a check on every letter.
Output dominates the bill because it is priced five times higher than input; cap each summary at 200 tokens first so the total fits.

items.explanation: Input: 60,000 x 6,000 = 360 million tokens, 1,080 USD. Output: 60,000 x 500 = 30 million tokens, 450 USD. One pass is about 1,530 USD and fits the 2,000 USD budget. A check on every letter adds 390 million input tokens (1,170 USD) and 12 million output tokens (180 USD), about 1,350 USD, for roughly 2,880 USD, which is over budget. The pilot eval has already located the risk: omissions occur only in the long letters, 6,000 a month. Checking those alone is 6,000 x 13,000 = 78 million input tokens (234 USD) plus 1.2 million output tokens (18 USD), about 252 USD, for a total near 1,782 USD, inside the budget. The prep course expects use cases to be sized from call volume and token consumption before they are committed; sizing against the evidence already in hand meets the deputy director's concern within budget instead of deferring it.

rationales.A: The arithmetic is right, but the pilot eval has already measured where omissions occur; running another eval before acting delays a check the evidence supports and leaves the long letters unprotected in the meantime.
rationales.B: This is an order-of-magnitude arithmetic slip; the single pass is about 1,530 USD, and dropping to the fastest tier on the basis of a wrong estimate trades away quality for no reason.
rationales.D: Output is pricier per token but input dominates here, 1,080 USD against 450 USD, because each call sends twelve times as many input tokens; capping summaries attacks the smaller line item and risks omissions.

items.objective: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
items.stem: An online fashion retailer is designing a customer support assistant. Its knowledge sources are a returns-and-sizing FAQ that changes a few times a year and the order management system, where shipping status changes many times a day. Most customers ask where their order is. How should the design supply order status to Claude?

options.text: Index the order table into the vector store alongside the FAQ, and re-index it every hour so the retrieved order status stays reasonably current.
Call the order management system through a lookup tool scoped to the signed-in customer, and keep the vector index for the FAQ content.
Load all open orders for the customer's region into a cached system prompt each morning, so the model sees every order without a lookup.
Give Claude a read-only SQL tool over the whole order database, so it can look up the status of any order a customer asks about.

items.explanation: Anthropic's customer support guide draws the line between retrieval and live state: embedding-based retrieval suits large, slow-changing knowledge, but for real-time facts such as account or order details it is not sufficient, and a tool call to the system of record is the documented pattern. The prep course names this skill directly as recognising when retrieval is doing a job that live state should own. The input stage therefore has two paths: retrieval for the FAQ and a live lookup for status, and that lookup is scoped to the signed-in customer so the model can reach only the data the conversation is entitled to.

rationales.A: Hourly re-indexing still serves status up to an hour old for data that changes many times a day, and turns a transactional lookup into a costly, fragile indexing pipeline.
rationales.C: A morning snapshot is stale within hours, loads other customers' orders into every conversation, and inflates the prompt with data that a single scoped lookup would supply.
rationales.D: This supplies live data, but the tool is not scoped to the customer: any order in the database is reachable, so one customer can extract another's order details. Least privilege means a lookup keyed to the signed-in customer's own orders, not open query access.

items.objective: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
items.stem: A city's 311 service-request platform is a vendor SaaS product. It exposes a REST endpoint that lists new requests but cannot send outbound webhooks, the vendor limits that list endpoint to 1,000 calls per day per tenant, and the city's security policy forbids exposing any new public endpoint. Each request must be classified and assigned to a department within 15 minutes. Which integration shape should the architect specify for the input stage?

options.text: A push-based receiver behind the city's API gateway, since webhooks are the more web-scalable pattern and avoid the delay that polling adds.
A pull-based service that polls the list endpoint every 3 minutes, well inside the 15-minute target, run as a monitored service.
A pull-based service that polls the list endpoint every 5 seconds, run as a monitored service, so each request is classified almost at once.
An hourly export of new requests that staff upload to a batch classification job, which keeps the integration simple and API-free.

items.explanation: Anthropic's ticket-routing guide describes two ways to connect Claude to an existing ticket system. Push (webhooks) has the ticket system call your routing service; pull has your code fetch new tickets on a schedule, which is easier to implement but makes unnecessary calls when the pull frequency is too high and is too slow when it is too low. Here push is impossible on both counts, so the decision is the poll interval. A day has 1,440 minutes: polling every 3 minutes is 480 calls a day, inside the 1,000-call quota, and the worst-case pickup delay of 3 minutes leaves most of the 15-minute target for classification and assignment. Running the poller as a monitored service makes the input stage observable rather than a script someone runs.

rationales.A: Push is the right idea at the wrong place: the vendor cannot send webhooks and city policy forbids a new public endpoint, so the more scalable pattern is simply unavailable.
rationales.C: Polling every 5 seconds is 17,280 calls a day, more than 17 times the vendor's 1,000-call quota, so the poller would be throttled or cut off within the first two hours of each day; this is the too-frequent polling the guide warns about, and it buys nothing against a 15-minute target.
rationales.D: An hourly manual export cannot meet a 15-minute assignment target and adds a human step where an API is already available to read from.

items.objective: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
items.stem: A hospital radiology department is taking a report-drafting pipeline from pilot to production. Claude drafts the impression section of each report from the radiologist's structured findings, and the radiologist edits and signs the report in the reporting system. The hospital calls the Claude API directly under Anthropic's Business Associate Agreement, with HIPAA readiness enabled for its organization. Which THREE elements belong in the end-to-end design? (Select THREE)

options.text: Validate each draft against the report template's required sections and send failures to an exception queue, not the reading worklist.
Retry only on HTTP 429 and 5xx responses, because any response that returns HTTP 200 contains a complete, usable draft.
A second Claude call, tuned against the eval set, reviews each draft and files it when it finds no omissions, so radiologists see only flagged ones.
Send drafting through the Message Batches API to halve the cost, since radiologists sign routine outpatient reports later in the shift.
Capture radiologist edits as structured diffs and feed recurring corrections into the eval set that gates prompt and model changes.
Set acceptance thresholds for omitted findings and laterality errors, and plan eval-gated migration because pinned model snapshots retire.

items.explanation: An end-to-end design covers the output path and the feedback loop, not just the call. On the output side, the production checklist names failure modes and a mitigation for each: a draft that is missing required sections or is malformed is caught by validation against the report template and sent to an exception queue, so it never reaches a radiologist looking like a finished draft and failures become countable. The feedback loop turns radiologist edits into evaluation data, and evaluations with explicit acceptance thresholds, here for omitted findings and wrong-side (laterality) errors, become the gate for every prompt or model change. Model IDs are pinned snapshots that Anthropic retires, with at least 60 days' notice for publicly released models, so an eval-gated migration path belongs in the design from day one rather than being improvised when a retirement notice arrives.

rationales.B: An HTTP 200 does not guarantee a complete, well-formed draft: a response can stop at max_tokens or leave out required sections, so the output stage has to check the content rather than trust the status code.
rationales.C: However well it scores on the eval set, a model check is not a substitute for radiologist review of a signed clinical report; letting it file the drafts it judges complete removes the human in the loop on exactly the omissions it failed to spot.
rationales.D: Anthropic's feature eligibility table marks Batch processing as not eligible under HIPAA readiness because of its 29-day retention, and a HIPAA-enabled organization's requests that use a non-eligible feature are rejected with a 400 error, so the half-price lever is not available to this PHI workload.

items.objective: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
items.stem: An asset manager streams Claude summaries of sell-side research notes into a compliance archive. About 0.3% of archived summaries stop mid-sentence. HTTP logs show only 200 responses for those calls, the affected notes are no longer than average, and they cluster on cybersecurity-sector research that describes intrusion techniques in detail. Which change to the pipeline's output stage should the architect specify?

options.text: max_tokens is set too low for detailed notes, so output is cut off; raise the limit and alert whenever stop_reason shows the ceiling was hit.
The writer treats every HTTP 200 as success, so mid-stream classifier refusals leave partial text; branch on stop_reason, discard it and fall back.
The streaming connection drops on long responses; add client-side reconnect logic and switch the archive writer to non-streaming calls.
The retrieval step passes truncated chunks of these notes; re-chunk the cybersecurity notes with larger overlap and rebuild their index.

items.explanation: Current Claude models include safety classifiers whose declines are not errors: the response is HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal', and the decline can arrive mid-stream after some output, which must be discarded. The symptoms point there: clean 200s, ordinary length, and clustering on content about intrusion techniques. The design defect is an output stage that treats every 200 as success and never reads stop_reason. The change to specify is to branch on it, drop the partial text, and route to a fallback (Anthropic offers a server-side fallback option) or to human handling, and to count refusals as their own signal, because monitoring built on error rates never sees them.

rationales.A: A max_tokens cut-off is the attractive near-miss, but it would correlate with length; these notes are of average length and cluster by topic, which points to a content classifier, not the output ceiling.
rationales.C: Dropped connections would surface as client errors or incomplete streams in the logs and would not cluster on one research topic; the logs show clean 200 responses.
rationales.D: Truncated retrieval chunks would degrade content, not stop the output mid-sentence, and nothing in the symptoms implicates the retrieval step; this is a fix at the wrong layer.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
items.stem: An online tutoring platform uses a capable Claude model for step-by-step maths help. Full replies take about 9 seconds, and analytics show students abandon after about 3 seconds of a blank screen. Product will not accept lower answer quality. After each reply, a second step tags it with curriculum skill codes for the teacher gradebook. Which output design fits?

options.text: Stream the tutor reply so students watch it build progressively, and run skill tagging as a separate non-streaming call on the complete reply.
Move the tutor to the fastest model tier so complete replies return in under 3 seconds, and keep the skill tagging in the same call as each reply.
Stream both the tutor reply and the skill codes, and write each code to the gradebook as its tokens arrive to keep records current.
Cap every tutor reply at 100 output tokens so that the complete answer arrives sooner, and show a progress spinner while students wait.

items.explanation: Anthropic's latency guidance says streaming lets the model start sending its response before the full output is complete, which can significantly improve perceived responsiveness; it does not shorten total generation time. That is why it fits when quality must be held: the architect can keep the more capable model and still put text on screen well before the 3-second abandonment point. A structured step that has to parse a complete response, such as assigning skill codes to the finished reply, runs non-streaming. Matching the output mode to who consumes the output, a person or a system, is an end-to-end design decision.

rationales.B: Product has ruled out lower answer quality, so downgrading the tutor model violates the stated constraint when streaming solves the abandonment problem without it.
rationales.C: Writing codes as tokens arrive means acting on partial, unparsed output; structured data for a system of record should be parsed from a complete response.
rationales.D: Capping replies at 100 tokens cuts the step-by-step explanation that is the product, and a spinner is still the blank-screen wait that students abandon.

items.objective: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
items.stem: A developer-tools company ships a feature that turns natural-language questions into SQL against each customer's schema and adds a short explanation of the query. Each week, questions whose generated SQL customers reported as wrong in production are added to the eval set. The team wants that evaluation to run in CI on every prompt or model change and block the merge on a regression. Which grading design should the architect specify for this feedback loop?

options.text: Two senior engineers hand-grade 50 sampled outputs from the eval set on each change, which gives the best possible signal per example.
An LLM grader reads each generated query and judges whether it looks correct, put to use at once so that the CI gate can ship this sprint.
Release changes behind a flag and gate each one on the production thumbs-up rate, measured over the week after it ships.
Run each query against fixture databases and compare result sets in code, adding a validated LLM grader only for the explanation text.

items.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to choose the fastest, most reliable, most scalable grading method: code-based grading where an objective check exists, LLM-based grading for nuanced judgement once its reliability is tested, and human grading only where unavoidable because it is slow and expensive. Generated SQL has an objective check, executing it and comparing result sets, so code grading fits that part; the free-text explanation is where a validated LLM grader earns its place. Because production failures flow into the eval set every week, the gate has to grade a growing set on every commit, which only a fast, repeatable automated design can sustain; that closes the loop from production back to the release gate.

rationales.A: Hand grading 50 cases per change is slow, costly and low in volume, the opposite of what a per-commit CI gate needs, when an objective automated check exists.
rationales.B: Judging whether SQL looks correct is weaker than running it, and adopting an LLM grader without first testing its reliability makes the gate untrustworthy.
rationales.C: Production thumbs-up is a lagging, noisy signal gathered after release; it is the wrong lifecycle phase for a gate meant to block regressions before merge.

items.objective: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
items.stem: A school district wants teachers to receive a rubric-aligned feedback draft for each student essay: one essay and one rubric in, a page of feedback out, and the teacher always edits it before students see it. A vendor proposes a planner agent, a critic agent and a writer agent. What should the architect recommend first?

options.text: An autonomous agent that decides which rubric criteria to examine per essay and how many revision passes to run before handing over the draft.
An orchestrator that assigns one worker per rubric criterion, followed by a synthesis step that merges the workers' comments into one page.
An evaluator-optimizer loop that keeps revising the feedback until a separate grader model's eval score shows it meets every rubric criterion.
A single augmented call with the rubric and a few graded examples in context, adding steps only if evaluations show that it falls short.

items.explanation: The prep course asks architects to choose between an augmented call, a workflow and an agent by naming what each choice costs, and to use evals as the gating mechanism for any change. Anthropic's prompting guidance adds that current models handle most multistep reasoning internally and that a few well-crafted examples improve accuracy and consistency. Three cooperating agents multiply calls, latency and cost, and add failure points, for a task with one essay and one rubric in and one page out. A human editor already reviews every draft, so the extra autonomy buys little safety either. The defensible start is a single augmented call with the rubric and graded examples in context, with evaluations deciding whether any extra step earns its cost.

rationales.A: The steps are known in advance (read the essay, apply the rubric), so model-directed control flow adds cost, latency and unpredictability for a task with no open-ended path.
rationales.B: Orchestrator-workers fits work whose subtasks cannot be predicted; one worker per criterion multiplies calls for a task one call can handle, before any evidence that it falls short.
rationales.C: An evaluator loop is justified only when iteration measurably improves output; making it the starting point adds repeated calls on every essay, and a loop that runs until every criterion scores as met has no sound stopping rule.

items.objective: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
items.stem: A cloud-hosting company wants Claude to investigate production incidents. Each investigation needs an unpredictable number of log queries, metric lookups and config diffs, and the next step depends on what the last one returned. Investigation is read-only; on-call engineers own every remediation. Which design fits?

options.text: An agent loop with read-only tools that checks each tool result as ground truth, stops at an iteration cap, and hands off to on-call when blocked.
A fixed prompt chain that queries logs, then metrics, then config diffs, with programmatic gates between steps and a final summary call.
A routing step that classifies the alert type and sends it to a specialised single-call prompt that was written for that type of incident.
An agent loop with the same read-only tools that keeps querying until it reaches a root cause it is confident in, with no iteration cap or hand-off.

items.explanation: Agents fit open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted and the next step depends on the last result, which is what an incident investigation is. In the agent loop each set of tool results feeds back to Claude for the next decision, so the agent should reason from what the logs, metrics and diffs actually returned rather than from assumptions. Because autonomy adds cost and room for compounding errors, the loop needs a designed stopping condition: the Agent SDK's turn and budget limits default to no limit, so a cap has to be set deliberately, and a blocked investigation should end with a hand-off to on-call rather than a guess. Keeping the tools read-only matches the stated boundary: the agent investigates, people remediate.

rationales.B: A fixed chain hard-codes a path, but the next query depends on what the last one returned, so a predefined sequence will miss the evidence trail most incidents need.
rationales.C: Routing chooses a prompt but each route is still a single call, which cannot run the variable sequence of queries an investigation requires.
rationales.D: The tools respect the read-only boundary, but with no cap the loop can run on and on against an incident it cannot resolve, and with no hand-off a stuck investigation ends in a confident guess instead of with an engineer; the model's own confidence is not a stopping condition.

items.objective: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
items.stem: A national tax authority is redesigning how it answers taxpayer letters. Letters fall into a few distinct categories (address change, payment-plan request, assessment dispute), each with its own handling rules, and every outgoing reply must pass a check against taxpayer-confidentiality disclosure rules. Which TWO pattern choices fit? (Select TWO)

options.text: Classify each letter and route it to a category-specific prompt, because tuning one prompt for every category degrades some of them.
Run the disclosure check as a separate screening call that gates each draft, so nothing is sent until the screen passes.
Give a single agent every category's tools and let it decide the processing path it takes for each incoming letter.
Put the disclosure check inside the drafting prompt so that one call both writes the reply and screens it for disclosures.
Use voting: draft each reply three times and send whichever version of the reply appears most often across the drafts.
Skip classification and send all letters to the most capable tier so that a single prompt can handle every category.

items.explanation: Routing fits distinct input categories that can be classified accurately: each category then gets a specialised prompt carrying its own handling rules, instead of one prompt compromising across divergent ones. Anthropic's ticket-routing guide notes that separate prompts per path allow more targeted, context-specific handling. Here the categories pull in different directions: an assessment dispute needs the assessment history and appeal rights, a payment plan needs affordability rules, and an address change needs identity checks, so tuning one prompt for all of them trades one category's accuracy against another's, while a router lets each category's prompt be evaluated and changed on its own. For the disclosure rule, the Responsible AI prep course asks architects to place output screening in the request path so the system fails closed instead of failing open, which calls for a screen outside the drafting call that blocks the send until it passes. Both are predictable workflow patterns, which suits a public body that must explain how each reply was produced.

rationales.C: The categories and their handling are known in advance, so model-directed control flow adds unpredictability and cost where a defined route works, and it is harder to audit.
rationales.D: Separating the screen from the drafting call gives an independent gate that fails closed; a self-screen inside the drafting call does not, because the same call that might disclose is the one judging whether it did.
rationales.E: Voting suits a judgement where agreement signals confidence, such as a yes or no check; for free-text replies the drafts rarely match, so majority selection is ill-defined.
rationales.F: A bigger model does not remove the trade-off of one prompt serving divergent categories with different rules, and sending routine address changes to the top tier wastes cost.

items.objective: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
items.stem: A home-improvement retailer piloted an agent that reviews return claims for fraud and writes a decision memo. Policy requires four checks on every claim (purchase verified, return window, serial-number match, customer history), and the fraud team must show each check's result when a customer disputes a decision. An audit found the agent skipped the serial check on about 4% of claims. What should the architect change?

options.text: Keep the agent and add a system-prompt rule that it must always complete all four checks, in order, before it starts writing the decision memo.
Recast the flow as a prompt chain with the four checks as fixed steps and programmatic gates, logging each step's output before the memo.
Keep the agent and move it to the most capable model tier, which plans multi-step work more reliably and is less likely to skip a check.
Recast the flow as a router that scores each claim's fraud risk and runs only the checks that the risk level calls for.

items.explanation: When the steps are fixed and known, the task is a workflow, not an agent problem. Prompt chaining runs fixed subtasks as separate calls with programmatic gates between them, and Anthropic's current prompting guidance says explicit chaining is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure, with each step a separate call so you can log, evaluate or branch at any point. Both conditions hold here: policy mandates every check on every claim, and dispute handling needs each result logged. Code that runs each step guarantees completion; a model choosing its own path cannot.

rationales.A: A prompt rule makes skipping less likely but cannot guarantee it, and a mandated control needs a deterministic one; it also does not create the per-check record disputes require.
rationales.C: A more capable model may skip less often but still decides its own path, so the guarantee is still missing, and the cost rises on every one of the claims.
rationales.D: Routing by risk skips checks on low-risk claims by design, which breaks the policy that all four checks run on every claim; routing chooses between paths, but here policy mandates a single path for every claim.

items.objective: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
items.stem: A hospital system's revenue-cycle team wants an agent to work through denied-claim appeal packets that contain protected health information. Each packet takes up to an hour of tool calls across the payer portal, the EHR and the payer's policy library, and runs asynchronously. The platform team is small, so the hosted loop of Claude Managed Agents is attractive. The hospital may send PHI only to services covered by a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement. Which build path should the architect choose?

options.text: Managed Agents, deleting each session and its files through the API as soon as a packet is done, so that no PHI is retained after processing.
Managed Agents with self-hosted sandboxes on the hospital's own infrastructure, so tool execution and packet files stay inside its boundary.
The Message Batches API, submitting each packet's steps as one batch so that the work runs asynchronously at half the standard price.
The Claude Agent SDK running in infrastructure the hospital operates, with every model call sent only to a route its BAA covers.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents three build paths: the Messages API (you write the loop), the Claude Agent SDK (the loop and tool execution run in a process you operate) and Claude Managed Agents (Anthropic hosts the loop, tools and runtime). Anthropic's feature eligibility table marks Managed Agents as not eligible for Zero Data Retention or HIPAA readiness, because sessions are stateful and transcripts persist until deleted. The Agent SDK is a library that runs the Claude Code binary, so BAA coverage turns on where its model calls go, and HIPAA readiness alone does not cover it: the retention page states that Claude Code is not covered under HIPAA readiness, and Claude Code's legal and compliance page says a BAA extends to Claude Code API traffic only when Zero Data Retention is also enabled for the organization. The covered routes are therefore a first-party organization with a signed BAA plus ZDR, or Amazon Bedrock or Claude on Google Cloud, where the cloud provider is the data processor and its own BAA governs. A governance constraint can rule out a build path before cost or convenience is weighed, so the hospital takes the SDK path, confirms one of those routes, and accepts the operational work.

rationales.A: Deleting sessions afterwards does not make the service BAA-covered; PHI would still be processed and held by a service outside the agreement while each packet runs.
rationales.B: Anthropic's feature eligibility table states that the Managed Agents exclusion applies to all of its sub-features, including self-hosted sandboxes: tool execution moves, but the session is still held by the hosted service, so the eligibility problem remains.
rationales.C: The feature eligibility table marks Batch processing as not HIPAA eligible because of its 29-day result retention, and a batch of independent requests cannot run a multi-step agent loop that depends on each tool result.

items.objective: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
items.stem: A card issuer's dispute intake maps each customer's free-text description to a network reason code and the evidence the customer must supply. The current design, a single call with retrieved rulebook sections and few-shot examples, scores 94% against a 92% acceptance bar at 2.5 s p95, inside the 4 s SLO for the intake screen. An agent prototype that browses the rulebook and asks follow-up questions scored 95.5% at 11 s p95 and four times the cost. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Adopt the agent, because higher accuracy matters most in dispute handling, and ask the business owner to relax the latency SLO for intake.
Keep the single augmented call, which meets the bar inside the SLO, and revisit the agent only if the bar rises or its gains land where errors cost most.
Adopt the agent and stream its output to the intake screen, so customers see progress at once and perceived latency falls inside the 4 s SLO.
Keep the single call but add a self-review call after it on every dispute, recovering part of the agent's accuracy gain at lower added latency.

items.explanation: The prep course asks architects to choose between an augmented call, a workflow and an agent by naming what each choice costs, and to map cost and latency to a budget before committing. The stem names the costs. The augmented call already clears the 92% acceptance bar at 2.5 s p95, inside the 4 s SLO. The agent buys 1.5 points the business did not ask for at four times the cost and an 11 s p95, nearly three times the permitted latency. Anthropic's evaluation guidance has teams set measurable success criteria before building; once a design meets them, any gain beyond the bar has to be bought with a stated business reason. The defensible recommendation keeps the simpler design and names the evidence that would justify revisiting it.

rationales.A: This trades away a stated constraint for a gain beyond the acceptance bar; asking the sponsor to relax the SLO to fit a design is backwards when a compliant design already exists.
rationales.C: Streaming helps when people read text as it forms, but an agent's follow-up turns and tool calls still take 11 s to produce a reason code, so the screen's SLO is still missed.
rationales.D: This adds a second call to every dispute on the untested assumption that self-review recovers accuracy, raising latency and cost when the current design already passes.

items.objective: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
items.stem: An online home-goods retailer runs a Claude Managed Agents session that prepares the weekly promotions. A coordinator delegates to three roster agents: a catalog researcher, a pricing analyst and a copywriter. The retailer's pricing-engine MCP server can change live prices. The team's platform notes record that the session's vault credentials and its environment's network rules apply to every agent in the session, while each agent definition lists its own tools and MCP servers. Security review requires that only the pricing analyst can ever reach the pricing engine, enforced in configuration rather than in prompts, and the weekly run must stay one automated session. Where should the architect draw that boundary?

options.text: Declare the pricing-engine MCP server only in the pricing analyst's agent definition, and in no other agent definition
Run the pricing analyst in a separate session with its own pricing-only vault, and have staff relay its output to the coordinator
Allow the pricing-engine host in the environment's network rules, and keep every other outbound host blocked for the session
Declare the server on every agent, but send its price-change tool through a human approval step before any change applies

items.explanation: The stem gives the scoping rule Anthropic documents for Managed Agents multiagent orchestration: every agent shares the session's sandbox, filesystem and vault credentials, but each agent uses its own configuration, and tools, MCP servers and context are not shared. MCP servers are therefore agent-scoped while vault credentials are session-scoped, so the per-agent boundary sits in the agent definition. In Anthropic's own example only the researcher declares the GitHub MCP server, so the coordinator has no access even though the session vault supplies the credential. Declaring the pricing server only on the pricing analyst is least privilege enforced in configuration, and it keeps the weekly run inside one automated session.

rationales.B: A separate session does isolate the credential, but it breaks the stated requirement that the weekly run stays one automated session, adding a manual relay to every run, when the same boundary is available in the agent definition at no cost.
rationales.C: Network rules belong to the environment the whole session runs in, so allowing the host opens it to every agent the coordinator can delegate to. A session-wide rule cannot separate one roster agent from another.
rationales.D: Approval is a compensating control, not least privilege: every other agent can still reach the server and its read tools, and a reviewer can approve a change requested by the wrong agent. Agents that never need the server should not have it.

items.objective: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
items.stem: A SaaS company's incident-response assistant runs on the most capable model tier at high effort. For each incident it reads one service's logs, which fit comfortably in a single context window, forms a hypothesis, queries a metric, revises the hypothesis and repeats until it names a root cause; every step depends on the result of the step before. To cut cost, an engineer proposes making the top-tier model an orchestrator that dispatches each step to lower-cost worker models. Nothing has been measured yet. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Adopt the orchestrator design now and measure the savings on the eval set after rollout, since workers bill most tokens at lower rates
Fan the investigation out to parallel workers, one per candidate hypothesis, and let the top-tier model merge their results
Sweep effort on the current model against an eval set, and price that solo model as the baseline any multi-model design must beat
Move every step to the fastest tier at default effort, then re-run the eval set to confirm the root-cause accuracy still holds

items.explanation: Anthropic's rule for multi-model strategies is that work splitting into independent pieces points to an orchestrator, while one answer reached through a chain of dependent steps points to an advisor, and that when unsure you should not build anything yet. The cheapest experiment, and where most workloads end, is an effort sweep on the current model; Anthropic adds that a multi-model configuration must beat the single model's whole curve. Anthropic measured that when the work is one dependent chain or fits in one context window, the coordinator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead in every case. This incident loop is both, so measuring the solo baseline comes before any multi-agent design.

rationales.A: Measuring after rollout puts the gate in the wrong place: Anthropic says a multi-model configuration must beat the single model's whole curve, so the solo baseline is priced first. Orchestration also paid off in Anthropic's measurements only as cost-tail insurance on routine work or for input larger than one context window, and here each step depends on the last and the logs fit in one context.
rationales.B: Parallel fan-out suits independent pieces of work, but here each hypothesis is formed from the previous metric result, so the hypotheses cannot be listed up front. Every worker also bills its own tokens, and Anthropic measured that a dependent chain that fits in one context ran cheaper on the solo model at lower effort.
rationales.D: Re-running the eval after the switch checks quality only once the cheaper tier is already in place, and it skips the cheaper experiment of tuning effort on the current model. Per-token list price is also the wrong basis; the comparison is cost per completed task, including failed and retried investigations.

sources.title: Optimizing for cost and intelligence (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
items.stem: A card issuer's chargeback-dispute agent uses the advisor strategy: a balanced-tier executor runs every turn and consults a top-tier advisor on hard calls. To save money the team lowered the executor's effort to its lowest setting. On the next eval run, dispute-decision accuracy fell below the score the executor had achieved alone with no advisor at all, and the logs show the advisor was consulted on 3 of 450 cases, against 60 of 450 before the change. What is the most likely root cause, and the right fix?

options.text: At low effort the executor stopped noticing it was stuck, so consults dropped; restore executor effort and log consult rate in evals
The advisor lacks dispute-policy context; pass it the full case history on every consult, then re-run the eval to confirm
Chargeback disputes are really single-turn tasks, so the advisor never fit; switch to an orchestrator that fans out by dispute type
The executor is ignoring advice it receives; add a rule that it must adopt every recommendation, and re-test on the eval

items.explanation: The advisor strategy pays off in proportion to the capability gap and the consult rate. Anthropic documents that a low-effort executor can stop detecting that it is stuck, so it rarely asks for help and the pairing can score below the executor alone; on one benchmark an executor consulted on 1 of 300 tasks and lost 7 points. Here consults fell from 60 to 3 immediately after the effort change, which is that signature. The fix is to restore executor effort and make consult rate a monitored health metric in the eval suite, so a future cost tweak that silently disables the advisor is caught before release.

rationales.B: The advice is not the problem: the advisor is barely being asked. Richer context on 3 consults cannot recover the hundreds of hard decisions the executor no longer escalates, and re-running the eval would only confirm a fix aimed at the wrong component.
rationales.C: The same pattern scored well before the effort change, so the task shape did not suddenly stop fitting. Orchestrators fit independent pieces; a dispute decision built from dependent steps is the advisor's documented shape.
rationales.D: The logs show advice was almost never requested, not that it was ignored. A rule to adopt every recommendation creates no new consults, so re-testing would show the same collapsed consult rate and the same accuracy loss.

sources.title: Optimizing for cost and intelligence (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
items.stem: A university's course-design assistant is built on the Claude Agent SDK. The parent agent spends several turns gathering an instructor's accessibility requirements (plain reading level, alt text for every figure, no timed questions), then calls a quiz-writer subagent with the prompt 'Write a 20-question quiz for week 4.' The quizzes come back ignoring every one of the accessibility requirements. What is the cause?

options.text: The subagent inherited the parent's long conversation; the requirements were truncated as its context window filled up
A subagent starts without the parent's conversation; only the delegation prompt carries context, and it omitted them
Subagents run on a lower-capability model by default; it cannot hold several formatting constraints at the same time
The subagent's restricted tool list blocked it; it could not open the parent's transcript, where the requirements live

items.explanation: In the Agent SDK a non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context window that has no parent conversation. It does receive its own system prompt, the project CLAUDE.md, its tool definitions and the parent's extended thinking configuration, but none of those carry what the parent gathered in this conversation: the only content passed from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string, and only the subagent's final message returns to the parent. That isolation is a deliberate benefit, keeping the parent's context clean and allowing parallel work, but it makes the delegation prompt a handoff contract: file paths, decisions and requirements gathered by the parent must be written into it, or into the subagent's definition when they are standing rules.

rationales.A: The premise is inverted. A subagent does not inherit the parent's conversation at all, so nothing was truncated; the requirements were simply never handed over.
rationales.C: No model can follow requirements that are absent from its context, so a capability explanation misdiagnoses a handoff defect. Upgrading the subagent's model would produce the same result.
rationales.D: The parent's conversation is not available to a subagent regardless of its tool permissions. Tool restrictions such as a read-only reviewer are a documented benefit of subagents, not the mechanism behind this failure.

sources.title: Subagents in the SDK (Claude Agent SDK docs)

items.objective: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
items.stem: A national statistics office built a research assistant on the Claude Agent SDK. One broad question ('summarise every regional employment survey since 2015') spawned subagents that spawned their own subagents, and that single query consumed most of the month's budget. The SDK documents three caps: subagent spawn depth (default 3 layers), concurrent subagents (default 20) and a per-query spend budget, which has no default and, when reached, refuses further spawns and ends the query. The office wants a hard ceiling on what any one query can spend and fewer needless delegations, while keeping parallel fan-out for genuinely independent work. Which three changes should the architect make? (Select THREE)

options.text: Set an explicit per-query spend budget, so a query that reaches it can spawn no more subagents and is then ended
Lower the maximum subagent spawn depth, so that one broad question cannot grow into a deep tree of nested subagents
Add a billing alert at 80% of the monthly budget, so staff are warned before any single query can exhaust the remainder
Require an analyst to approve each subagent spawn in the interface, so every delegation is reviewed by a person before it runs
Instruct the agent to reserve subagents for parallel, isolated or independent workstreams, and to do simple sequential steps itself
Raise the concurrent-subagent limit so the fan-out finishes sooner, which cuts the bill in line with the wall-clock time

items.explanation: Agent SDK subagents can spawn their own subagents, so one prompt can grow into a tree of agents, each billing its own requests to the query. Of the three caps the stem lists, only the spend budget is a hard ceiling on cost, and because it has no default it must be set explicitly; a lower depth cap stops the runaway tree. Caps bound the damage but do not change when the model chooses to delegate, so Anthropic's prompting guidance adds a damping instruction that reserves subagents for work that can run in parallel, needs isolated context or forms independent workstreams. That cuts needless delegation without removing the legitimate fan-out the office wants to keep.

rationales.C: An alert is a notification, not a ceiling. It fires on the monthly total, after the money is spent, and nothing stops a single query from running on while staff react.
rationales.D: Per-spawn approval is a fallible compensating control (Anthropic reports roughly 93% of permission prompts are approved as attention fades) and it slows the independent work the office wants to keep. It is not a hard spending ceiling.
rationales.F: Parallelism shortens elapsed time to roughly the slowest subtask, but every subagent still bills its own tokens. More concurrency can raise burst spend; it does not cut the bill.

How we contain Claude across products (Anthropic Engineering)

items.objective: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
items.stem: A pharmaceutical manufacturer's drug-safety team is building a three-agent pipeline for adverse-event reports, which contain patient health information. An intake agent extracts the event, suspect drug, dates and patient details; a causality agent assesses whether the drug plausibly caused the event; a drafting agent writes the regulatory case narrative. The build path is settled: the team runs its own orchestration loop on a route covered by its Business Associate Agreement. Privacy requires that the causality agent never sees patient identifiers, Quality requires proof of what each agent was given, and in testing the drafting agent sometimes omits the causality reasoning. How should the architect design the hand-offs between agents?

options.text: Run all three agents in one shared conversation, so each later agent sees everything the earlier agents read and nothing is lost
Have each agent pass its free-text final message to the next, and let the drafting agent check the whole chain for consistency
Give every agent read access to the full case store, with a system-prompt rule telling the causality agent to ignore identifiers
Have the orchestrator build each agent's input as a schema-checked record of only the fields it needs, logged at each hand-off

items.explanation: In Anthropic's agent designs each agent works in its own context and receives only what it is handed: in the Agent SDK the only content passed from parent to subagent is the delegation prompt and only the subagent's final message returns, and in Managed Agents each thread is context-isolated, with tools and context not shared. That makes every hand-off a contract the orchestrator owns. Building each input from a record that holds only the fields that agent needs enforces the identifier rule in code rather than in a prompt; a programmatic check on the record, the gate Anthropic describes for intermediate steps, catches a missing causality rationale before drafting starts; and logging each record gives Quality evidence of exactly what each agent received.

rationales.A: A shared conversation hands the causality agent every patient identifier the intake agent read, which is the privacy breach the design must prevent, and it bloats every agent's context with material it does not need.
rationales.B: Free-text hand-offs are how the causality reasoning goes missing today. Nothing checks that a required field is present until the last step, and the trail of what each agent received is prose rather than an auditable record.
rationales.C: Access to the full store is itself the exposure. A prompt rule is a probabilistic control, not an enforced boundary, and it cannot prove to Quality that identifiers never reached the causality agent.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
items.stem: A fashion retailer classifies inbound customer emails into 64 intent categories with a single Claude prompt that lists all 64. Accuracy is poor, and most errors confuse near-identical intents within the same area, such as the different kinds of return request. What should the architect change to fix the confusions between near-identical intents?

options.text: Add several more few-shot examples per intent to the single 64-intent prompt, focusing on the most-confused pairs
Build a taxonomic tree: a top-level classifier picks the area, then a targeted sub-classifier per area picks the intent
Run the single 64-intent prompt on a larger, more capable model tier, and keep the prompt structure exactly as it is
Split the 64 intents across eight parallel calls of eight each, then keep whichever call reports the highest confidence

items.explanation: Anthropic's ticket-routing guide warns that as the number of classes grows, the number of examples required expands too, potentially making a single prompt unwieldy, and for 20 or more intent categories it recommends a taxonomic tree of classifiers: a top level such as Orders, Returns and Product, with a sub-classifier under each, so every parent path gets a prompt targeted at the fine distinctions inside it. That is exactly where these errors live. The documented trade-off is extra latency, because the classifiers run in sequence, which is why Anthropic pairs the cascade with the fastest model. The guide does also mention a larger model for a large volume of intent categories, but only the tree gives each fine-grained distinction its own targeted prompt.

rationales.A: Examples are the strongest single lever, but the guide notes that as classes grow the examples needed grow with them and the single prompt becomes unwieldy; the tree is its documented answer for 20 or more intents, and each sub-classifier can then carry targeted examples.
rationales.C: It leaves one prompt choosing among all 64 intents, which is exactly where the within-area confusions occur. A larger model may lift overall accuracy, but it gives no area's fine distinctions a prompt of their own, which is what the guide's taxonomic tree is for once there are 20 or more intents.
rationales.D: Sectioning is misapplied here: seven of the eight calls must choose from a set that lacks the true intent, and self-reported confidences from different prompts are not comparable enough to pick a winner.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
items.stem: A multi-site physiotherapy clinic piloted a patient-facing booking assistant built on one long system prompt that covers identity checks, symptom questions, appointment search, insurance questions and confirmations. Pilot satisfaction is mediocre, but the team cannot say which part of the conversation is failing, and every prompt edit seems to fix one behaviour while breaking another. What should the architect do next?

options.text: Add an upfront intent classifier that routes each patient to a dedicated specialised agent with its own prompt and its own tools
Write out the ideal patient interaction and break it into discrete tasks, each with its own prompt or tool and its own eval
Move the assistant to the most capable model tier and re-run the pilot eval, because the prompt already holds everything it needs
Gather far more end-to-end satisfaction scores from the pilot, so each prompt edit can be measured by its overall effect

items.explanation: Anthropic's customer-support guide prescribes writing out the ideal interaction and then breaking it down into every task Claude must perform, such as identity verification through a tool, information lookup and booking through an API call, precisely so each task can be prompted and evaluated on its own. Without per-task evaluation, every edit is a blind trade-off measured only by an aggregate score. The guide also says to exhaust prompt engineering and tooling before adding architectural layers such as an intent router, which costs an extra call's latency; decomposition comes first and tells you whether routing is even needed.

rationales.A: A router is an architectural layer added before anyone knows which task fails, and it adds a sequential call. Anthropic advises exhausting prompt engineering and tools first, and the routes can only be designed sensibly after the interaction has been decomposed.
rationales.C: A bigger model scored by the same pilot eval still yields one aggregate number, so there is no way to tell which behaviour improved or regressed, and the edit-whack-a-mole pattern points to a structure and evaluation gap, not a capability gap.
rationales.D: An end-to-end satisfaction score is the aggregate that is already hiding which task fails; collecting more of it does not localise the defect.

Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 1.5 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
items.stem: A commercial bank uses one Claude call to turn each loan file into a five-section credit memo, and the call meets its accuracy bar on four sections. Error analysis of 300 graded memos traced 41 of the 44 failures to one figure: the prompt says only 'report covenant headroom', and the model sometimes reports the dollar margin and sometimes the percentage of the covenant threshold, while credit policy defines headroom as that percentage. An engineer proposes splitting the memo into a five-step prompt chain with a code check after each step. What should the architect do?

options.text: Keep the single call, and define headroom in the prompt as a percentage of the threshold, with the formula and an example
Adopt the five-step chain, with a code check after every step, so each memo section is generated and verified on its own
Hold all prompt and design changes until a larger graded set confirms the cause, since 44 failures are too few to act on
Move the single call to the most capable model tier, which is better at inferring which headroom figure credit policy means

items.explanation: The failure is an underspecified instruction, not a task too large for one call: 41 of 44 failures share one cause, and the missing piece is a definition the bank already has. Anthropic's prompting guidance says Claude responds well to clear, explicit instructions and should be treated as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms; credit policy's definition of headroom is exactly such a norm. Prompt chaining is ideal when a task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks and you need to inspect intermediate outputs, and it trades latency for accuracy. Here four sections already pass, so a chain adds four round trips per memo while the headroom step would still receive the same ambiguous instruction. The corrected prompt is then re-scored on the existing graded set as a routine regression check.

rationales.B: A chain earns its latency when intermediate outputs need inspecting, but four sections already pass, and the headroom step would still get the same ambiguous instruction; a code check could flag the inconsistency but not supply the definition.
rationales.C: 41 of 44 failures share one documented cause and the policy definition is known, so more graded memos would not change the fix, while waiting keeps shipping memos with the wrong figure.
rationales.D: Both readings of 'headroom' are reasonable, and the bank's definition is not in the prompt, so no tier can reliably infer which one policy intends; a stronger model may simply pick one reading more consistently.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
items.stem: A state human-services agency runs a resident help line where one Claude call both answers benefit questions and decides whether the message discloses a risk, such as abuse or self-harm, that legally requires referral to a caseworker. Testing shows referral detection drops sharply on long, complex benefit questions, while answer quality is fine. The latency budget allows two model calls at the same time but not two calls in sequence. How should the architect decompose the work?

options.text: Chain the calls, screening the message for referral risk first; generate the benefit answer only once that screen passes
Split it into two parallel calls, one answering and one dedicated to referral screening; refer whenever the screen flags
Run the combined answer-and-screen call three times in parallel; refer whenever a majority of the three runs flag a risk
Keep one call, moving the referral instruction to the top of the system prompt; label it the single most important duty

items.explanation: This is parallelization by sectioning. Anthropic's documented guardrail pattern is a dedicated screening call with its own prompt that returns a constrained classification the application branches on, rather than folding the screen into the main response prompt. Anthropic also notes that agents working in their own isolated context improve output quality and, run in parallel, time to completion. The symptom here, screening failing only when the answering task is demanding, is exactly that competition for attention inside one call. Running the answer and the screen as two parallel calls separates the jobs and meets the stated latency budget, and the referral is acted on from the dedicated screen's result.

rationales.A: Anthropic's harmlessness-screen example does pre-screen input before the main conversation, and that would separate the jobs and fail closed, but it runs the two calls in sequence, which the stated latency budget rules out.
rationales.C: Voting repeats the same combined call, so each run suffers the same diluted attention; a majority rule then further suppresses rare true flags, and the agency pays three times.
rationales.D: Reordering the prompt is a prompt-only fix that leaves one call juggling both jobs, which is the structural cause of the missed referrals.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
items.stem: An exam board's coursework-feedback service makes four sequential Claude calls per essay: draft the feedback, review the draft against the marking rubric, refine it, then assign a provisional grade band. Logs show the review output from the second call is never stored, inspected or branched on; it is passed straight into the refine call. The grade band, by contrast, is logged and signed off by a human moderator before release. Latency and cost per essay are both over budget. Which two changes should the architect make? (Select TWO)

options.text: Merge drafting, review and refinement into one adaptive-thinking call that self-checks against the rubric
Keep all four calls but run them at the same time, since every one of the calls reads the same essay as input
Fold the grade band into that same single call too, so each whole essay is handled in just one request
Add a call that summarises each rubric review for the logs, so the review output becomes auditable
Keep the grade band as its own logged call, because a moderator audits and signs off that output

items.explanation: Current guidance says that with adaptive thinking Claude handles most multistep reasoning internally, and that explicit prompt chaining is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure; the draft-review-refine chain exists so each step can be logged, evaluated or branched on. Here nobody logs, inspects or branches on the review, so the chain buys nothing but extra round trips and resent context. Collapse those three steps into one call, with an instruction to verify the draft against the rubric before finishing, and keep a separate call only where an intermediate output is genuinely inspected: the grade band a moderator audits and signs off.

rationales.B: The calls are not independent: review needs the draft and refinement needs the review, so they cannot run at the same time. Sharing an input does not make dependent steps parallel.
rationales.C: The grade band is the one output a human audits and signs off, which is exactly the case where a separate, logged call is justified; folding it in removes the inspection point.
rationales.D: This adds a fifth call to create an audit trail nobody has asked for. The problem is a chain step with no consumer, so the fix is to remove the step, not to add cost to document it.

items.objective: 1.5 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
items.stem: A developer-platform company wants Claude to apply an internal API deprecation across a monorepo of 140 services. Which files need changing depends on how each service calls the deprecated API, which nobody can list in advance; some of the changes cross service boundaries, and the repository as a whole is far too large for one context window. Which decomposition fits this task?

options.text: A fixed prompt chain of search, edit, test and commit steps, applied across the whole repository in one long sequential pass
An orchestrator that inspects the repository, decides which changes are needed and where, and dispatches workers for them
Fixed sectioning with one worker per service for all 140 services in parallel, each told to edit only its own service
A single call given as much of the repository as fits, rerun with different slices until every service has been covered

items.explanation: Orchestrator-workers looks like parallelization but differs in flexibility: the subtasks are not predefined, they are determined by the orchestrator from the specific input. Anthropic names multi-file code changes as the canonical fit, because you cannot predict which files must change. It also suits input larger than one context window, since workers each handle a bounded piece while the orchestrator holds the plan and merges the results, including edits that cross service boundaries.

rationales.A: A fixed chain assumes the steps and their scope are known and runs in one context, which this repository exceeds; it cannot adapt to a change set nobody can list.
rationales.C: Fixed sectioning presumes the subtasks are known in advance. It spends calls on services that never touch the API, and each worker sees only its own service, so cross-boundary changes are missed.
rationales.D: Arbitrary slices cut through the cross-service call paths, and with no orchestrating plan nothing coordinates or merges the edits made in different slices.
