items.objective: 1.6 Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
items.stem: A grocery chain will regenerate product descriptions for 200,000 items over a weekend; nobody waits on any single result. Each request carries a 6,000-token shared prefix (brand voice guide and examples) plus 500 item-specific input tokens, and returns about 400 output tokens. Assume $3 per million input tokens, $15 per million output tokens, cache reads at 10% of the input price, and a 50% batch discount on every token. Assume a 90% cache-hit rate for batched requests, since batch cache hits are best effort, and 100% for synchronous requests; bill cache misses at the base input price and ignore cache writes. The fastest model tier failed the brand-voice eval. The budget is $1,200. Which plan fits the budget?

options.text: Send the requests synchronously with prompt caching on the shared prefix, and cap every description at 200 output tokens
Submit through the Message Batches API without caching, as the 50% discount alone cuts the most cost per token
Submit through the Message Batches API with caching on the shared prefix, keeping the model and description length
Send the requests synchronously with prompt caching on the shared prefix, keeping the current model and description length

items.explanation: Cost estimation from volume and tokens is the arithmetic the prep course expects. Uncached and synchronous, each request costs (6,500 x $3 + 400 x $15) / 1,000,000 = $0.0255, or $5,100 for 200,000 items. Synchronous with caching bills the 6,000 prefix tokens at $0.30 per million: (6,000 x $0.30 + 500 x $3 + 400 x $15) / 1,000,000 = $0.0093, or $1,860. Batch halves every token, so with a 90% hit rate the prefix costs 6,000 x (0.9 x $0.15 + 0.1 x $1.50) = $0.00171, the item tokens 500 x $1.50 = $0.00075 and the output 400 x $7.50 = $0.0030, a total of $0.00546 per request or $1,092 for the job, inside the budget. Batch alone is $2,550, and synchronous caching with a 200-token cap is $1,260. Batch cache hits are best effort (Anthropic reports typical hit rates of 30% to 98%), so the estimate should state its hit-rate assumption, and Anthropic recommends the 1-hour cache duration for batches with shared context. The workload qualifies for batching because no one is waiting on it, and neither lever touches the model or the output that passed the brand-voice eval.

rationales.A: Caching plus a 200-token cap costs about $1,260 (input $0.0033 plus output $0.0030 per request), over budget, and halving description length is a quality trade-off the batch discount makes unnecessary.
rationales.B: Batch alone is about $2,550. The 6,000-token prefix dominates the bill, so caching is the larger lever here and the two discounts must be combined.
rationales.D: Synchronous caching brings the job to about $1,860, still well over the budget, while leaving the 50% batch discount unused on work nobody is waiting for.

items.objective: 1.6 Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
items.stem: A software company's agent attempts automated fixes for customer-reported bugs; any bug it fails to fix goes to an engineer at an average loaded cost of $30. On a 1,000-bug eval set, the balanced model tier averaged $0.72 per attempt and fixed 40% of bugs. The most capable tier at low effort averaged $1.20 per attempt and fixed 80%, although its per-token list price is about five times higher. Finance asks which option gives the lower total cost per 1,000 bugs. What should the architect answer?

options.text: The top tier at low effort: it costs less per fixed bug, and far less once unfixed bugs' engineer cost is counted
The balanced tier, because its per-token price is five times lower and its average attempt costs about 40 percent less
The balanced tier with two automatic retries per failed bug, which lifts its fix rate while keeping the lower token price
Neither yet: price the median bug on both tiers first, since the median attempt is the fair basis for comparing models

items.explanation: Anthropic says to compare models on cost per completed task, not per token, because a more capable model can finish with fewer turns and less backtracking. Per fixed bug the balanced tier costs $720 / 400 = $1.80 and the top tier $1,200 / 800 = $1.50. Adding the downstream cost of failures, the balanced tier totals $720 + 600 x $30 = $18,720 per 1,000 bugs against $1,200 + 200 x $30 = $7,200 for the top tier. Anthropic's documented example shows the same flip: a frontier model at low effort solved more tasks for 35% less per solved task despite a 5x per-token price.

rationales.B: Per-token and per-attempt prices ignore what the attempt achieves. Failed attempts still bill, and each unfixed bug adds $30 of engineer time, so the cheaper tier is far more expensive per outcome.
rationales.C: Retries bill tokens too, and failures concentrate on the hardest bugs, so retrying on the same tier has no measured fix-rate gain. Anthropic says to price the retry and the downstream cost, not assume it.
rationales.D: The median hides the cost tail; Anthropic says to price the hardest tenth of tasks because failures and retries live there. The eval already gives the outcome data needed to decide.

items.objective: 1.6 Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
items.stem: A radiology group's revenue-cycle team uses Claude on the first-party API to assign billing codes to 30,000 imaging reports each night, in an organisation with HIPAA readiness enabled; nobody reads the codes until morning. Compliance requires every API feature in the PHI path to be on Anthropic's HIPAA-eligible list, and Batch processing and the advisor tool are not on it. The bar is 95% code accuracy on a 500-report hand-coded eval set. Last week's sweep on that set: top tier at high effort (current), 98.1% at about $900 a night; top tier at low effort, 97.8% at $610; balanced tier at medium effort, 97.4% at $380; fastest tier, 92.6% at $140. Finance wants the lowest nightly cost that meets the bar. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Pick the balanced tier at medium effort, the cheapest setting that clears the bar, shadow it on live traffic, then cut over
Keep the top tier and drop it to low effort; it also clears the bar, and staying on one model avoids any migration risk
Keep the current model at high effort and move the nightly job to Message Batches, since nobody reads the codes until morning
Hold every change and re-run the full sweep on a fresh 500-report set first, since a single sweep could just be noise

items.explanation: Governance first: the stem puts Batch processing and the advisor tool outside the permitted features, so the decision is made among settings the team can actually use, and effort is on the eligible list. The sweep already answers Finance's question. The balanced tier at medium effort clears the 95% bar by 2.4 points, more than three standard errors on 500 reports, at $380 a night against $610 for the next cheapest passing setting; the fastest tier is cheapest but fails the bar. Anthropic's cost guidance is to baseline tiers across effort levels, plot score against spend, then run the winner in shadow on a traffic slice before cutover and keep the suite running. That is the remaining step, not another offline sweep.

rationales.B: Passing the bar is necessary but Finance asked for the lowest cost: this setting costs about $230 a night more than one that also passes, and the sweep already shows the tier change holds on this task.
rationales.C: The stem states Batch processing is not on the eligible list, and under HIPAA readiness the API rejects requests that use ineligible features, so the discount is unavailable however well the overnight timing fits.
rationales.D: The evidence is already sufficient: 97.4% sits more than three standard errors above 95% on 500 reports, and delay costs about $520 a night. Live-traffic risk is what the shadow run before cutover is for.

items.objective: 1.6 Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
items.stem: A state motor-vehicle agency's resident chat assistant has a service-level objective written into its contract: 99.5% monthly availability, and responses that begin to appear within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile. The vendor's original proposal relied on a Priority Tier capacity commitment, but the agency's procurement team reports the vendor could not obtain a new one. What should the architect tell the agency?

options.text: Rewrite the SLO around the Standard tier's availability guarantee, so the contract matches what the API itself commits to
Keep a single route on the Standard tier and add exponential backoff retries on every 5xx and 429 response to absorb overload
Engineer the SLO in the design: stream responses, fail over to a route with separate capacity, and agree capacity with sales
Route the chat through the Message Batches API, whose separate processing queue isolates the assistant from peaks in live traffic

items.explanation: Priority Tier capacity commitments are no longer available for purchase, the Standard tier is documented as best-effort, and organisations needing guaranteed capacity are directed to sales, so a performance SLO has to be engineered into the design. Streaming lets the model start sending its response before the full output is complete, which addresses a time-to-first-content target. A second delivery route that draws on a separate capacity pool, such as Claude Platform on AWS, which Anthropic says can be used to fail over, keeps the service up when one route is saturated. Refusals arrive as normal HTTP 200 responses with a refusal stop reason, so the client should also detect them and retry on a fallback model rather than count them as successes.

rationales.A: The Standard tier carries no availability guarantee; it is documented as best-effort, so there is no figure to write into the contract and no mechanism behind the SLO.
rationales.B: Retries on one best-effort route add delay without supplying capacity during a sustained overload, and they leave a single point of failure against a 99.5% availability target.
rationales.D: Batches are asynchronous, do not support streaming and may take up to 24 hours, so they cannot meet a 2-second interactive response target.

sources.title: Claude Certified Architect - Professional Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 1.6 Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
items.stem: A community-college district is deploying a Claude support agent for its student IT help desk. The sponsoring vice-president wants go/no-go criteria that demonstrate business value without hiding failures. The vendor's draft lists one headline metric: 75% of conversations resolved without a human. Which two additions should the architect make to the criteria? (Select TWO)

options.text: Escalation accuracy and response relevance as task criteria, so high deflection cannot hide a failing handoff
The total number of conversations the agent handles each month, reported as a measure of help-desk productivity
Average tokens consumed per conversation, trending down over time, as evidence of the help desk's efficiency
Raise the deflection target from 75% to 85%, so the bar the agent must clear before go-live is stricter
Cost per ticket and time to resolution against today's human-only help desk baseline

items.explanation: Anthropic's support-agent guidance separates task-performance criteria (comprehension, response relevance, escalation accuracy, topic adherence) from business-impact criteria (deflection, sentiment, CSAT, handle time), and its success-criteria guidance says most use cases need multidimensional evaluation. A deflection rate on its own can rise while the escalation path fails silently. The ticket-routing guide also expresses go/no-go thresholds relative to the incumbent process, such as cost per classification against the current method, because value has to be shown against what the business does today.

rationales.B: Volume measures activity, not value: an agent can handle more conversations while resolving them badly, so the count cannot support a go/no-go decision.
rationales.C: Tokens are an input cost, not an outcome; they can fall simply because answers became shorter and less useful, so the trend says nothing about efficiency for students.
rationales.D: A stricter target is still the same single aggregate. It can even reward an agent for failing to escalate, so it hides a broken handoff rather than exposing it, and it shows no gain against today's process.

items.objective: 1.6 Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
items.stem: A regional commercial insurer quotes small-business policies. Underwriters decline about 35% of submissions without quoting, mostly businesses with mixed operations, because reading their loss runs, inspection reports and contracts takes longer than the premium justifies. The sponsor's case for a Claude underwriting assistant is not faster work on today's book: it is that the insurer can write that declined segment profitably for the first time. Which success measure most directly shows whether this transformation goal is being met?

options.text: Underwriter hours per quote on mixed-operation submissions, compared with the manual hours those files took before launch
Share of previously declined mixed-operation submissions that now receive a quote, tracked monthly against the pre-launch decline rate
Model and tooling cost per quoted mixed-operation submission, held under the per-quote budget the sponsor approved
Bound premium and the loss ratio on mixed-operation risks that were once declined, tracked against the segment's pricing targets

items.explanation: The exam guide lists transformation as its own value pillar, beside efficiency, productivity, cost and performance SLAs. The sponsor's outcome is a new line of business: profitably writing a segment the insurer declines today. Anthropic's success-criteria guidance asks for criteria that are specific, measurable and relevant to the application's purpose, and notes that most use cases need several dimensions. Relevance here means the outcome the sponsor named: premium actually bound in the new segment shows the business is being written, and the loss ratio shows whether it is profitable. Hours per file, quote rate and cost per quote are useful operating measures, but each can look healthy while the transformation fails.

rationales.A: Hours per file is an efficiency measure. Reading mixed-operation files faster says nothing about whether the resulting quotes bind or whether their losses fit the price.
rationales.B: Quote rate shows activity in the new segment, but quotes that never bind, or that bind underpriced, would raise it while the goal fails; it measures only half of writing the segment profitably.
rationales.C: Cost per quote belongs to the cost pillar. It can sit under budget while the new segment loses money, so it cannot show the transformation the sponsor is funding.

items.objective: 2.1 Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
items.stem: A retail bank runs its KYC document-review assistant on a balanced-tier Claude model. After a vendor demo, the head of onboarding wants to move to the newest most-capable tier next sprint because it 'looked sharper'. The bank's model-risk policy requires documented evidence for any change to a production model. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Switch to the new tier behind a feature flag, measure analyst escalations for a month, and roll back if they rise above the baseline.
Build an eval set from labelled past KYC files and success criteria, then score the current model at higher effort and the new tier on it.
Approve the new tier for complex multi-entity ownership files only, where the demo looked strongest, and keep the balanced tier for the rest.
Adopt the new tier and attach its published system-card eval scores on financial-document benchmarks to the change ticket as the evidence.

items.explanation: A model swap is gated on evaluation evidence built from the workload's own data, not on impressions or generic benchmarks. The prep course for this domain expects candidates to use evaluations as the gate before any model swap, and the model-selection docs call a good task-specific eval set the most important step. Including the current model at higher effort matters because tuning effort inside one model is often a better lever than switching tiers, and it may close the gap at lower cost and with less change-control overhead.

rationales.A: Measuring escalations after the switch moves the decision to after deployment and relies on a lagging, noisy production signal; it does not satisfy a policy that wants evidence before a production model changes.
rationales.C: Routing only the hardest files to the new tier is still a production model change made on a demo impression; it skips the pre-change evidence the policy requires for exactly the riskiest cases.
rationales.D: System-card eval scores are generic benchmarks that were not run on this bank's KYC files or success criteria, so they cannot show whether the new tier beats the current model on the actual task.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 2.1 Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
items.stem: A hospital network drafts radiology report impressions with Claude. On top of its HIPAA safeguards, the network's contracts with partner health systems commit it to zero vendor-side retention, so it runs under a zero data retention (ZDR) arrangement that its compliance office treats as non-negotiable. Quality falls short on complex multi-modality studies, and engineers propose moving the whole pipeline to the most capable tier. The provider's data-retention documentation states that this tier requires 30-day retention and that ZDR is unavailable for it unless expressly authorized. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Move to the most capable tier now, because the hospital's business associate agreement already covers PHI and so makes the retention requirement irrelevant.
Stay on a ZDR-eligible tier with higher effort and better grounding for complex studies, and move tiers only after express retention approval.
Send only complex studies to the most capable tier through an advisor call, which stays within ZDR, and confirm the gain on the evals.
Move the complex admissions to the Batch API on the most capable tier, since asynchronous jobs are processed without the retention requirement.

items.explanation: Governance and data-handling constraints rule options out before any capability trade-off is weighed. The most capable tier is a Covered Model that requires 30-day retention, so a workload bound by contract to ZDR cannot simply escalate to it. The defensible path is to exhaust levers that stay inside the constraint first: higher effort on a ZDR-eligible model, better grounding, and measurement on the impression evals. If those still fall short, the tier change becomes a compliance decision rather than an engineering default. The documented route is to enable 30-day retention on one dedicated workspace used only for that workload while other workspaces keep ZDR, and here that needs compliance sign-off and agreement under the partner contracts first.

rationales.A: A BAA governs how PHI is handled, but it does not override the model's documented retention requirement, and the partner contracts separately commit the network to zero vendor-side retention.
rationales.C: Routing only some studies through an advisor still sends those patients' data to the tier that requires 30-day retention, so the ZDR constraint is breached for exactly the hardest cases, and a better eval score does not cure a contractual breach.
rationales.D: Batch processing has to store jobs and is itself not eligible for ZDR or HIPAA, so it makes the retention problem worse rather than avoiding it.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 2.1 Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
items.stem: A grocery chain's compliance team reviews about 40 new private-label product specifications a month for allergen labelling against food-law rules. Each review means reading supplier spec sheets, ingredient sub-declarations and factory cross-contact statements, and a missed allergen carries recall and legal exposure. Volume is tiny, so model cost is a minor line item, and the team wants a reliable tool in production within a quarter. What should the architect recommend as the starting approach to model selection?

options.text: Start on the fastest, cheapest tier, test it on labelled specs, and move up a tier only for the allergen gaps that testing reveals.
Start on the strongest starting-point model for the task, tune prompts and evals on it, then test lower effort or cheaper tiers.
Start on the balanced tier and patch its misses with extra allergen rules in the prompt, moving up a tier only if eval scores stall.
Run two cheaper tiers on every spec and send only their disagreements to a frontier model, so the strongest model bills on very few items.

items.explanation: The model-selection docs describe two starting strategies. Efficiency-first (start on a faster, cheaper model and upgrade only for specific capability gaps) suits high-volume, straightforward, cost-sensitive work. Capability-first suits complex tasks where accuracy outweighs cost: 'implement with the strongest starting point for your task, then optimize to more efficient models down the line', which means optimizing prompts for that model, evaluating, then increasing efficiency by lowering effort or downgrading over time. The docs add one more step: if evals at the highest effort levels still fall short on demanding reasoning, move up to the frontier model, so the starting point is not automatically the most capable model on offer. A low-volume, safety-critical review where cost barely matters fits capability-first, because starting weak spends the quarter debugging capability gaps instead of building the evals that later justify any step down.

rationales.A: Efficiency-first is meant for high-volume, straightforward, cost-sensitive work; here volume is tiny, cost is minor and accuracy is critical, so starting at the bottom wastes iteration cycles on capability gaps.
rationales.C: Patching a weaker model with ever more prompt rules treats capability gaps as prompt defects; watching eval scores for a stall delays the evidence of what a stronger model can do and leaves brittle rules the team must maintain.
rationales.D: Agreement between two weaker models is not correctness, since both can miss the same hidden allergen, and the ensemble adds complexity to save a cost that is already negligible at this volume.

items.objective: 2.1 Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
items.stem: A developer-tools company runs a code-migration agent on its most capable model tier at high effort. Finance asks for a 40% cost reduction, and engineering leadership will accept no more than a 2-point drop on the team's own migration eval suite. Which TWO actions are the best first steps? (Select TWO)

options.text: Move straight to the fastest, cheapest tier, since efficiency-first is the documented starting point for cost-sensitive work.
Route each request through a difficulty classifier to a cheaper tier, keeping one shared cached prompt prefix across the tiers.
Re-run the migration eval suite at lower effort levels on the current model and record cost and score at each level against the tolerance.
Price the current tier and the next tier down in cost per completed migration on the suite, and keep any within the 2 points.
Adopt an advisor pattern with a cheap executor at its lowest effort setting, then run the migration suite to confirm the saving.
Halve max_tokens on every request so that the agent physically cannot spend as much on output as it does today.

items.explanation: The documented order is to measure before changing and to try the cheapest-to-reverse lever first. Effort trades intelligence for cost and latency inside one model; the docs say to start with an effort sweep on the current model, and that curve is also the baseline any multi-model design must beat. Comparing tiers should be done in cost per completed task, not per-token price, because a cheaper model that fails or needs more turns can cost more per finished migration, and any candidate must stay within the agreed 2-point tolerance.

rationales.A: Efficiency-first is a starting strategy for new, straightforward work; jumping a complex migration agent to the cheapest tier skips the 2-point tolerance check and the cost-per-completed-task comparison, and failed migrations still bill their tokens.
rationales.B: Prompt caches are per model, so a router that switches tiers request by request causes model_changed cache misses; a shared cached prefix across tiers is not possible and the lost cache reads can erase the saving.
rationales.E: Confirming afterwards does not fix the order: a multi-model build is a larger change than the levers inside one model, the docs say to draw the single-model effort curve first as the baseline, and an executor's consult rate is sensitive to how low its effort is set.
rationales.F: max_tokens is a hard ceiling; cutting it truncates migrations mid-output with stop_reason max_tokens instead of making the agent more economical.

items.objective: 2.1 Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
items.stem: An online university grades capstone reports against a 12-criterion rubric. To cut cost, the team piloted a cheaper executor model at low effort with a frontier advisor it can consult. Over 400 reports the executor consulted the advisor on 88% of them. Agreement with faculty graders matched the frontier model running alone at a reduced effort setting, within run-to-run noise, but the pairing cost about 1.8 times as much per report. The provost's goal was lower cost at the same grading quality. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Drop the pairing and run the advisor's model alone at the reduced effort setting, re-checking it on the grading eval set.
Keep the pairing but swap in an even cheaper executor model, then re-run the grading eval to confirm the per-report saving.
Replace the pairing with an orchestrator that hands each rubric criterion to parallel cheap workers and merges their scores.
Keep the pairing, since matching frontier quality was the main goal and grading cost per report is a secondary concern.

items.explanation: An advisor saves money only when a few short consultations replace running the frontier model for the whole task. The cost-and-intelligence guidance says that if the executor asks on most of its tasks, you are paying advisor rates across the whole workload, and running the advisor's model itself is the cheaper way to the same score; its own measurement found a pairing that consulted on nearly every task matched the frontier model alone at a reduced effort within noise, at about 1.8 times the cost per task. The opposite failure also appears in the docs: a low-effort executor that consulted on 1 of 300 tasks scored 7 points below that executor model running alone. Either way, the advisor's model alone at a reduced effort is the baseline the pairing must beat.

rationales.B: A weaker executor gets stuck more often, so it would consult even more; the bill is driven by advisor rates on almost every report, not by the executor's token price, so the re-run would most likely confirm a higher cost, not a saving.
rationales.C: Rubric judgements on one report form a dependent chain rather than independent pieces; the orchestrator guidance says that when work is one chain, the coordinator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead in every measured case.
rationales.D: The pilot's stated purpose was lower cost at the same quality; paying 1.8 times as much for a score the frontier model already reaches alone fails that goal.

items.objective: 2.1 Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
items.stem: A state agency's caseworker assistant drafts long eligibility determinations on a top-tier Claude Opus model at its default effort and misses its internal p95 latency target. Its evals show that both lower effort and the balanced tier fall below the accuracy bar. Traces show the time goes on generating long answers, not on time to first token. The agency calls the Claude API directly and has approved extra spend for this tool. The provider offers fast mode for this model: a research preview that raises output speed up to 2.5 times at premium per-token pricing, with no change to the model. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Move to the balanced tier anyway, since a small accuracy loss is the normal price of meeting a latency target.
Enable fast mode on the current model, budget for its premium rate, and fall back to standard speed when fast capacity is limited.
Lower effort anyway, because the docs call effort a better lever than switching models for trading quality against latency.
Stream the responses so caseworkers see text sooner, and report time to first token as the latency measure instead.

items.explanation: Model selection weighs capability, speed and cost together. Here the evals have already ruled out the cheaper levers: lower effort and the balanced tier both miss the accuracy bar, so capability has to stay where it is. Fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration, so quality is unchanged, and its gain is in output tokens per second, which is where the traces put the time. The trade is paying premium rates for speed, which the agency has approved. Because it is a research preview with its own rate limit, the design should fall back to standard speed on a fast-mode 429 rather than fail.

rationales.A: The agency's own eval shows the balanced tier below the accuracy bar; trading correctness on eligibility determinations for speed is not acceptable when a same-quality option exists.
rationales.C: Effort is often the better lever, but this agency has already measured it and lower effort fails the accuracy bar; generic guidance does not override the workload's own evidence.
rationales.D: Streaming improves perceived responsiveness, but caseworkers need the complete determination; redefining the metric hides the miss instead of meeting the target.

items.objective: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
items.stem: A home-goods retailer classifies customer return reasons into one of eight labels. The old prompt ended with a prefilled assistant turn containing an opening quote mark to force a bare label. After moving to Claude Sonnet 5.5, every request returns a 400 error. The returns system rejects any value that is not exactly one of the eight labels, so every response must be a valid label. What should the architect change?

options.text: Keep the prefill but shorten it to a single space, which current models still accept as the opening of the assistant's reply.
Add 'CRITICAL: You MUST reply with ONLY the label' to the system prompt and strip anything extra with a regex.
Lower temperature to zero so the model reliably emits only the label and no surrounding explanation or preamble.
Use structured outputs with a schema whose label field is an enum of the eight labels, so decoding is constrained to them.

items.explanation: Prefilling the last assistant turn is not supported from Claude 4.6 models onward and returns a 400. The prefill-migration guidance points classification and forced formats to structured outputs or tools with an enum field, and says instructions plus post-processing are for removing preambles. Because the returns system accepts only the eight exact labels, the design needs a guarantee. Structured outputs (output_config.format with an enum) give one: constrained decoding means the response must match the schema. The tool route is weaker on this model. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (like Claude Opus 5.5) rejects forced tool use, so tool_choice of type any or tool returns a 400. With tool_choice auto, a strict tool constrains the input only when Claude actually calls it, and the model can still reply in text, so that route needs a prompt instruction saying when the tool applies plus handling for a text reply, and it still does not guarantee a valid label.

rationales.A: Any prefilled final assistant turn is rejected on Claude 4.6 and later models; shortening it does not change that.
rationales.B: Instructions plus post-processing are documented for removing preambles, but they cannot guarantee that every response is exactly one of the eight labels, which constrained decoding through structured outputs does.
rationales.C: Non-default temperature returns a 400 on Claude 4.7 and later models, and temperature never guaranteed format in the first place.

items.objective: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
items.stem: A hospital pharmacy uses Claude to extract dosing data from manufacturers' package inserts into its drug formulary, returning each record through a strict JSON schema with fields for drug, single dose, dose unit and maximum daily dose. Every record parses, but an audit finds a few where the unit is mg although the insert says mcg, and some where the daily maximum is lower than the single dose. A pharmacist must approve any record that fails a check. What should the architect add?

options.text: Nothing in the pipeline: constrained decoding already guarantees valid records, so the faults must come from the inserts themselves.
Add minimum and maximum keywords to the dose fields of the strict schema, so constrained decoding itself rejects any out-of-range dose.
Add an emphatic system-prompt rule to verify every unit against the insert and never confuse mg with mcg before returning a record.
Keep the schema for format and add rule checks in code after generation (unit matches the source, daily maximum at least the dose).

items.explanation: Structured outputs guarantee that a response is valid, parseable and schema-compliant: the right fields and types every time. They do not guarantee that the values are correct, and a schema cannot express cross-field business rules. The guardrail for that is deterministic validation in application code after generation, checking each value against the source text and domain rules, with failures routed to the pharmacist. Format comes from constrained decoding; correctness comes from checks the model cannot talk its way past.

rationales.A: Constrained decoding guarantees format, not correctness: a record with the wrong unit or an impossible daily maximum is still schema-valid, so the faults are model errors the schema cannot catch.
rationales.B: Numerical constraints such as minimum and maximum are not supported in structured-output schemas and return a 400 error, and a range limit still could not catch a wrong unit or a cross-field rule.
rationales.C: A stronger instruction may reduce the error rate but is still only a request; it gives no deterministic guarantee and no route to the pharmacist when a record is wrong.

items.objective: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
items.stem: A wealth-management firm's research assistant fetches news articles about client holdings. Articles already arrive JSON-encoded in tool_result blocks, and the tool definitions and system prompt form a cached prefix that must stay stable. The model in use accepts system-level messages inserted later in a conversation, which keep operator authority and are appended after the latest turn. After each fetch, compliance checks the holding against the firm's restricted list and wants an operator-level instruction added when it is restricted: 'Do not present any view on this security; state only that it is restricted.' Where should the architect place that instruction?

options.text: After the tool_result block, as a system-level message inserted at that point, leaving the cached prefix untouched.
Prepend it inside the tool_result, ahead of the article text, so Claude reads the restriction before it reads the content.
Append it to the top-level system prompt whenever a fetched holding is restricted, so it carries full operator authority.
Add it to the news tool's description whenever a restricted holding is fetched, so it travels with the tool that fetched the article.

items.explanation: Two constraints decide the placement: trust and the cache. The injection guidance says not to put your own instructions in tool results, because Claude treats tool-result content as untrusted data and may ignore or flag instructions there as an injection; send them in a user turn that follows the tool_result block or, on supported models, as a mid-conversation system message. A mid-conversation system message keeps operator-level priority over user text and is appended at the end of the history, so the cached tools and system prompt are untouched. That suits an instruction that depends on what was fetched and changes from turn to turn.

rationales.B: Instructions placed inside a tool result sit in the untrusted channel next to third-party text, so Claude may ignore them or flag them as a possible injection, which defeats a compliance control.
rationales.C: Editing the top-level system prompt per turn changes the start of the hashed prefix and invalidates the cache for everything after it, which the stem rules out; a mid-conversation system message gives the same authority without that cost.
rationales.D: The tools array sits at the very start of the cached prefix, so editing a description per fetch invalidates the cache for the whole conversation, and a tool description is meant to describe the tool, not carry per-turn rules.

items.objective: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
items.stem: A state benefits agency is launching a public chatbot that answers eligibility questions. Before launch, the security team saw repeated jailbreak attempts in testing, including role-play framings meant to extract other claimants' details. The agency wants guardrails that follow Anthropic's documented guidance. Which THREE controls should the design include? (Select THREE)

options.text: Pre-screen each user message with a lightweight model that returns a structured yes-or-no harm classification before the main call.
Write a system prompt that sets the assistant's legal and ethical boundaries and states exactly how it should decline out-of-scope requests.
Give the chatbot a claimant-lookup tool keyed on any ID the user supplies, and have the system prompt refuse other claimants' records.
Screen only the model's output with a regex for national-ID patterns, skipping input screening so citizens see lower latency.
Use a static keyword denylist of words such as 'pretend' and 'role-play' as the only input filter, with no model-based screen.
Throttle or block repeat offenders and continuously monitor outputs so new jailbreak patterns are caught and fed back into the controls.

items.explanation: The jailbreak guidance recommends combining controls: harmlessness pre-screens with a lightweight model returning a structured classification, input validation (which can itself be an LLM screen generalised from known jailbreak examples), a system prompt that sets boundaries and spells out how to refuse, throttling or banning repeat offenders, and continuous output monitoring. Least privilege matters too: a successful manipulation should find nothing sensitive within reach, which a prompt-only refusal cannot ensure.

rationales.C: This is prompt-enforced authorisation: the tool can return any claimant's record, and the role-play jailbreaks seen in testing target exactly the prompt rule that is meant to stop it. Access must be scoped in code to the authenticated claimant.
rationales.D: An output regex catches only well-formed ID numbers, not names, addresses or paraphrased details, and dropping the input screen removes the layer that stops the jailbreak before the main model sees it.
rationales.E: A fixed word list is trivially evaded by rephrasing and blocks legitimate questions that use the words; the docs suggest a model-based screen generalised from known jailbreak examples rather than a static list.

items.objective: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
items.stem: A school district runs one prompt template for 300 teachers to generate lesson plans. Each request fills in teacher notes, the district's own vetted state-standards text and class reading-level data. Nothing in the inputs is adversarial, but some outputs follow imperative sentences inside the standards, such as 'Students will compare fractions', as if they were instructions to the model, and others mix up which text is the standard and which is the teacher's note. What is the best template change?

options.text: Separate the inserted inputs with blank lines and add one sentence before them saying that everything below this point is reference data only.
Move the standards text into the system prompt and keep the teacher notes in the user turn, so role separation tells Claude which text is which.
Wrap each input in its own consistently named XML tag, nest multiple standards documents inside a parent tag, and keep instructions outside them.
Move the teacher notes and the standards text into few-shot example blocks, so the model treats them as patterns rather than as instructions.

items.explanation: A robust template separates fixed instructions from variable inputs with tagged slots. The docs recommend wrapping each kind of content (instructions, context, examples, variable input) in its own XML tag, using consistent descriptive names, and nesting where there is natural hierarchy, such as documents inside a documents tag. This lets one fixed template carry variable inputs without Claude confusing data with instructions, and it keeps the fixed part stable for reuse. The failure here is confusion over which text is which, not an attack: for adversarial third-party content, tags help structure a prompt but do not change its trust level, so other controls are needed there.

rationales.A: Blank lines and a single caveat sentence give the model weak, ambiguous boundaries; it is the minimal version of the right idea and does not distinguish one input type from another.
rationales.B: This puts long reference text in the system prompt, where its imperative sentences carry even more weight as instructions, and the inputs are still not delimited by tags that say what each one is.
rationales.D: Examples are for demonstrating the desired output; putting live inputs there misuses the slot and invites the model to copy them as patterns.

items.objective: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
items.stem: A SaaS company moved its support agent to a current Claude model and kept the old system prompt, which says: 'IMPORTANT: Run search_kb FIRST on every single message. No exceptions, ever.' The agent now calls search_kb even for greetings and thank-you messages, adding latency. What is the best fix?

options.text: Rewrite it plainly, e.g. 'Use search_kb when the user asks about product behaviour, because answers must match the docs.'
Add a second rule: 'NEVER call search_kb for greetings or thanks', written in capitals so that it carries the same weight as the first.
Remove search_kb from the agent's tool list entirely, since least privilege says an agent should not hold tools it misuses.
Keep the rule, and send tool_choice none on turns that a keyword filter classifies as greetings or thanks, so search_kb is skipped there.

items.explanation: Current models respond strongly to the system prompt, so emphatic always-do wording written for older models causes over-triggering. The docs recommend dialling back aggressive language into plain, conditional instructions that say when to use the tool, and explaining why a rule exists so Claude can generalise from the reason.

rationales.B: Stacking an emphatic negative onto an emphatic positive compounds the problem; the docs advise saying what to do, in plain language, rather than adding more prohibitions.
rationales.C: The agent genuinely needs the knowledge base for product questions; removing a needed tool trades an over-use problem for a capability gap.
rationales.D: This leaves the defect in the prompt and adds a brittle code-side classifier that only covers the phrasings it knows; other turns that need no lookup, such as clarifications, still trigger the tool.

items.objective: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
items.stem: A supermarket chain drafts replies to online product reviews. Zero-shot instructions produced an inconsistent brand voice, so the team added one example reply praising fast delivery. Now nearly every draft copies that example's structure and mentions delivery speed, even for complaints about product quality. What should the team change?

options.text: Use three to five diverse examples, including complaints and edge cases, and wrap them in example tags apart from the instructions.
Remove the example and expand the instructions with a longer list of adjectives that describe the desired brand voice in detail.
Keep the single example and add an instruction not to copy its structure or mention delivery unless the review itself does.
Move to the most capable model tier, which is less prone to copying examples and better at inferring the right tone from instructions alone.

items.explanation: Few-shot examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure, but a single example teaches unintended patterns. The docs recommend three to five examples that are relevant to the real use case, diverse enough to cover edge cases so Claude does not latch onto one surface feature, and structured in example tags so they are distinct from instructions.

rationales.B: Going back to zero-shot discards the most reliable tone lever; the voice problem that prompted the example in the first place returns.
rationales.C: A negative instruction patches one symptom while the single example remains the only pattern to imitate; the docs steer with diverse examples that show the range, not with prohibitions.
rationales.D: This is a bigger-model fix for a prompt-design defect; any model given one narrow example has a single pattern to imitate.

items.objective: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
items.stem: A lender's credit-memo assistant runs on a model with adaptive thinking always on. Its system prompt describes the house underwriting method in prose. Memos are well formed, but for self-employed applicants the reasoning skips reconciling declared income against bank statements and does not exclude one-off income. The credit team has several past memos in which analysts annotated their reasoning step by step, including self-employed cases. Which prompt change best teaches the house method?

options.text: Add the annotated memos as examples, with each analyst's step-by-step reasoning in thinking tags ahead of the finished memo.
Add three to five diverse past memos, including self-employed cases, as finished-memo examples with all the annotations removed.
Raise effort to its maximum for self-employed applications, so adaptive thinking spends longer reasoning about their declared income.
Turn the annotations into a reference guide placed above the applicant file, and tell Claude to consult it before drafting.

items.explanation: What the model is missing is a reasoning method, so the examples must show the reasoning, not just the conclusions. The thinking guidance says multishot examples work with thinking: put the reasoning inside thinking tags in each example and Claude generalises that reasoning style to its own thinking. Annotated memos that include the self-employed cases demonstrate the reconciliation and the exclusion of one-off income being applied, which the prose description already fails to convey. The number and diversity of examples matter less here than whether the step the model skips is visible in them.

rationales.B: A diverse set of finished memos shows the format of the conclusion but not the reconciliation steps behind it, so the reasoning pattern the team wants copied is missing from every example, however well the set covers the edge cases.
rationales.C: More effort buys more thinking, not the firm's method; the model can reason longer and still skip a step it was never shown how to apply.
rationales.D: This restates the method as prose a second time, which is what is already failing; demonstrating the reasoning in examples is the documented way to transfer a reasoning pattern.

items.objective: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
items.stem: A drug manufacturer's pharmacovigilance assistant receives about 80,000 tokens per adverse-event case (reporter narratives, hospital notes, lab results) plus the company's seriousness-assessment guideline, then answers whether the case meets the criteria for expedited reporting. The current prompt states the question first, then the instructions, then the documents pasted one after another. Reviewers find answers that cite findings not in the case file and attribute findings to the wrong document. Which TWO prompt changes should the architect make? (Select TWO)

options.text: Put the case documents and guideline at the top of the prompt, with the instructions and the question placed after them.
Wrap each case document and the guideline in its own document tag, with content and source subtags plus date and type metadata.
Split the 80,000 tokens into ten chunks, ask the question of each chunk separately, and take the majority answer.
Keep the question at the very top so the model knows what to look for before it begins reading the case documents.
Move the guideline into the system prompt and keep the question first in the user turn, ahead of the case documents.

items.explanation: For long-context work the docs recommend placing long documents near the top, above the query, instructions and examples, and say that a query at the end can improve response quality by up to 30% in tests. When there are several documents, each should be wrapped in its own document tag with document_content and source (and other metadata) subtags, so Claude can tell the records apart and attribute each finding to the right one. These changes reduce errors rather than eliminate them, so reporting decisions still need human review.

rationales.C: A seriousness decision needs the whole case at once; per-chunk answers lose evidence that spans documents, and a majority vote over partial views can outvote the one chunk that holds the deciding finding.
rationales.D: This is the current layout and the opposite of the documented guidance; with long inputs, the query belongs at the end.
rationales.E: The question still comes before the long case documents, against the long-context guidance, and the individual documents are still pasted together with no labels to tell one from another.

items.objective: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
items.stem: An exam board uses Claude to check worked solutions to A-level mathematics problems. The model applies adaptive thinking, which cannot be switched off, and the board has a cost cap per checked solution that the current setup meets with little headroom. To lift accuracy on the hardest problems, a team member proposes a 12-step 'think step by step' script and a large fixed thinking-token budget. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Adopt the 12-step script and the fixed budget, since manual chain-of-thought plus a large budget gives the most accurate checks.
Drop the script, add a general 'think thoroughly' instruction, and set effort per problem tier from an eval run against the cap.
Keep the 12-step script but run it as a separate pre-processing call whose output is pasted into the checking prompt.
Use manual thinking and answer tags in the visible output, and score the tagged reasoning against the eval set for examiners.

items.explanation: On current models adaptive thinking decides when and how much to think, steered by effort. The docs prefer general instructions such as 'think thoroughly' over hand-written step-by-step plans, because Claude's reasoning often exceeds what a human would prescribe, and fixed thinking budgets are rejected on the newest models, where effort sets depth. Because effort trades accuracy against cost, choosing it per problem tier from an eval keeps spend on the hardest problems within the cap. Manual chain-of-thought with tags is the fallback for when thinking is off.

rationales.A: Prescriptive scripts tend to underperform general guidance on current models, and a fixed thinking budget returns a 400 on the newest models, where effort controls depth.
rationales.C: A second call adds cost and latency against a tight cap, and it keeps the prescriptive script that the guidance says tends to underperform general instructions.
rationales.D: Manual tags are the fallback when thinking is off; with adaptive thinking always on they duplicate reasoning in billed output and push cost toward the cap, and scoring that visible reasoning on an eval does not make the checks more accurate.

items.objective: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
items.stem: A cloud-hosting provider routes support tickets into five queues with a zero-shot prompt that gives a one-line definition per queue. On a 500-ticket eval it scores 91% against a 95% target while meeting a tight p95 latency SLO. Error analysis shows that almost every miss is a server suspended after a failed payment, which the definitions could place in Billing or in Infrastructure. Support policy routes these to Billing, but the prompt never says so, and two senior agents relabelling the misses blind also split on them until shown the policy. What should the architect do?

options.text: Add 40 labelled examples spread across all five queues, so the model infers the boundaries between queues from the patterns.
State the support policy in both queue definitions: suspensions caused by a failed payment go to Billing, with the reason why.
Add a visible step-by-step reasoning section that weighs each of the five queue definitions against the ticket before choosing one.
Build a larger 2,000-ticket eval before touching the prompt, so the miss pattern is confirmed at higher statistical confidence.

items.explanation: Zero-shot prompting falls short here because the instructions are incomplete, not because the technique is wrong. The prompting guidance starts with being clear and direct and with giving the context or reason behind a rule so Claude can apply it. The error analysis traces the misses to a routing policy the prompt never states, and the blind relabel shows that even experts need that policy to agree. Stating it in one sentence is the smallest fix, adds almost no tokens under the latency SLO, and is checked on the existing 500-ticket eval. Examples and visible reasoning are levers for patterns that are hard to put into words, not for a rule that can simply be written down.

rationales.A: Forty examples add input tokens and latency under a tight SLO and leave the deciding rule implicit for the model to infer, when the policy can simply be stated.
rationales.C: Visible reasoning adds output tokens and latency against the SLO, and the model cannot reason its way to a routing policy it has never been told.
rationales.D: The error analysis and the blind relabel already identify the cause; a bigger eval only delays a one-sentence fix that the existing 500-ticket eval can verify.

items.objective: 2.4 Optimize context windows and manage token usage
items.stem: A state benefits agency runs a caseworker assistant on a current Claude model with a 1M-token context window. Every request includes the agency's full eligibility manual (about 700,000 tokens), cached with a 1-hour TTL, plus the case file and the conversation so far. On complex cases the API now returns a 400 'prompt is too long' error. A developer argues that cached tokens should not count against the context window and suspects a platform bug. What should the architect tell the team?

options.text: The error comes from reserving output space: input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, so lowering max_tokens on complex cases will let those requests through.
Cached tokens still occupy the window; caching changes their price, not their size. Send only the manual sections a case needs, checking fit with token counting.
The 1-hour cache entry has expired between case updates, so the manual is resent as uncached input; a shorter TTL reused more often keeps it out of the window.
Route complex cases to the Message Batches API, which accepts larger inputs than interactive calls, and return eligibility answers once each batch completes.

items.explanation: Everything in a request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, every message, tool definitions and the output. Prompt caching changes what the cached prefix costs and how fast it is processed, not whether those tokens occupy the window. When the input alone exceeds the window, every model returns a 400 'prompt is too long'. The fix is to send less, for example by retrieving only the manual sections relevant to the case, and to check fit before sending with the free token counting endpoint. Sending less also helps quality, because the docs warn that recall degrades as context grows (context rot).

rationales.A: On Claude 4.5 and newer models, a request whose input plus max_tokens exceeds the window is accepted and stops with stop_reason 'model_context_window_exceeded' if generation reaches the limit. A 400 'prompt is too long' means the input alone is too large, so lowering max_tokens changes nothing.
rationales.C: Cache state never affects whether tokens count toward the window. An expired entry only changes the price of the tokens, and a shorter TTL would make expiry more likely, not less.
rationales.D: Batch processing changes price and turnaround, not the model's context window, and it turns an interactive caseworker question into an asynchronous job (most batches finish within an hour, but results can take up to 24 hours) without fixing the oversized input.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 2.4 Optimize context windows and manage token usage
items.stem: A hospital pharmacy runs a drug-shortage agent that, for each shortage, calls a wholesaler-inventory tool 30 to 40 times (each result about 6,000 tokens) and a formulary-substitution-rule tool a few times. The workload contains no patient data and runs in a separate API organization that is not HIPAA-ready. By the end of a session only the latest inventory results matter, but the pharmacy and therapeutics committee requires every substitution-rule result to stay in context exactly as returned. Sessions are reaching context limits, and finance has noted that each earlier attempt to trim the history triggered an expensive new cache write. The platform offers two server-side options: compaction, which replaces older turns with a model-written summary, and tool-result clearing, which removes old tool results once input passes a trigger and can keep the N most recent tool uses, exempt named tools from clearing, and skip any clear smaller than a set minimum. Which context-management design best fits these constraints?

options.text: Enable threshold-based compaction with the default summarization prompt, so that older turns, inventory results and substitution rules alike are condensed into one summary.
Have the application delete the oldest inventory results from its stored history before each request, so the prompt stays small and the client controls exactly what is removed.
Enable tool-result clearing set to keep the 40 most recent tool uses so that no substitution-rule result is cleared, and leave its other options at their default settings.
Enable tool-result clearing, exempt the substitution-rule tool from clearing, and set the minimum clear size to an amount that justifies the cache write each clear causes.

items.explanation: Context editing clears content by rule instead of summarizing it. Tool-result clearing removes old tool results server-side once input passes a trigger, while the client keeps its full history. Two of its settings map directly to the constraints here: exempting a tool (exclude_tools) means its uses and results are never cleared, so the substitution rules stay verbatim, and a minimum clear size (clear_at_least) means that if that many tokens cannot be cleared the strategy is not applied, which makes each clear worth the new cache write it causes, because every clear invalidates the cached prefix. Bulky inventory results that go stale are exactly the content tool-result clearing is designed to remove. Context editing and compaction are not HIPAA-eligible (a HIPAA-ready organization gets a 400 error for them), so this design is valid only because the workload holds no PHI and runs in an organization without HIPAA readiness.

rationales.A: Compaction replaces older turns with a model-written summary. Summaries can paraphrase or drop details, which breaks the requirement that substitution-rule results stay exactly as returned; a custom summarization prompt reduces that risk but still does not guarantee verbatim text.
rationales.B: Editing history instead of appending to it changes the prefix on every request (a messages_changed cache miss), which recreates the finance problem on each call and puts deletion bookkeeping in the client. It is also a correctness risk: on Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, client-side edits to earlier turns can invalidate the thinking blocks in every later assistant turn, and for accounts created on or after August 31, 2026 a request that replays an invalidated block is rejected unless it opts into dropping it. Server-side context management never invalidates thinking blocks.
rationales.C: Keeping the 40 most recent tool uses keeps almost every stale inventory result, so little context is freed, and once a session passes 40 tool uses the oldest substitution-rule results are cleared anyway; with no minimum clear size set, small clears each still force a new cache write.

sources.title: API and data retention (Feature eligibility, HIPAA readiness)

items.objective: 2.4 Optimize context windows and manage token usage
items.stem: A software company's internal platform-operations agent connects to six MCP servers exposing about 140 tools. Before the agent reads the user's request, tool definitions alone consume roughly 60,000 tokens, and incident reviews show it increasingly picks the wrong tool among similar ones. Most requests use the same handful of tools. The team wants to cut per-request tokens and improve tool selection without losing access to the rarely used tools. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Place all 140 tool definitions behind a cache breakpoint so they are billed at the cache-read rate, which removes their cost and frees the context they occupy.
Move the agent to the most capable model tier, since a stronger model selects well among similar tools and a 1M-token window has room for all definitions.
Shorten every tool description to one line so the full set fits in about a quarter of the tokens, keeping all 140 tools loaded on every request.
Adopt the tool search tool with defer_loading for the long tail, keeping the most-used tools loaded, so only definitions a request needs enter context.

items.explanation: Tool definitions are part of the context window and can consume tens of thousands of tokens before any work starts; the docs also note that tool-selection accuracy degrades beyond 30 to 50 tools. The tool search tool with defer_loading: true loads only the definitions a request needs (typically 3 to 5 per search), cuts definition tokens by over 85% and keeps deferred tools out of the cached prefix. The docs recommend it at 10 or more tools or more than 10k tokens of definitions, and recommend keeping the 3 to 5 most-used tools non-deferred.

rationales.A: Caching lowers the price of the definitions but they still occupy the context window, and it does nothing for the selection errors that come from too many similar tools in view.
rationales.B: A bigger model is offered for a context-bloat problem. Loading 140 tools still degrades selection and adds context rot, and model changes should be gated on evals rather than assumed to fix selection errors.
rationales.C: Thinner descriptions make similar tools harder to tell apart, which worsens the selection errors, and all 140 tools remain in context on every request.

items.objective: 2.4 Optimize context windows and manage token usage
items.stem: A university admissions office scores about 30,000 application essays each night against a fixed 12,000-token rubric, and the scores must be ready when reviewers start at 8 a.m. The office's model budget has been cut by 40%, and the admissions director will not accept any change that puts scoring quality at risk without evidence. Which TWO changes cut cost without that risk? (Select TWO)

options.text: Count each essay with the token counting endpoint before submission, since the counts reflect cache discounts and let the job skip tokens that are already cached.
Turn on fast mode for the overnight run so the job finishes sooner, which reduces the billed processing time and so lowers the cost of each essay scored.
Submit the nightly run through the Message Batches API, which halves input and output prices and normally completes well inside the overnight window.
Put the rubric in a cached prefix with the 1-hour TTL so its tokens are read at the cache rate across the batch, a discount that stacks with the batch price.
Trim the rubric to its 4,000 most important tokens so each request carries a third of the current rubric, cutting the input cost of the run by about two thirds.

items.explanation: Overnight scoring is asynchronous work with a deadline hours away, which is what the Message Batches API is for: it halves input and output prices, most batches finish within an hour, and requests expire only after 24 hours. The rubric is identical in every request, so caching it as a prefix means most requests read it at the cache rate instead of paying full input price. Caching stacks with the batch discount; cache hits inside a batch are best-effort, and the docs recommend the 1-hour TTL for context shared across a batch. Neither change alters the model, the rubric or the scoring logic, so quality is not put at risk.

rationales.A: Token counting is free and useful for sizing, but it returns an estimate that does not apply prompt-caching logic, and counting tokens does not by itself reduce what the scoring requests cost.
rationales.B: Fast mode raises output speed at premium per-token pricing, so it raises cost; billing is per token, not per unit of time, and fast mode is not available through the Batch API.
rationales.E: Cutting two thirds of the rubric removes scoring criteria, which is exactly the unproven quality risk the director has ruled out; caching gets most of the input saving with the full rubric intact.

items.objective: 2.4 Optimize context windows and manage token usage
items.stem: A bank moved its KYC document-review pipeline from an older-generation model to a current Sonnet-tier model after evals showed better extraction accuracy; both have a 1M-token context window. The cost forecast reused per-document token counts measured on the old model. In the first month, input tokens per document run about 30% above forecast. A replay of last quarter's identical documents shows the same rise, cache read tokens are the same share of input as before the move, and a few of the longest dossiers now stop early with stop_reason 'model_context_window_exceeded'. What is the most likely cause, and what should the architect do?

options.text: Caches are per model, so the move caused model_changed misses on every request; holding the model constant will let the cache bring input cost back to forecast.
The newer model's tokenizer turns the same text into more tokens; recount sample documents against the new model ID, then re-baseline both cost and window fit.
Requests above 200,000 tokens now carry a long-context premium; split the longest dossiers into chunks below that size so all tokens bill at the standard rate.
The new model defaults to a higher effort level, which inflates the input tokens of each document; setting effort to low on routine dossiers brings input back in line.

items.explanation: Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces about 30% more tokens for the same text, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 and earlier models use the previous one. The docs warn against reusing token counts measured on an older model to estimate cost or context fit after a migration; instead, count the same requests against the target model ID with the token counting endpoint and compare. The symptoms point here: identical documents now produce more input tokens, caching behaves as before, and the largest dossiers have less headroom in the window, so generation reaches the limit and stops with model_context_window_exceeded.

rationales.A: Caches are per model, but a model switch causes a one-time miss per cached prefix, not a lasting rise. The stem rules this out: cache reads are the same share of input as before.
rationales.C: Claude 4.6 and later models price the full 1M-token window at standard rates, so there is no long-context premium to avoid, and chunking dossiers would complicate review for no saving.
rationales.D: Effort governs how many output tokens the model spends (text, tool calls and thinking); it does not change how many tokens the input documents tokenize to, so it cannot explain a 30% input rise.

items.objective: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
items.stem: An online retailer's customer-service assistant sends 15 order-management tools, which its API gateway assembles on each request from a plugin registry, followed by a byte-stable 6,000-token system prompt of returns policy and tone guidance with a cache_control breakpoint at its end. Traffic is steady at several requests per second, all in one workspace and on one model. Monitoring shows cache_creation_input_tokens of about 8,500 on every request and cache_read_input_tokens always zero. A diff of two consecutive request bodies shows the same system text, messages and set of tools; the only differences are the order of JSON keys inside some tool input schemas, which the gateway team says is semantically meaningless. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: The prompt is below the model's minimum cacheable length, so the breakpoint is silently ignored; pad the system prompt with more policy text until caching starts.
The 5-minute TTL keeps expiring between requests; move the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the entry lives long enough to be read by the requests that follow.
Caching matches bytes, not meaning, so the reordered schema keys change the prefix on each request; send the tools in one fixed order with sorted schema keys.
Tools sit outside the prefix that a system-prompt breakpoint covers; add a second breakpoint on the last tool definition so the tool block is cached on its own.

items.explanation: Prompt caching needs a byte-for-byte match of the prefix up to the breakpoint, and the prefix is built in the order tools, then system, then messages. Tools come first, so a schema serialized with a different key order changes the very start of the prefix and invalidates the tools, the system prompt and everything after them, even though the JSON means the same thing. Each request therefore writes a new entry (the 8,500 creation tokens) and none is ever read. Cache diagnostics reports this as tools_changed, which covers tools added, removed or reordered and input_schema JSON serialized non-deterministically; the documented fix is to send the same tool list in a fixed order with deterministically serialized schemas, for example with sorted keys. The system prompt is already static, so reordering static and dynamic content would change nothing here.

rationales.A: Tools plus a 6,000-token system prompt are above every current model's minimum cacheable length. A prompt below the minimum would show zero for both creation and read tokens, not about 8,500 creation tokens on every request.
rationales.B: With several requests per second, a 5-minute entry would be read and refreshed long before it expired. The entry is never matched, so a longer TTL only makes each wasted write cost more.
rationales.D: The cache hierarchy is tools, then system, then messages, so the system-prompt breakpoint already covers the tools. A breakpoint on the last tool would still include the reordered schemas, so its prefix would also change on every request and never hit.

items.objective: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
items.stem: A commercial insurer's underwriting assistant already opens every request with a byte-stable 40,000-token underwriting-guideline pack behind a cache breakpoint with the default 5-minute TTL; each underwriter's question follows it. Traffic is sparse: about 20 requests across a 10-hour working day from one workspace, typically 10 to 30 minutes apart, and underwriters expect answers within seconds. Usage shows nearly every request writing the cache instead of reading it. Pricing for this model relative to base input: 5-minute cache write 1.25x, 1-hour cache write 2x, cache read 0.1x. What should the architect change?

options.text: Set the pack's breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL: one write costs 2x, but each later request, 10 to 30 minutes on, reads at 0.1x and refreshes the entry.
Keep the 5-minute TTL and send a small keep-alive request every four minutes so the entry never expires, avoiding the 2x write price of the 1-hour TTL.
Remove the breakpoint, since the 1.25x write premium is paid on almost every request and sending the pack as ordinary input at 1x would cost less.
Gather the day's underwriter questions and send them through the Message Batches API at half price with the pack cached, returning each answer afterwards.

items.explanation: TTL choice is an economic decision about the gap between reuses. A 5-minute entry pays off after one read, but only if the next request arrives within five minutes; here the gaps are 10 to 30 minutes, so nearly every request pays the 1.25x write. The 1-hour TTL costs 2x to write and breaks even after two reads, and each read refreshes the entry at no extra cost, so a day of requests at these intervals becomes roughly one 2x write followed by 0.1x reads. The docs recommend the 1-hour TTL for prompts reused less often than every 5 minutes but more often than hourly.

rationales.B: At the stated 0.1x read price, keep-alives pay a read of the full 40,000-token pack every four minutes across the 10-hour day, about 150 extra paid reads, or roughly 15x the pack's base input price before the real requests are counted, against about 3.9x for the whole day with the 1-hour TTL (one 2x write plus 19 reads at 0.1x); they also add a scheduler to operate. The trade-off is model-specific: some current models price cache reads at 0.05x or 0.025x, where keep-alives cost proportionally less and can come out cheaper, so the comparison must be rerun with the target model's prices.
rationales.C: Dropping caching makes every request pay 1x for the pack, whereas the 1-hour TTL brings most requests down to 0.1x. The fault is the TTL, not caching itself.
rationales.D: Batching turns an interactive tool that must answer within seconds into an asynchronous one, which breaks the latency expectation, and cache hits inside a batch are only best-effort.
