items.objective: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
items.stem: A software company's Claude Code rollout uses a project CLAUDE.md that has grown to about 1,500 lines. Besides coding conventions, it now holds a 20-step release procedure, a database-migration runbook and an incident checklist, all loaded into every session even though most sessions are routine feature work. Developers report that conventions are followed less reliably and that sessions start with much of the context already used. The release procedure must never run unless a release manager starts it. What restructuring should the architect recommend?

options.text: Keep everything in CLAUDE.md, since the large context window easily holds 1,500 lines, and add a line telling Claude to prioritize the coding conventions.
Have Claude summarize CLAUDE.md to about 150 lines, compressing the release procedure and runbook to a few sentences each so that all of it still loads.
Keep standing conventions in CLAUDE.md and move each procedure into its own Skill, loaded only when invoked, with model invocation disabled for the release Skill.
Expose the procedure, runbook and checklist through a new internal MCP server whose tools return each document's text when Claude decides to call them.

items.explanation: In Claude Code, CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session and suits standing conventions, while a Skill loads its full content only when invoked and suits procedures and multi-step tasks. The documented rule of thumb is to move a CLAUDE.md section that has grown into a procedure into a Skill. That restores context for routine sessions and keeps each procedure intact and exact. For a Skill with side effects such as a release, disable-model-invocation: true stops Claude from triggering it on its own, so it runs only when a person such as the release manager invokes it, which is exactly the stated constraint.

rationales.A: A large window does not prevent context rot; loading three procedures into every routine session is what is diluting the conventions, and one more instruction adds to the problem rather than solving it.
rationales.B: Compressing a 20-step release procedure into a few sentences loses the exact steps a fragile operation needs, and the procedures would still load into sessions that never use them.
rationales.D: Building a custom MCP server is heavier than the documented Skills pattern, adds its own tool definitions to every session's context, and leaves the release procedure without a guard against automatic invocation.

items.objective: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
items.stem: A regional health system's revenue-cycle team is building a claim-denial appeals assistant on the Claude API. The organization has zero data retention (ZDR) and HIPAA readiness in place, and the compliance officer requires every feature in the request path to be eligible under both. Each request combines general appeal-writing guidance shared by every payer, then the policy modules of the denying payer (one of about a dozen), all stable for weeks, and finally one patient's claim and chart extract. All appeal traffic runs in one workspace. The architect wants as much prompt reuse across patients and payers as possible. Which THREE design choices meet both the compliance requirement and the reuse goal? (Select THREE)

options.text: Put one cache breakpoint after the shared appeal guidance and another after the payer's modules, so a request for a different payer still reads the shared part.
Package each payer's appeal procedure as an Agent Skill on the API, so that only the matching procedure is loaded into context for a given request.
Run the nightly re-review of pending appeals through the Message Batches API, so the policy content is processed at half price with caching stacked on top.
Give each payer its own workspace so that its cached policy modules are kept apart from other payers' traffic, an isolation the compliance officer can cite.
Assemble each payer's policy modules in a fixed, versioned order with deterministic serialization, so a given payer always yields a byte-identical prefix.
Track cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens for each request in monitoring, rather than assuming every marked prefix is actually being reused.

items.explanation: Prompt caching is eligible for ZDR and HIPAA: prompts are not stored, and the cached representations are held in memory only for the TTL. Cache entries are written only at breakpoints, and up to four breakpoints let sections that change at different rates be cached separately; a breakpoint after the shared guidance gives every payer's requests a common entry to read, and a second one after the payer's modules gives each payer its own longer entry. Reuse depends on a byte-identical prefix, so modules assembled in a fixed order with deterministic serialization keep it stable, which is also the documented fix for tools_changed and system_changed misses. Because caching fails silently, reuse is confirmed only through the usage fields, so they belong in monitoring. Agent Skills and the Batch API are not ZDR- or HIPAA-eligible, so they fail the compliance requirement however much they would help.

rationales.B: Agent Skills are not eligible for ZDR or HIPAA, because Skill data follows standard retention, so they fail the compliance officer's requirement even though progressive loading suits modular procedures.
rationales.C: The Message Batches API must store jobs, so it is not eligible for ZDR or HIPAA; the half-price saving cannot be taken on this workload.
rationales.D: On the Claude API caches are isolated per workspace, so splitting traffic across a dozen workspaces makes the shared guidance a separate entry in each, multiplying cache writes and cutting reuse. Payer policy text holds no patient data and caches are never shared across organizations, so the split adds no compliance value.

items.objective: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
items.stem: A grocery chain's merchandising assistant runs long sessions: a 9,000-token system prompt and tool set, then many turns. In some turns the merchandiser attaches 25 or more shelf photos, each sent as its own image block, with a short text question. The team puts one explicit cache_control breakpoint on the final block of every request. History is append-only, the model never changes and requests are a minute or two apart. The platform writes cache entries only at breakpoints, and a read looks back at most 20 block positions from each breakpoint for an entry that an earlier request wrote. Usage shows strong cache reads on turns with a few photos, but every request whose new turn carries 20 or more photos reads zero cached tokens and rewrites the whole prompt, including the system prompt. What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.text: Uploading many photos delays each request until the 5-minute entry expires; switch the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the previous write is still alive.
Image blocks cannot be cached, so photo-heavy requests fall back to uncached input; send text descriptions of the photos so the whole turn can be cached.
Each photo is a separate block, so the previous write falls outside the lookback; add a second breakpoint on the last block before the new photos arrive.
Enable context editing to clear older photos from the history so that each request stays within 20 blocks of the previous cache write and keeps hitting.

items.explanation: Cache writes happen only at breakpoints, and a read checks at most 20 positions back from each breakpoint, counting the breakpoint itself, for an entry an earlier request wrote. The docs note that 'a run of consecutive tool_use blocks counts as one position, and so does a run of consecutive tool_result blocks', so parallel tool calls do not push the previous entry out of reach; ordinary content blocks such as attached images get no such grouping. A turn with 25 photos therefore moves the final-block breakpoint more than 20 positions past the last write, the lookback finds nothing, and with no other breakpoint even the unchanged system prompt is rewritten. The docs say the final block works as long as each turn adds fewer than 20 blocks, and that when a growing conversation pushes the breakpoint 20 or more blocks past the last write you should add a second breakpoint closer to that position. A breakpoint on the last block of the prior history is within reach of the previous write, so the history before the photos is read from cache; a breakpoint on the stable system prompt and tools also guarantees that prefix always hits (up to 4 breakpoints per request).

rationales.A: Requests are a minute or two apart, the TTL is measured from the start of each request, and every read refreshes the entry, so nothing expires; the miss pattern tracks the number of blocks a turn adds, not elapsed time.
rationales.B: Images in user turns are cacheable content blocks, the same as text; the problem is how far the breakpoint moves, and replacing photos with descriptions throws away the visual evidence the merchandiser needs analyzed.
rationales.D: Context editing clears old tool results and thinking blocks, not image blocks a user attached, and every clear invalidates the cached prefix; the miss also comes from the blocks one turn adds, not from the total length of the history.

items.objective: 3.1 Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
items.stem: A developer-tools company rolls out Claude Code to the engineers who maintain its public documentation site. The repository holds only Markdown, the team never needs to run shell commands, and the engineers work on a mix of Windows and macOS laptops. The security lead requires that Claude have no way to run any shell command in these sessions, including commands nobody has thought to block. Which configuration meets that requirement?

options.text: Add deny rules naming the bare Bash and PowerShell tools, which take both shell tools out of Claude's context in every session.
Add deny rules for Bash(rm *), Bash(curl *) and Bash(sudo *) so the riskiest shell commands are blocked and the rest stay usable.
Enable sandboxing so every shell command Claude runs is confined by OS-level filesystem and network isolation on each laptop.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction stating that Claude must never run shell commands of any kind while working in this repository.

items.explanation: When a role needs none of a capability, least privilege means removing it, not containing or filtering it. In Claude Code a deny rule that names a bare tool removes that tool from Claude's context entirely, so the model cannot select it at all, whereas a scoped rule such as Bash(rm *) leaves the tool available and blocks only matching calls. Claude Code has two shell tools: Bash, and a separate PowerShell tool that is on by default on Windows for claude.ai and Console accounts. With Windows laptops in the fleet, only bare deny rules for both tools leave Claude with no shell at all.

rationales.B: Scoped deny rules leave the Bash tool in context and block only the listed patterns; every other shell command, and the PowerShell tool on Windows, remains available.
rationales.C: Sandboxing contains what shell commands can touch, but it leaves the shell tools in place and usable; the requirement is that no shell command can run at all.
rationales.D: CLAUDE.md shapes what Claude tries to do but is not enforced; permission rules, not instructions, decide what Claude Code allows.

items.objective: 3.1 Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
items.stem: A consumer bank's account-servicing agent was assembled from tools contributed by three teams. It now exposes 26 read-only tools, including get_account, get_account_v2, fetch_account_details and account_summary_lookup, which overlap heavily. Traces show the agent alternating between them and returning inconsistent fields to customers. Every underlying lookup is still needed. Which change best addresses the root cause?

options.text: Move all 26 tools behind tool search with deferred loading, so only the three to five tools a request needs are loaded into context.
Move the agent to the most capable model tier, whose stronger reasoning should settle on the right account tool more consistently.
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that map common customer questions to the tool each contributing team prefers to use.
Consolidate the overlapping lookups into one namespaced account tool that returns a single, stable set of fields.

items.explanation: The root cause is capability bloat in the form of overlapping tools: when several tools do nearly the same job, Claude has no principled way to choose between them, and each returns a different shape. Anthropic's tool-definition guidance is to consolidate related operations into fewer tools, namespace them by service, write detailed descriptions and return high-signal fields with stable identifiers. Collapsing the duplicates into one account tool with one output shape removes the ambiguity at its source instead of working around it.

rationales.A: Tool search reduces how many definitions sit in context, but a search over four near-identical account tools still surfaces the duplicates, so the selection ambiguity and inconsistent fields remain.
rationales.B: A larger model cannot resolve an ambiguity that is in the tool set itself; the overlapping tools are genuinely interchangeable from the model's point of view, so this spends money on the wrong layer.
rationales.C: Prompt-level routing is brittle, grows with every new question type and leaves all the duplicates in place; it treats the symptom while the tool surface keeps the ambiguity.

items.objective: 3.1 Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
items.stem: A large school district's teaching assistant runs on the Messages API and connects through the MCP connector to six MCP servers (curriculum, gradebook, attendance, library, timetabling and special-education plans) that expose 140 tools, and classroom teachers and special-education coordinators share one agent configuration. An audit shows classroom teachers use about 25 tools from four servers, while the plan tools are used only by coordinators. The district's privacy officer requires that classroom-teacher sessions cannot read or change special-education plans, and tool definitions consume tens of thousands of tokens per request. Which change BEST meets both needs?

options.text: Put all 140 tools behind tool search with deferred loading for every role, so only the definitions a request needs are loaded.
Give each role its own toolset that enables only the servers and tools that role uses, so teacher sessions never carry the plan tools.
Keep the shared toolset, and have the plan server reject each plan call unless the signed-in user is a coordinator.
Add a system-prompt section listing the servers each role may use, and tell Claude to leave the plan tools alone in teacher sessions.

items.explanation: Two problems share one cause: a single configuration gives every role every tool. Deferred loading and per-role enablement both shrink the definitions in context, but only enablement changes what can be called. The MCP connector's toolset configuration can enable or disable whole servers and individual tools, so a teacher configuration that enables only the roughly 25 tools teachers use cuts the token load and takes the plan tools out of reach, which tool search alone cannot do because deferred tools stay discoverable and callable. A server-side role check on the plan server is still worth keeping as defence in depth behind the per-role configuration.

rationales.A: Deferral addresses the token load, but deferred tools remain enabled and can be found through search and called, so teacher sessions could still reach special-education plans.
rationales.C: A backend role check is a sound second layer for the privacy rule, but it leaves all 140 definitions in every teacher request, so the token load and selection noise remain.
rationales.D: A prompt rule depends on model behaviour for a privacy requirement and leaves every definition in context, so it fixes neither problem in configuration.

items.objective: 3.1 Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
items.stem: A state benefits agency is building a caseworker assistant on the Messages API. It connects through the MCP connector to a vendor-hosted document-management MCP server that currently exposes 35 tools, including read, upload, redact and delete operations, and the vendor adds tools without notice. The connector's toolset configuration can set a default for every tool on a server, override that default for named tools, and mark tools for deferred loading. The assistant must stay read-only, and the agency wants the limit enforced in configuration rather than by model behaviour. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: Add a system-prompt rule stating that the assistant must never call any tool whose name implies a write, upload or delete operation.
Disable the upload, redact and delete tools by name, leaving the server default of enabled for every other current and future tool.
Set the server default to disabled and enable only the named read tools, so any tool the vendor adds later arrives disabled.
Mark the upload, redact and delete tools for deferred loading, so their definitions enter context only when a tool search finds them.

items.explanation: With a vendor that adds tools without notice, the read-only limit has to hold for tools nobody has seen yet, so the default must be deny. Setting the server default to disabled and enabling named read tools (in the mcp_toolset, default_config with enabled false plus per-tool configs) is an allowlist: anything new arrives disabled. Disabling known write tools by name is a denylist, which blocks only what you already knew about, and deferred loading changes when a definition enters context, not whether the tool can be used.

rationales.A: A system-prompt rule depends on model behaviour, which the agency explicitly ruled out, and relies on tool names describing their effects accurately.
rationales.B: A denylist is a documented pattern, but any write tool the vendor adds later inherits the enabled default, so it fails the stated constraint.
rationales.D: Deferred tools stay enabled and can be discovered through tool search and then called; deferral controls context size, not capability.

sources.title: Claude Certified Architect - Professional Exam Guide v1.0 (Domain 3 objectives)

items.objective: 3.1 Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
items.stem: A hospital's patient-scheduling agent, built on the Claude Agent SDK, has four tools: appointment_get, appointment_book, appointment_cancel and appointment_purge, which permanently erases a duplicate appointment record. The records team now wants the agent to handle duplicate cleanup, a few purges a week, but the retention policy requires a records officer to approve each purge before it runs. To reduce tool-selection errors, an engineer proposes consolidating all four into one appointments tool with an action parameter. What should the architect approve?

options.text: Consolidate all four into one tool, and state in its description that purge needs a records officer's approval before it is used.
Consolidate all four into one tool, and have the agent ask the patient to confirm in the chat before it runs any purge on the record.
Consolidate get, book and cancel, and take purge away from the agent so that records officers keep running every purge by hand.
Consolidate get, book and cancel, and keep purge as its own tool, with every purge call held until a records officer approves it.

items.explanation: Consolidating related operations behind an action parameter is good practice for selection accuracy, but a destructive action that needs per-call human approval should stay a separate tool. Permission rules and approval callbacks in the Agent SDK match on tool names: an ask rule naming the purge tool routes every purge call to the approval callback, where a records officer decides, even in permissive modes, while get, book and cancel run normally. Folded into one tool, purge could only be gated by gating every scheduling action or by custom parsing of arguments. A backend check that rejects a purge without a recorded approval is still worth adding as defence in depth.

rationales.A: A description asking for approval is a prompt-only control; nothing stops the purge action running without an approval, which the retention policy requires.
rationales.B: The patient is not the approver the retention policy names, and a chat confirmation is still decided inside the conversation rather than enforced outside it.
rationales.C: Removal is right when a role never needs a capability, but here the records team has asked the agent to do this work; removing it fails the requirement instead of gating it.

items.objective: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
items.stem: A SaaS company is building a remote MCP server over Streamable HTTP that fronts its internal ticketing API. A developer proposes that when an MCP client calls a tool, the server simply forwards the user's access token from the client to the ticketing API. Under the current MCP authorization specification, how should the architect assess this design?

options.text: Acceptable; the ticketing API checks each forwarded token's signature and expiry before it serves any request.
Acceptable; the MCP server also logs the calling user's ID beside every forwarded request for later audit.
A gap; the server should hold one shared admin key for the ticketing API, so user tokens never leave the client.
A gap; the server must accept only tokens issued for it and obtain its own token for the ticketing API.

items.explanation: The MCP authorization specification forbids token passthrough. An MCP server must validate that a token was issued for it as the audience, must not accept or transit other tokens, and when it calls an upstream API it acts as a separate OAuth client using a token from the upstream authorization server. Passthrough bypasses audience-based controls such as validation and rate limiting, breaks the audit trail and creates confused-deputy risk.

rationales.A: Signature and expiry checks do not establish audience; a valid token minted for the MCP server is still the wrong token for the ticketing API, which is exactly what the spec prohibits.
rationales.B: Extra logging is a detective measure; it does not restore audience binding or prevent the confused-deputy problem the passthrough creates.
rationales.C: A shared admin key swaps one gap for a worse one: every user acts with full privileges through the server and per-user authorization is lost.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
items.stem: A bank's platform team deploys Claude Code with a managed-settings deny rule for Bash(curl *). A payments team needs to download build artifacts from an internal repository, so it adds an allow rule for Bash(curl https://artifacts.bank.internal/*) to its project settings. Calls to the artifact host are still blocked. Which analysis is correct?

options.text: The more specific allow rule should win over the broader deny, so re-test the URL pattern to confirm a typo is not the cause.
Project settings take precedence for rules scoped to that project, so the allow belongs in the repository's shared settings.
Deny is checked before allow and no level overrides a managed rule, so only the platform team can resolve it by narrowing the deny.
A PreToolUse hook that returns an allow decision for the artifact host will override the deny rule and unblock these calls safely.

items.explanation: Claude Code evaluates permission rules deny first, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins; specificity does not change that order, so an allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny. Managed settings also sit at the top of the precedence order and nothing set at another level, including --settings on the command line, overrides them. The correct path is a governed change by the platform team that owns the managed rule, for example narrowing or replacing the curl deny and allowing the artifact host through WebFetch domain rules or the sandbox network allowlist.

rationales.A: Specificity does not reorder evaluation; deny is checked first and wins however narrow the allow rule is, so re-testing the pattern will not change the result.
rationales.B: Project settings cannot override managed settings; managed settings have the highest precedence of all levels.
rationales.D: PreToolUse hook decisions cannot override deny or ask rules, so a hook returning allow does not unblock a denied call.

items.objective: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
items.stem: A government digital service runs Claude Code headlessly with claude -p in its CI pipeline to triage pull requests. The CI job's environment holds a repository write token and a deployment credential, which any stdio MCP server the run starts inherits. The repository's .mcp.json defines project-scoped MCP servers, and a contributor's pull request added a new server entry. The service wants a control enforced by the pipeline at runtime, not by human review. Which control closes the authorization gap?

options.text: Rely on the project-scope approval prompt, because a person must approve project servers before Claude Code will load them.
Run claude -p with --strict-mcp-config and an explicit, centrally owned MCP config, so .mcp.json additions are ignored.
Move every server definition into local scope, so server entries are no longer shared with contributors through version control.
Pin each server's tool list on first connection, so a newly added server cannot change the tools Claude sees during a run.

items.explanation: The gap is that an unapproved server can gain the pipeline's credentials. Project-scoped servers in .mcp.json need approval in interactive sessions, but that approval is skipped in non-interactive contexts such as claude -p and the Agent SDK, so a server added through a pull request can start inside the job and inherit its write and deployment credentials without anyone approving it. Running with --strict-mcp-config and an explicit, centrally owned MCP configuration makes the pipeline start only the servers the service controls; managed allow and deny lists for MCP servers are the organisation-wide complement.

rationales.A: The approval prompt only appears in interactive sessions; it is skipped under claude -p, which is precisely why the gap exists in CI.
rationales.C: Local scope is per-user configuration and does not stop the pipeline loading a server that a pull request adds to the project file.
rationales.D: Tool-list pinning is a Messages API MCP connector feature that freezes a known server's tools; it does nothing to stop an unapproved server starting and inheriting the job's credentials.

sources.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

items.objective: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
items.stem: An HR-software vendor commissions a design review of its remote MCP server and client integration, which use OAuth over Streamable HTTP. Which THREE findings are genuine security gaps under the current MCP authorization specification? (Select THREE)

options.text: The server accepts any unexpired token signed by the corporate identity provider, without checking it was issued for this server.
The client sends the access token in the URI query string of each MCP request instead of in an Authorization header.
The server publishes OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata so that clients can discover which authorization server protects it.
The client includes the resource parameter naming the server's canonical URI in both the authorization and token requests.
A companion stdio server that runs locally reads its credentials from environment variables instead of running an OAuth flow.
The client continues the authorization flow even when the authorization server's metadata gives no sign that it supports PKCE.

items.explanation: The 2026-07-28 MCP authorization specification requires servers to validate that tokens were issued for them as the audience, requires clients to send access tokens in the Authorization header and never in the URI query string, and makes PKCE mandatory: its security considerations say that if authorization server metadata omits code_challenge_methods_supported, the client must refuse to proceed. Publishing Protected Resource Metadata, sending the RFC 8707 resource parameter in both requests, and taking stdio credentials from the environment are all what the specification asks for.

rationales.C: Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) is a MUST for HTTP MCP servers using authorization; publishing it is compliance, not a gap.
rationales.D: Clients MUST include the resource parameter, set to the MCP server's canonical URI, in both authorization and token requests; this binds the token to its audience.
rationales.E: The specification says STDIO implementations should not follow the OAuth flow and should take credentials from the environment, so this is correct.

items.objective: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
items.stem: An online retailer's returns assistant calls the company's order MCP server, which uses OAuth. About 2% of conversations end in a refund; the rest only look up orders. Product managers want to avoid repeated consent prompts, so the team proposes requesting orders:read, orders:refund and customers:write at first sign-in. Security requires least privilege per user. Which design best satisfies both groups?

options.text: Request only the scope from the server's 401 challenge, then step up to orders:refund on an insufficient_scope 403 when a refund starts.
Request all three scopes at sign-in, then review scope use each month and revoke refund and write scopes from users who never needed them.
Give the MCP server one long-lived service token holding all three scopes, so that customers never see a consent prompt for any action.
Request orders:read and orders:refund at sign-in since refunds are a core flow, and defer only customers:write to a later consent prompt.

items.explanation: The MCP authorization model is built for this trade-off: clients request only the scopes needed, starting from the scope in the initial 401 challenge, and acquire extra privilege through step-up authorization when a 403 insufficient_scope arrives, unioning the new scope with those already granted. The 98% of users who only look up orders never hold refund rights, and the 2% who refund see one extra consent at the moment it makes sense, which is the least friction compatible with least privilege.

rationales.B: Granting everything up front and revoking later is a detective cleanup; for a month every user holds refund and write rights they do not need.
rationales.C: A shared service token removes per-user authorization altogether, turns the server into a confused deputy and breaks per-user audit.
rationales.D: This looks like a compromise but still grants refund rights to the 98% of users who never refund, when step-up would grant it only to those who do.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 3.3 Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
items.stem: A furniture retailer's shopping assistant answers delivery questions such as 'can I get this sofa by Saturday' with three read-only tools: stock by store, price, and delivery slots. Answers are accurate, but shoppers wait about nine seconds before any text appears. Traces show that on the first turn Claude requests all three tools together, yet the app runs them one after another at about two seconds each and returns each result in its own message; on later turns Claude calls one tool per turn. A developer proposes streaming. Answer quality must not change. Which change BEST cuts the wait?

options.text: Stream the final answer so that text appears as soon as generation starts, which removes most of the wait shoppers complain about.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to invoke all independent tools simultaneously rather than one after another.
Run the independent lookups concurrently and return all their results together in a single user message after each tool turn.
Switch to the fastest model tier, so that each model turn between the lookups finishes sooner than it does at the moment.

items.explanation: Most of the wait happens before Claude writes a word: three independent lookups run in series, and the app's message format is making it worse. Anthropic's parallel tool use guidance is that independent, read-only calls are usually safe to run concurrently for lower latency, and that every tool_result must come back in one user message; returning each result in its own message teaches Claude to stop making parallel calls, which is why later turns degrade to one tool per turn. Fixing execution and formatting cuts the lookup time to roughly the slowest single call without touching the model or its answers. Streaming helps only once answer generation starts, so it cannot recover time spent on tools.

rationales.A: Streaming improves perceived latency during generation, but the first token still waits for the serial lookups, which are most of the nine seconds.
rationales.B: Claude already requests the tools together on the first turn; the serial execution and the one-message-per-result format are in the app, so an instruction does not fix them.
rationales.D: The lookups, not model turns, dominate the wait, and a tier change risks the answer quality the stem says must not change.

items.objective: 3.3 Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
items.stem: A wealth-management firm generates quarterly portfolio commentary with a Claude Opus model at high effort. Accuracy on the firm's eval set is 96% against a 93% bar, but p95 latency is 38 seconds against a new 20-second SLO. Last month's effort sweep on that eval set scored medium effort at 91%. Traces show almost all the time goes on output: drafts average about 2,400 output tokens, but the client template publishes only a three-paragraph summary and an allocation table, and the formatter discards the rest. Fast mode is offered for this model, but Finance has frozen the AI budget, so premium-priced options are out. What should the architect do?

options.text: Enable fast mode on the current model, which raises output speed without changing the model or the commentary it writes.
Rewrite the instructions to ask only for the three-paragraph summary and allocation table that the template publishes.
Lower max_tokens to about the size of the published sections, so generation stops once the useful part has been written.
Re-run the effort sweep at low and medium on the eval set, then adopt the lowest level that still clears the 93% bar.

items.explanation: The traces put the latency in output length, and about three quarters of that output is thrown away. Anthropic's latency guidance is to minimise output tokens by asking Claude directly for shorter responses, with paragraph or sentence limits rather than word counts, and the Effort documentation notes that on recent Opus models effort controls thinking volume rather than visible length, so length should be prompted for. Asking only for what the template publishes cuts generation time roughly in proportion to the tokens removed, at no extra cost and without touching the model or effort level; the existing eval then confirms accuracy holds as a routine release check.

rationales.A: Fast mode raises output speed at premium pricing, which the frozen budget rules out, and it still generates the 2,400 tokens the formatter discards.
rationales.C: max_tokens is a hard cut-off that can stop mid-sentence, and nothing guarantees the published sections are written first, so it can truncate the very content the client sees.
rationales.D: The stem already holds the evidence: medium effort scored 91%, below the bar, and low effort will not do better; effort also does not reliably shorten the visible output that drives the latency.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P prep course)

items.objective: 3.3 Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
items.stem: A hospital's clinical-documentation assistant runs long conversations over a 60,000-token formulary and guideline prefix that is prompt-cached. To speed up simple follow-ups, an engineer set the request-level effort to low on follow-up turns while the first turn stays at high; cache reads then fell sharply and median latency rose. The team has confirmed that the request-level effort value is part of the rendered prompt, so changing it between requests starts the cache over. A per-message effort change that keeps the cache exists only as a beta, and the hospital's change board bars beta features from clinical systems. On follow-ups, a cache hit saves about 4 seconds and low effort about 1 second, and evals show first-turn answers fall below the accuracy bar at low effort. What should the architect do?

options.text: Hold effort at high for the whole conversation, so every follow-up matches the cached prefix and regains the cache saving.
Switch follow-ups to the per-message effort change, which keeps both the cached prefix and the low-effort saving on each turn.
Run every turn at low effort, the first turn included, so that the effort value never changes and the cached prefix holds.
Move the prefix to the longer cache lifetime option, so cached content survives the switches between high and low effort.

items.explanation: Each constraint removes one option. The beta that would keep both savings is barred by the change board, and low effort on every turn fails the first-turn accuracy bar. Of what remains, a constant effort level keeps every follow-up on the cached prefix: giving up about 1 second of effort saving to regain about 4 seconds of cache saving is a net gain of roughly 3 seconds per follow-up. Anthropic's guidance matches: hold top-level effort constant within a conversation that relies on cache hits, and vary it across workloads instead.

rationales.B: This is the documented way to keep both savings on supported models, but it is a beta and the change board bars betas from clinical systems.
rationales.C: A constant low effort would keep the cache, but the evals show first-turn answers fall below the accuracy bar at low effort.
rationales.D: A longer lifetime keeps an unchanged prefix warm for longer; it cannot make a request with a different effort value match the cached prefix.

items.objective: 3.3 Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
items.stem: A school district's analytics agent answers questions such as 'which ninth-grade students fell behind in maths this term' by calling get_student_progress once per student, often 300 times per question. Every result lands in the context window, answers take minutes and token costs are high, though accuracy is acceptable. The deployment uses the Claude API directly and has no zero-data-retention requirement. Which change best reduces latency and tokens together?

options.text: Apply prompt caching to the tool definitions and system prompt, so the repeated prefix on each of the 300 turns is cheaper to process.
Move to the fastest model tier, so each of the roughly 300 model round trips per question completes in less time than it does today.
Enable context editing to clear older tool results as the loop runs, keeping the context window small while all 300 calls proceed.
Use programmatic tool calling, so Claude writes code that loops over the tool in the sandbox and only the aggregate enters context.

items.explanation: The cost driver is the shape of the work: hundreds of sequential tool calls, each needing a model round trip and each dumping its result into context. Programmatic tool calling lets Claude write code in the code-execution sandbox that calls the tool, so intermediate results never enter the context window and there is no model round trip per call, cutting latency and tokens together. The stem's note that ZDR is not required matters, because programmatic tool calling is not ZDR-eligible.

rationales.A: Caching lowers the price and processing time of a repeated prefix but leaves all 300 round trips and all 300 results in context.
rationales.B: A faster tier shortens each round trip but keeps 300 of them and the same token volume, and it risks accuracy the team is currently happy with.
rationales.C: Context editing trims stale results to relieve window pressure, but every call still needs its own model round trip, so latency barely moves.

items.objective: 3.3 Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
items.stem: A state unemployment agency is designing an eligibility-triage agent. Evals show the most capable tier meets the accuracy bar on all cases but misses the latency SLO and the budget; the fastest tier meets both but fails the accuracy bar on the roughly 10% of cases with complex legal edge conditions. The latency SLO applies to median decision time, and complex legal cases are allowed a longer turnaround. Which configuration should the architect propose?

options.text: Use a faster model as executor that escalates hard decisions to the most capable model, then confirm it on evals split by case type.
Run the most capable tier with fast mode on every case, buying back the latency without changing the model that already passes the evals.
Run the fastest tier with extended thinking and a large thinking budget on every case, so extra reasoning closes the gap.
Run the fastest tier and add retrieval over past adjudicated decisions, so it can copy the reasoning used on similar complex cases.

items.explanation: When one tier is accurate but too slow and expensive and another is fast and cheap but fails a minority of cases, a multi-model design bills most tokens at the cheaper rate. Anthropic documents an executor that escalates hard decisions to an advisor model as one such pattern. Because the SLO is on median time and complex cases may take longer, the escalated 10% does not set the SLO. The failure is concentrated in an identifiable segment, so the design must be validated on evals segmented by case type, not just on an overall average that could hide the edge cases.

rationales.B: Fast mode is offered only for certain Opus models and only on the Claude API, so it may not exist for the most capable tier at all; where it does, it raises output speed at premium pricing, which addresses latency while making the budget miss worse.
rationales.C: This is an untested assumption: a large thinking budget adds latency and cost to the 90% of routine cases that did not need it, which threatens the median SLO, and the evals already show the tier failing the hard segment.
rationales.D: The failure is reasoning on complex legal conditions, not missing information; retrieving similar past decisions risks pattern-matching to cases that differ in exactly the edge condition that matters.

items.objective: 3.4 Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
items.stem: A software company rolled Claude Code out to 800 engineers and stood up an OpenTelemetry collector with dashboards for sessions, token usage and cost. A week later the dashboards are still empty, and the collector shows no inbound connections at all. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Telemetry is opt-in, and nothing is exported until each machine is configured both to enable it and to name an exporter.
Claude Code reports usage only through the Admin API, so OpenTelemetry dashboards cannot be filled from developer sessions.
Prompt redaction is on by default and drops every event that would have contained a prompt before it is ever exported.
The collector has to be registered in the Claude Console before Claude Code will send it any data from organisation members.

items.explanation: Claude Code telemetry is opt-in: nothing is exported until CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 is set and an exporter is chosen. An empty collector with no inbound connections is the signature of telemetry never being enabled, not of filtering further down the pipeline. At fleet scale the reliable fix is to push these variables to every machine through managed settings, where OTLP endpoint variables also override conflicting developer-set ones.

rationales.B: Claude Code exports metrics and events over OpenTelemetry; the Admin API is a separate usage source and does not replace OTel export.
rationales.C: Redaction removes prompt text and tool content from events but still exports the events and metrics, so it cannot explain zero connections.
rationales.D: There is no collector registration step in the Console; the exporter is configured through environment variables and settings on the client side.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 3.4 Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
items.stem: A payments fintech runs a support agent built on the Claude Agent SDK for 40 merchant tenants, all through one service credential. Compliance asks which merchant user triggered each refund-tool call, but the exported telemetry events identify only the service account. Which change makes these actions attributable going forward?

options.text: Turn on tool-content logging so the full input and output of each tool call is exported along with its event.
Issue one API key per merchant tenant and group the Usage and Cost API report by key to see who triggered refunds.
Instruct the agent to state the requesting user's ID in every reply, then parse those replies from the logs.
Attach the end user's and tenant's IDs as resource attributes on each query, so tool events record whom they acted for.

items.explanation: In a multi-tenant agent the built-in identity attributes describe the service's credential, not the person the agent acted for. The Agent SDK observability guidance is to inject end-user identity such as enduser.id and tenant.id into OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES on each query(), which turns tool_decision and tool_result events into a per-user audit trail a SIEM can query. Identity is attached deterministically at the instrumentation layer rather than inferred later.

rationales.A: Tool content opt-in adds payload data, not identity; it widens sensitive-data exposure in telemetry and still does not say which user triggered the call.
rationales.B: Per-tenant keys give cost and token totals per tenant, not per-user attribution of individual tool calls, and they multiply credentials to manage.
rationales.C: Asking the model to report identity is a prompt-only control on an audit requirement; it is unreliable and can be manipulated by user input.

items.objective: 3.4 Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
items.stem: A pharmaceutical company's pharmacovigilance team triages incoming adverse-event reports with Agent SDK jobs in serverless functions; each run lasts about three seconds and the platform kills the process as soon as the handler returns. Traces are missing from the collector for roughly a third of runs, the collector keeps 100% of what it receives, its receiver metrics show zero refused or dropped spans, and application logs show no errors. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

options.text: Batched telemetry is lost when the process exits before export, and export errors are silent by default; flush before exit.
Content redaction strips spans that carry case data before export; turn on tool-content logging so those spans are kept.
TRACEPARENT is not propagated, so subagent spans land in separate traces; pass W3C trace context into every run of the job.
The collector rate-limits bursts from serverless functions; add a second collector and balance the load across both.

items.explanation: Agent SDK telemetry is batched (traces and logs every few seconds), so a short-lived process killed as soon as its handler returns can die before the batch is exported; and export failures are silent by default, which is why the logs show nothing. The fix is to make each run flush (or shorten the export interval) before exit and to enable CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_DIAG_STDERR=1 so export errors become visible. The intermittent, roughly one-in-three pattern fits a timing race, not a configuration that drops data consistently.

rationales.B: Redaction removes content attributes from events; it does not delete spans, and turning on tool-content logging would add case data to telemetry without solving the loss.
rationales.C: Missing trace context produces disconnected traces, not missing ones; the spans would still arrive at the collector.
rationales.D: The collector's receiver metrics show zero refused or dropped spans, so the missing data never reached it; rate limiting also would not explain why the loss tracks very short process lifetimes.

items.objective: 3.4 Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
items.stem: A retail group runs five brands, each in its own Claude API workspace under one organization. Finance wants a daily token chargeback per brand, and the platform team wants to spot a prompt-caching regression within an hour of each deployment. Which TWO approaches meet these needs? (Select TWO)

options.text: Query the Cost endpoint in hourly buckets after each deployment and alert when spend per brand rises above the previous week.
Query the Usage API with an Admin key, grouped by workspace, to produce the daily token totals that finance charges back per brand.
Query the Usage API in 1-hour buckets and compare cached-input and cache-creation tokens with uncached input before and after deploys.
Call the usage endpoints with each brand's own workspace API key, so each brand team can pull and reconcile its own token usage.
Read the anthropic-ratelimit headers on every response and sum them per brand to estimate the token cost behind each workspace.

items.explanation: The Usage API reports tokens in 1-minute, 1-hour or 1-day buckets, can be grouped by workspace, and separates uncached input, cached input, cache creation and output tokens. Grouping by workspace gives finance its per-brand chargeback, and hourly buckets of cache reads versus cache writes versus uncached input reveal a caching regression soon after a deploy. The API requires an Admin credential, and data typically appears within minutes.

rationales.A: The Cost endpoint is daily-only, so it cannot show hourly movement after a deployment, and spend is a lagging, indirect signal for cache efficiency.
rationales.D: The Usage and Cost API requires an Admin credential; workspace API keys do not work against it.
rationales.E: Rate-limit headers report remaining capacity against limits, not billed token usage or cache behaviour, so summing them does not produce a chargeback.

items.objective: 3.4 Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
items.stem: A university moved its student-support assistant from a direct Claude API pilot to Claude in Microsoft Foundry, on a US Data Zone deployment, because its student-records agreement requires inference to stay in the United States under the university's Azure agreement. The SRE team's rate-limit alerts read Anthropic's anthropic-ratelimit-* response headers, and the team has confirmed that Foundry responses do not carry them, so the alerts stayed silent through enrolment-week peaks. What should the team do?

options.text: Rebuild the rate-limit and error alerts on Azure Monitor and Log Analytics, which report usage and errors for Foundry.
Route enrolment-week traffic back to the direct Claude API, where the response headers that feed the existing alerts are returned.
Pull one-minute usage buckets from the Usage and Cost Admin API with an Admin key, and alert when use nears the pilot's limits.
Compute remaining capacity from each response's usage object, and alert at 80% of the rate limits that applied during the pilot.

items.explanation: On a partner route, operational monitoring lives in the cloud provider's tooling. Foundry does not return Anthropic's rate-limit headers, and rate limits for a Foundry deployment are managed in Azure, so the alerts must be rebuilt on Azure Monitor and Log Analytics, which track usage, latency and error rates for the deployment. Anthropic also recommends retaining activity logs on at least a 30-day rolling basis. The university's records agreement rules out moving traffic off the Azure deployment to get the old signal back.

rationales.B: Moving student traffic off the Azure deployment breaks the records agreement the move was made to satisfy, just to restore an alerting signal.
rationales.C: The Admin API, including Usage and Cost, is not available for Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and the pilot's direct-API limits no longer apply.
rationales.D: The usage object reports tokens per request, not remaining capacity, and the pilot's direct-API limits are not the limits Azure applies to the Foundry deployment.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (CCAR-P prep course) - learning objectives

items.objective: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
items.stem: A regional hospital network is building a Claude assistant that answers nurses' questions from 1,400 clinical protocols. Each protocol has numbered sections and dosing tables whose rows carry only a weight band and a dose; the drug name and indication appear only in the section heading above the table. The pilot indexes fixed 400-token windows. In evaluation, dosing answers quote correct-looking numbers for the wrong drug in about one case in eight, while narrative questions score well. Which change to the chunking and indexing design best addresses this?

options.text: Raise the chunk overlap from 10% to 50%, so that each dosing-table row is more likely to land in a window that also holds the heading above it.
Switch to semantic chunking, so that chunk boundaries fall where the topic changes rather than at a fixed token count in each protocol.
Chunk on section boundaries, keep each dosing table whole with its heading, and prefix every chunk with the protocol title and section path.
Index each dosing-table row as its own small chunk, so that every weight band and dose can be matched precisely against the query.

items.explanation: Fixed-size windows ignore document structure, so they cut a table away from the heading that gives its rows meaning; a row reading '10-20 kg: 5 mg/kg' is semantically similar to the same row for a different drug. Structure-aware chunking keeps each unit of meaning (a section, a whole table) intact, and carrying the document and section context into every chunk is the idea behind contextual retrieval, which Anthropic Academy's Claude in Amazon Bedrock course teaches as a stage of its RAG pipeline. The fix belongs in the indexing design, because the defect is created there; no generation-side change can recover a fact that the retrieved chunk does not contain.

rationales.A: More overlap makes it likelier, not certain, that a row shares a window with its heading, and long tables still span several windows; it also inflates the index with duplicated text while leaving the structural cause in place.
rationales.B: Semantic chunking breaks where neighbouring sentences diverge in meaning, and a heading that names a drug reads very differently from rows of weights and doses, so the break can land exactly between them. It also adds nothing about which protocol or section a chunk came from.
rationales.D: Row-level chunks are the most ambiguous of all: each is a weight band and a dose with no drug name, so it buys precision on the numbers by discarding the very context that is missing today.

items.objective: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
items.stem: A wealth-management firm is choosing an embedding model for RAG over 90,000 internal research notes that advisers query in plain language. Its model-risk policy requires a documented, evidence-based rationale for any model that shapes client advice, and re-embedding the corpus later would need a fresh approval. The shortlist is a finance-domain model, a current general-purpose model and a contextualized-chunk model. Which selection approach should the architect recommend?

options.text: Choose the finance-domain model outright, since domain models are documented for finance retrieval and the notes are written by analysts.
Choose whichever model ranks highest on a public embedding leaderboard, which gives model-risk reviewers an independent, auditable benchmark.
Build a labelled set of real adviser questions, set input_type for questions and notes, and pick the model with the best recall in budget.
Choose the contextualized-chunk model outright, as every note is split into chunks and advisers' questions often depend on whole-note context.

items.explanation: Anthropic's embeddings guide frames the choice as a trade-off of domain specificity, inference performance and customisation, recommends assessing a variety of embedding vendors, and lists finance-domain, general-purpose and contextualized-chunk models as options rather than naming a winner. Which one serves this corpus is an empirical question, and the evidence the model-risk policy asks for is a retrieval eval on the firm's own questions and notes. Each candidate should be tested as it will run: the guide says to set input_type to query for questions and document for the notes in every retrieval use. The same eval becomes the baseline for any later re-embedding request.

rationales.A: Being documented for finance describes a model's training focus, not its recall on these notes. Choosing without a comparison puts an assumption, not evidence, in the model-risk file and risks a costly re-embed later.
rationales.B: Public leaderboards measure other corpora and query styles. They do not show how adviser questions match these notes, so they are weak evidence for a decision the policy says must rest on evidence.
rationales.D: Contextualized embeddings help when chunks lose meaning without their document, which may or may not be this corpus's main weakness. That is a hypothesis for the eval to test, not a reason to skip it.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (CCAR-P Prep Course): evals as the gating mechanism for any change

items.objective: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
items.stem: A national archives agency indexes 410 million chunks of digitised records as 1024-dimension float32 embeddings. The vector tier now needs about 1.7 TB of memory, the approved hosting budget covers 550 GB, and records may not be removed from search. The retrieval eval sets a hard floor: recall@10 may fall no more than one point below today's baseline. A pilot on a 1% sample measured recall@10 against that baseline: int8 storage 0.3 points below, Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions 2.1 points below, and binary quantization 6 points below. Which plan best fits both constraints?

options.text: Switch to binary quantization, which cuts memory about 32x and leaves wide headroom under the budget for the collection to keep growing for years.
Truncate the Matryoshka vectors from 1024 to 256 dimensions and renormalise, a fourfold cut to about 420 GB, and confirm recall@10 on the full eval.
Store the vectors as int8, a roughly fourfold cut to about 420 GB, and confirm recall@10 on the full retrieval eval before the cutover.
Move the 60% of records least used in five years into a cold store that is searchable only on request through a ticket to the reading room.

items.explanation: Anthropic's embeddings guide sets out the levers: float32 gives the highest retrieval accuracy, int8 cuts storage, memory and cost by about 4x, binary by about 32x, and Matryoshka vectors can be truncated by keeping the leading dimensions. Here the budget does not separate int8 from 256-dimension truncation, because both take 1.7 TB to about 420 GB, inside 550 GB. The pilot does: int8 lands 0.3 points below baseline, inside the one-point floor, while truncation (2.1 points) and binary (6 points) fall outside it. The sample is only 1% of the corpus, so the full eval still gates the cutover, but the evidence already says which option to take to that gate.

rationales.A: Binary quantization meets the budget many times over, but the pilot already puts it 6 points below baseline, far outside the one-point floor. It buys headroom the constraints never asked for with recall the floor protects.
rationales.B: Truncation is a valid Matryoshka technique and reaches the same 420 GB, but the pilot measured it 2.1 points below baseline, outside the floor. Confirming it on the full eval would most likely just confirm the failure and force a second migration.
rationales.D: Making most records searchable only by ticket is effectively removing them from search, which the mandate forbids; it solves the memory problem by breaking the service.

items.objective: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
items.stem: A home-improvement retailer's store-associate assistant answers from 18,000 product installation guides. The pilot indexed 1,000-token chunks, and precise questions ('how long must this tile adhesive cure before grouting?') often missed, because each vector blended several steps. A trial with 150-token chunks raised the retrieval hit rate from 61% to 88%, but answer review found that about a quarter of answers now omit a prerequisite step or a safety warning stated elsewhere in the same section, which associates must pass on to customers. Which change to the indexing design best fits both findings?

options.text: Keep the 150-token chunks and switch to contextualized chunk embeddings, so each small vector also captures the context of the whole guide.
Index each guide as a single whole-document chunk, so that every answer receives the full guide with all its prerequisite steps and warnings.
Embed 150-token child chunks for matching, link each to its parent section, and give Claude the parent section instead of the child.
Store every guide twice, as 150- and 1,000-token chunks in one index, and let similarity decide which size of chunk reaches Claude.

items.explanation: The two findings pull in opposite directions: small chunks give precise vectors, but a complete answer needs the section around the matched passage. Hierarchical (parent-child, or small-to-big) chunking resolves this in the index design: child chunks are embedded and matched, and each retrieved child is replaced by its parent section before it reaches the model. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documents the pattern directly: small text embeddings are more precise, but retrieval aims for comprehensive context, so retrieved child chunks are replaced with broader parent chunks. Anthropic's RAG curriculum treats chunking strategy as a design choice for the same reason: the unit you match on need not be the unit you hand to Claude.

rationales.A: Contextualized embeddings improve how a small chunk is matched, but Claude still receives only the 150-token passage, so the warning elsewhere in the section is still missing from the answer.
rationales.B: Whole-guide vectors are diluted far more than the 1,000-token chunks that already missed precise questions, and every answer would carry an entire guide into context at much higher cost.
rationales.D: Two unlinked sizes in one index let the precise small chunk win most queries, which reproduces the snippet-only answers already seen; it doubles the index without tying a match to its section.

items.objective: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
items.stem: A developer-tools company is designing a RAG index over its public API documentation and 2.3 million lines of SDK source code, so its support assistant can answer integration questions with working code. During the build the team will also move from an older general-purpose embedding model to a newer one. Which THREE design decisions are sound? (Select THREE)

options.text: Chunk source files on function and class boundaries rather than fixed windows, so each retrieved chunk is a complete unit of code.
Evaluate a code-specialised embedding model for the source index, since domain-specific models are documented for code retrieval.
Re-embed the whole corpus with the new model before cutover, since vectors from different models do not share a comparable space.
Use one fixed 200-token window for both prose and code, so the pipeline stays uniform and every chunk is scored on the same footing.
Skip the index and put the whole codebase in the system prompt with prompt caching, which removes retrieval error from the design.
Keep the old model's stored vectors, embed only new queries with the new one, and confirm recall on the retrieval eval after cutover.

items.explanation: A sound RAG index matches its chunking and embedding choices to the shape of the data and keeps the query and document sides consistent. Code has natural units (functions, classes), and splitting along them keeps each chunk meaningful. Anthropic's embeddings guide lists domain-specific Voyage models, including one optimised for code retrieval, as options worth evaluating. And the exam guide's own rationale for a confidently wrong RAG system names mismatched embeddings as a retrieval failure: query vectors and stored vectors must come from the same model, so a model change means re-embedding the corpus before the switch.

rationales.D: A single fixed window splits functions mid-body and treats prose and code alike, which loses the structure that makes code chunks retrievable and self-contained.
rationales.E: Millions of lines far exceed any context window, and caching changes price and latency, not the fact that cached tokens still occupy the window; this is a monolithic design where retrieval is required.
rationales.F: Queries embedded by the new model would be compared with documents embedded by the old one, and similarity scores across different embedding spaces are meaningless. An eval after cutover would only confirm that retrieval had already broken in production.

items.objective: 3.6 Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
items.stem: A state judiciary runs a Claude assistant over its rules of court and local rules for court clerks. Clerks mostly paste exact citations such as 'Rule 12-4-301(b)(2)' or form numbers such as 'CV-7A'. With dense-vector search alone, the assistant returns similar rules from neighbouring sections, and clerks are losing trust. Retrieval logs show that for about a third of citation queries, the cited rule does not appear anywhere in the top 50 dense results. Conceptual questions ('when may a filing deadline be extended?') already work well. Which retrieval change BEST fits this query pattern?

options.text: Fine-tune a custom embedding model on the rules of court, so that its vectors learn to separate neighbouring rule numbers from one another.
Add BM25 lexical search next to the dense index and merge the two result lists, so citations match literally and concepts match semantically.
Raise the similarity threshold so only chunks scoring above 0.9 reach Claude, filtering out the near-miss neighbouring sections before generation.
Add a reranking stage over the top 20 dense results so the exact rule is promoted, without changing how the candidates are first retrieved.

items.explanation: Dense embeddings capture meaning, so strings like rule numbers and form codes that differ by one character land close together. Lexical search such as BM25 matches the literal tokens and is strong exactly where dense search is weak. Anthropic Academy's RAG lessons teach BM25 lexical search and a multi-index pipeline that merges lexical and semantic results, and managed retrieval services expose the same choice: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases offers a hybrid search type that queries both the vector embeddings and the raw text, in place of semantic-only search. Because this workload mixes exact-identifier lookups with conceptual questions, the retrieval strategy should serve both query patterns rather than replace one with the other.

rationales.A: Fine-tuning is costly and slow to iterate, and it still asks a semantic model to do an exact-match job; a lexical index solves the identifier problem directly and cheaply.
rationales.C: A threshold filters by the same similarity scores that are already wrong. The neighbouring rules score as high as the right one, so the filter removes good results without fixing the ranking.
rationales.D: A reranker can only reorder what the first stage returns. The logs show the cited rule is absent from the top 50 dense results for about a third of citation queries, so reranking the top 20 cannot promote it; literal matching belongs in candidate generation.

items.objective: 3.6 Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
items.stem: A sporting-goods retailer's merchandising assistant answers buyers' questions from two sources: 30,000 product descriptions and vendor fact sheets, and a sales table with one row per SKU, store and week for the last three closed fiscal years. The sales data is final and never changes. The pilot embedded each sales row as a text chunk in the same vector index as the descriptions. Questions such as 'which fact sheets mention recycled insulation?' work well, but 'which ten outerwear SKUs sold the most units in the Northeast in fiscal 2025?' return confident totals that are wrong. Which retrieval strategy should the architect recommend?

options.text: Keep the row chunks but raise top-k from 10 to 200, then re-run the retrieval eval to confirm that the totals now come out right.
Add BM25 next to the dense index so that SKU codes, region names and fiscal years in each question match the stored sales rows literally.
Pre-compute text summaries of sales by category, region and year, and embed them as extra chunks so common questions find a ready answer.
Give Claude a read-only query tool over the sales table, with the schema described in the tool, and keep vector retrieval for the descriptions.

items.explanation: The data shape decides the strategy. The descriptions are unstructured text, where similarity search fits. The sales table is structured, schema-conformant rows, and the failing questions are aggregations: filter by region and year, sum units, rank. Similarity search returns the k rows most like the question, not every row that satisfies a predicate, so any total Claude computes from them is a sum over a sample. A query tool lets the database compute the exact answer, and read-only access keeps the tool to the least privilege the job needs. Managed retrieval documents the same split: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can connect to structured data stores and convert natural-language questions into SQL, so existing structured data is used directly instead of being converted to another format. Freshness is not the issue here, because the data is closed; the mismatch is between an aggregation query pattern and a similarity index.

rationales.A: A larger k is still a similarity-ranked sample rather than every row matching the region, category and year, and 200 rows of figures crowd the context. Claude would still be summing a partial set; the eval would only measure the gap.
rationales.B: Literal matching changes which rows rank first, but retrieval still returns a top-k sample rather than all matching rows, so the totals stay partial. The defect is the aggregation, not the matching.
rationales.C: Pre-built summaries answer only the groupings someone anticipated. A ranking by SKU within one region and year, or any new cut a buyer asks for, falls through to the same partial rows.

items.objective: 3.6 Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
items.stem: A university's advising assistant answers degree-requirement questions from twelve years of academic catalogs. Students are bound by the catalog of the year they enrolled, and consecutive catalogs are nearly identical apart from a few changed requirements. Students who enrolled in 2021 are being told the 2025 rules, because the 2025 chunk often scores slightly higher for the same wording. Which retrieval strategy matches this data shape?

options.text: Index only the current catalog and tell students on older catalogs to confirm their requirements with a human adviser at the registrar.
Tag every chunk with its catalog year at indexing time and filter retrieval to the student's enrollment year before ranking by similarity.
Switch to a larger, higher-quality embedding model so the small year-to-year differences in wording separate cleanly in the vector space.
Tell Claude in the system prompt to prefer passages from the student's enrollment year whenever two retrieved passages say different things.

items.explanation: The data shape here is many near-duplicate versions of the same document, where the correct version is decided by an attribute of the user (enrollment year), not by the meaning of the question. Similarity ranking cannot make that distinction, because the passages are nearly identical. The retrieval strategy should therefore restrict candidates deterministically on the version attribute, recorded as metadata when the chunk is indexed, and only then rank by similarity. Managed retrieval services expose exactly this: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases lets each document carry metadata attributes and applies a retrieval filter (for example, equals on a catalog-year attribute) to the metadata before returning results. It is the same principle as keeping a decision in deterministic code rather than leaving it to ranking or a prompt.

rationales.A: Dropping older catalogs removes the very content most current students are bound by and pushes routine questions to human staff; it shrinks scope instead of fixing retrieval.
rationales.C: Near-identical text produces near-identical vectors in any model. The deciding fact is the student's enrollment year, which no embedding of the passage can know.
rationales.D: A prompt preference only works if the right year's passage is retrieved at all and is visibly labelled; it is a probabilistic fix where a deterministic filter is available and required.
