items.objective: 3.6 Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
items.stem: A health system's revenue-cycle assistant helps denial-management staff by retrieving from 60,000 payer-policy and coding-guideline chunks and passing the top 5 to the generator. The retrieval eval shows the correct chunk is in the top 50 dense results for 95% of test questions but in the top 5 for only 58%. The p95 latency budget has about 300 ms of headroom, and the cost per worked claim is near its ceiling. Which change is the best next step?

options.text: Pass the top 50 chunks straight to the generator instead of the top 5, so the right policy chunk is almost always somewhere in its context.
Replace the embedding model with a larger one and re-embed the corpus, since better first-stage vectors are the only way to fix top-5 order.
Move generation to the most capable model tier, which is better at spotting the relevant policy among weakly related chunks in the top 5.
Add a reranker that rescores the top 50 dense candidates against the question and keeps the best 5, sized to fit the latency headroom.

items.explanation: The eval separates recall from precision: the first stage already finds the right chunk 95% of the time, but it ranks it poorly. That is the job a reranker does: it takes a query and a candidate list and reorders them by relevance with a more expensive model than the first-stage similarity score. Anthropic's embeddings guide lists rerankers with an accuracy tier and a latency-and-cost tier, so the reranker can be sized to the 300 ms headroom. Anthropic Academy's Claude in Amazon Bedrock course likewise teaches reranking results as a stage of its RAG pipeline. Fix the stage the metrics point to, and leave the stages that are working alone.

rationales.A: Ten times more context per call breaks a cost ceiling that is already tight and adds noise that degrades answer accuracy; it moves the ranking problem into the generator rather than solving it.
rationales.B: Recall at 50 is already 95%, so the first stage is not the bottleneck; re-embedding 60,000 chunks is the expensive fix at the wrong stage and may not change top-5 order at all.
rationales.C: In 42% of cases the right chunk is not in the top 5 at all, so no generator can find it there; a bigger model for a retrieval problem also raises cost against a ceiling.

sources.title: Claude in Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Academy): RAG module, 'Reranking results' lesson

items.objective: 3.6 Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
items.stem: A cloud software company's site-reliability assistant answers from runbooks held in the company's own search service. Every answer must cite the runbook passages it used, so the team returns passages as search_result blocks with citations enabled. Two uses are planned: on-call engineers investigating incidents ask open-ended, multi-step questions whose next lookup depends on what the last one found, and a deploy gate asks one fixed question per change ('which runbook covers rollback for this service?') under a tight latency budget. Which delivery design best fits both query patterns?

options.text: Expose search as a custom tool for both uses, so one code path serves incidents and the deploy gate and Claude decides when to search.
For incidents, expose search as a custom tool returning search_result blocks; for the deploy gate, pre-fetch into the user message.
Pre-fetch the top results for both uses and pass them in the user message, so every request completes in one call with no tool round trip.
For incidents, pre-fetch the top results into the user message; for the deploy gate, expose search as a custom tool that Claude calls.

items.explanation: search_result blocks can reach Claude in two ways: returned from a custom tool, for dynamic retrieval where Claude decides what to fetch at runtime, or placed as top-level content in the user message, for results the application has already fetched. The choice follows the query pattern. Investigations are multi-step and Claude must be able to search again based on what it learns, which only the tool path allows. The deploy-gate question is fixed, so the application can run the search itself and send a single request; the tool path would add a model round trip (Claude asks for the search, the application runs it, Claude answers) to a latency-bound step for no benefit. Citations work the same way on both paths. They are off by default, and every search_result block in a request must use the same setting, which is why the design enables them explicitly.

rationales.A: This suits incidents, but every change at the deploy gate pays an extra model round trip for a search whose query never varies, spending the latency budget for nothing.
rationales.C: Pre-fetching fixes the context before Claude has seen anything, so an investigation cannot follow up on what the first results reveal; the agent gets one guess at what to retrieve.
rationales.D: This inverts the match: the open-ended investigation loses the ability to search again, and the fixed deploy-gate query gains a tool round trip it does not need.

items.objective: 3.7 Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
items.stem: A B2B ticketing vendor wants its customers' engineers to search and update tickets from Claude Code, from claude.ai, and from the customers' own Agent SDK applications. Today the vendor maintains three hand-written tool integrations, and each change to its API breaks one of them. Which integration mechanism should the architect recommend?

options.text: Package the ticket functions as an Agent Skill with bundled scripts, and upload it once so that every Claude surface picks it up automatically.
Publish an A2A agent with an Agent Card, so each client delegates ticket tasks to the vendor's agent instead of calling the functions itself.
Build one remote MCP server over Streamable HTTP with OAuth, so every MCP-capable client reaches the same tool definitions and implementation.
Publish an OpenAPI specification and ask every customer to generate their own function-calling tool definitions from it in each application.

items.explanation: MCP exists so a capability is implemented once, as a server, and consumed by any MCP-capable client; Claude Code, claude.ai connectors and the Agent SDK can all reach a remote MCP server. Streamable HTTP is the standard remote transport in the current MCP revision (HTTP+SSE is deprecated), and OAuth lets each customer authorise access to its own tickets. One server replaces three integrations, so an API change is absorbed in one place. Match the mechanism to the boundary: the vendor is exposing tools to many hosts, which is MCP's shape.

rationales.A: A Skill reaches only the organization that installs it: an owner can provision one to their own Team or Enterprise members, and on to their Claude Code sign-ins, but nothing pushes a vendor's Skill into its customers' organizations or into their Agent SDK applications. Skills on the Claude API also run in a sandbox with no network access, so they could not reach the ticketing API.
rationales.B: A2A connects independent agents across an organisational boundary. Here the clients need tools for their own agents, so inserting a second agent adds a hop, latency and opacity without solving distribution.
rationales.D: An OpenAPI file pushes integration work onto every customer and multiplies the number of hand-built integrations, which is the maintenance problem the vendor is trying to escape.

items.objective: 3.7 Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
items.stem: A regional health system runs its patient-scheduling assistant on Claude on Google Cloud. Its business associate agreement, committed cloud spend and data-residency controls all sit under its Google Cloud contract, and the compliance office will not approve sending patient data through any other provider. A design review finds the team plans to reach the EHR scheduling MCP server through the Messages API MCP connector, as it did in a Claude API prototype. What should the architect change?

options.text: Move the workload to Claude Platform on AWS or Microsoft Foundry, where the MCP connector is offered, keeping the prototype's request shape.
Package the scheduling operations as an Agent Skill that runs in the managed code-execution sandbox, so no MCP connector is needed at all.
Run the MCP client in the application, list the server's tools, pass them to Claude as ordinary tools and execute the calls locally.
Expose scheduling as an A2A agent for Claude on Google Cloud to call directly, as A2A is the documented replacement for the connector there.

items.explanation: Route constraints come first: the prep course asks architects to identify which delivery routes are ruled out by governance or regulated-industry constraints before any other trade-off, and here the compliance office has fixed the route. Anthropic's Google Cloud page lists the MCP connector and Agent Skills among the features not supported there. The portable pattern is client-side MCP: the application acts as the MCP client, converts the server's tools into standard tool definitions (the SDKs' client-side MCP helpers do this conversion) and executes the tool calls itself. Standard tool use is supported on Google Cloud, so the integration fits the route instead of forcing the route to change.

rationales.A: Both routes do list the connector, but they move patient data outside the Google Cloud contract, BAA and residency controls that the compliance office requires. One integration feature does not outrank the route constraint.
rationales.B: Agent Skills and code execution are listed as not supported on Google Cloud, and on the Claude API Skills run in a sandbox with no network access, so they could not reach the EHR server anyway.
rationales.D: No documentation makes A2A a replacement for the MCP connector, and Claude on Google Cloud does not call A2A agents for you. It adds an agent boundary the design does not need.

items.objective: 3.7 Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
items.stem: A commercial bank's onboarding agent must obtain fraud-risk assessments from a consortium partner. The partner runs its own agent on a different framework and will not expose its internal tools, models or data; it will only accept assessment tasks and return results, some of which take hours. Which integration mechanism fits this boundary?

options.text: Ask the partner to publish its internal fraud tools as an MCP server, so the bank's agent can call each scoring function directly as a tool.
Have the bank's agent use computer-use tooling to operate the partner's analyst web portal, entering cases and reading results on screen.
Use an agent-to-agent protocol such as A2A: find the partner agent through its Agent Card and exchange tasks and artifacts with it.
Copy the partner's fraud data into the bank's own vector index each night, so the onboarding agent can retrieve risk signals without calling out.

items.explanation: The boundary is between two independent, opaque agents owned by different organisations. A2A is designed for that horizontal case: agents discover each other through an Agent Card that declares identity, skills, the service endpoint and supported auth schemes, then manage Tasks and exchange Messages and Artifacts, with polling, streaming or push notifications for work that runs for hours or days. Agents collaborate without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans or tool implementations. MCP is the vertical case, where an agent uses structured tools; the two are complementary. Choosing the mechanism starts with what each side is willing to expose.

rationales.A: The partner has refused to expose its tools. MCP would require it to give the bank's agent direct access to its scoring functions, which is exactly what it will not do.
rationales.B: Driving a human portal through the screen is brittle, hard to audit and slow, and it bypasses a machine interface the partner is willing to offer for regulated decisions.
rationales.D: The partner will not share its data, and nightly copies of risk signals would also be stale. This is retrieval doing a job that a live exchange should own.

items.objective: 3.7 Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
items.stem: A university's research-computing team supports several hundred researchers who run Claude Code on the cluster's login nodes, where each researcher signs in through university single sign-on to a personal account. The scheduler's command-line tools for submitting, listing, accounting and cancelling jobs are installed there, enforce per-account quotas and log every action against the account that ran it. An engineer proposes building an MCP server that wraps the scheduler so Claude Code can submit and monitor jobs. The security office requires every cluster action to stay attributable to an individual researcher. Which integration mechanism should the architect recommend?

options.text: Build a remote MCP server over Streamable HTTP that wraps the scheduler under one service account, with OAuth sign-in for each researcher.
Publish the scheduler as an A2A agent that accepts job requests from each researcher's Claude Code session and reports the results back.
Have Claude Code run the existing scheduler CLI under each researcher's own login, with permission rules and a short skill on site conventions.
Upload the job scripts as an Agent Skill through the Claude API so that every researcher's session runs the same tested submission code.

items.explanation: The exam guide's objective lists API/CLI beside MCP and agent-to-agent, and the right mechanism can be the interface that already exists. Claude Code's best-practices guide says CLI tools are the most context-efficient way to interact with external services, and that Claude can learn an unfamiliar CLI from its help output. Here the CLI already runs under each researcher's own account, so quotas, permissions and attribution are enforced by the scheduler, with nothing new to build, host or secure. Permission rules can allow the read-only listing and accounting commands while keeping submissions and cancellations behind an approval prompt, and a skill carries site conventions such as partitions and module loads on demand. An MCP server earns its place when no suitable interface exists or when many hosts outside the cluster need the same tools; neither applies here.

rationales.A: OAuth identifies the researcher to the server, but the scheduler sees only the service account, so attribution is lost unless the server re-implements identity mapping the CLI already provides. It adds a networked service to build, secure and run for no new capability.
rationales.B: A2A connects independent agents across an organisational boundary. The scheduler is a tool inside the researchers' own environment, so a second agent adds a hop and hides who acted without solving anything.
rationales.D: Skills uploaded through the Claude API run in a sandbox with no network access, so the scripts could never reach the scheduler, and Claude Code loads its Skills from the filesystem, plugins or organization provisioning, not from API uploads.

items.objective: 3.7 Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
items.stem: An online fashion retailer's merchandising tool calls the Claude Messages API and wants Claude to use the company's promotions MCP server, which requires OAuth and today runs as a stdio process on the application host. Merchandisers also want the server's MCP prompt templates for campaign briefs, and requests from the loyalty desk carry customer data covered by the retailer's zero data retention (ZDR) arrangement. Which THREE design decisions follow? (Select THREE)

options.text: Rely on the MCP connector to run the OAuth flow on first use, then store and refresh the access token on the retailer's behalf.
Pull the prompt templates through the MCP connector by listing them in the mcp_toolset configuration beside the promotion tools.
Move the workload to Amazon Bedrock, whose data-handling terms let the MCP connector run under the retailer's ZDR arrangement.
To use the MCP connector, host the server over Streamable HTTP at a public https URL, since the connector cannot launch a stdio process.
Use a client-side MCP connection with the SDK's MCP helpers for the prompt templates and for loyalty-desk requests under ZDR.
Have the application obtain the OAuth access token, pass it as authorization_token, and refresh it before it expires.

items.explanation: The MCP connector lets the Messages API call a remote MCP server without the developer writing an MCP client, but each of the retailer's constraints meets one of its documented limits. The server must be publicly exposed over HTTP (Streamable HTTP or SSE) at an https URL, so the stdio process has to be hosted remotely before the connector can reach it. Only MCP tool calls are supported, and the feature is not ZDR-eligible, so the prompt templates and the ZDR-covered traffic need the application's own MCP client; the SDKs' client-side MCP helpers exist for local servers, prompts and resources. The connector does not perform OAuth: the API consumer obtains the token, passes it as authorization_token and refreshes it as needed.

rationales.A: The documentation puts the OAuth flow and token refresh on the API consumer; the connector only forwards the token it is given.
rationales.B: Only tool calls are supported through the connector. MCP prompts and resources are not, so the templates need a client-side connection.
rationales.C: The MCP connector is not available on Amazon Bedrock at all, so the move would lose the very feature it was meant to keep.

items.objective: 3.8 Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
items.stem: A telehealth provider's symptom-intake agent has six small tools (find patient, check allergies, record symptoms, triage score, book slot, notify clinician), about 2,000 tokens of definitions in total, and nearly every conversation uses all six. Its first-response latency target is tight. A platform engineer proposes moving all six behind the tool search tool with defer_loading, 'to follow best practice'. What should the architect decide?

options.text: Keep all six tools loaded up front, because with a few small tools used on every call a search step adds latency and saves little context.
Adopt tool search for all six tools, since deferring definitions always lowers latency by shrinking what Claude must read on every call.
Adopt tool search but leave the triage tool non-deferred, so the most safety-critical tool is always visible and the rest load on demand.
Merge the six tools into one tool with an action parameter, then defer that one tool behind tool search to minimise baseline context.

items.explanation: Progressive discovery pays off when definitions crowd the context or selection accuracy falls as a library grows. Anthropic's tool search documentation says standard tool calling is a better fit when you have fewer than 10 tools or every tool is used in every request; both apply here. The context-management guidance also notes that tool search costs an extra lookup step in exchange for a smaller baseline context. With almost nothing to save and a tight latency target, loading all six tools up front is the right strategy. The judgement is to match the strategy to the toolset, not to apply a pattern because it is labelled best practice.

rationales.B: Deferring does not always lower latency: a tool that is needed on almost every call must first be found, adding a step each time, while the context saved on 2,000 tokens is negligible.
rationales.C: Keeping one tool visible still forces searches for the other five that nearly every conversation needs, adding lookups to most turns for no meaningful saving.
rationales.D: Consolidation can reduce selection ambiguity, but deferring the agent's only working tool means every conversation starts with a search for it; it adds latency to save almost nothing.

items.objective: 3.8 Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
items.stem: A SaaS company's pull-request review agent on the Claude API checks every diff against the company's secure-coding standard: about 18,000 tokens, revised once a quarter, with rules that interact (a logging rule changes what the PII rule allows). The current design retrieves the four sections of the standard most similar to each diff. In the eval, 22% of missed findings trace to a rule that applied but was not retrieved, usually one triggered by an interaction rather than by the diff's wording. The agent reviews about 3,000 diffs a day, and the largest diff plus the full standard fits in the window with ample room. Which context strategy is BEST?

options.text: Keep retrieval, raise it from four sections to eight, and re-run the eval every week for a quarter before deciding whether to change the design.
Package each section of the standard as an Agent Skill with a precise description, so only the sections a diff triggers load into context.
Load the full standard into the system prompt on every review, with a cache breakpoint after it, and retire retrieval for the standard.
Keep retrieval but move reviews to the most capable model tier, so that it can infer the interacting rules from the sections it is shown.

items.explanation: Progressive discovery pays off when most of a large body of context is irrelevant to each request. This standard is the opposite case: small enough to fit with room to spare, stable for a quarter, and relevant to every review as a whole, because its rules interact. Claude Code's documentation draws the same line between always-loaded context, for rules that should always apply, and on-demand skills, for reference needed only sometimes. Any retrieve-or-trigger scheme decides from the diff's wording which rules to show, and the eval shows that is exactly where the misses come from. Loading the whole standard removes that failure; as a stable prefix sent 3,000 times a day it is what prompt caching is for, and a quarterly revision simply starts a new cache. The evidence is already in hand, so further delay only keeps a known miss source in production.

rationales.A: Doubling k still picks sections by similarity to the diff, the mechanism the eval shows missing interaction-triggered rules. A quarter of weekly reruns keeps a known 22% miss source live while confirming what the eval already says.
rationales.B: Skills load when a request matches their description, so a rule triggered by an interaction rather than the diff's wording would still fail to load. It is progressive discovery applied to content every review needs.
rationales.D: No model can apply a rule it is never shown. A stronger tier raises the cost of 3,000 daily reviews without putting the missing rules into context.

items.objective: 3.8 Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
items.stem: A school district's teacher-support assistant runs on the Claude API with code execution enabled. Its system prompt carries 35 procedure guides (grading rubrics, accommodation plans, report-card steps) of about 3,500 tokens each, over 120,000 tokens per request. A typical request needs one or two guides, and several guides include a Python script that calculates grades. Which context strategy fits best?

options.text: Keep all 35 guides in the system prompt but add a cache breakpoint after them, which removes both their cost and their effect on the context window.
Package each guide as an Agent Skill with a precise what-and-when description, so only metadata loads up front and bodies and scripts load on demand.
Merge the 35 guides into one condensed 20,000-token digest written by Claude, and load that digest into the system prompt on every single request.
Move the guides from the system prompt into the user turn, so that Claude treats them as reference material rather than as standing instructions.

items.explanation: Agent Skills are Anthropic's progressive-disclosure mechanism for instructions. Level 1 metadata (a name and description, about 100 tokens per Skill) is always loaded; the SKILL.md body loads only when a request triggers it; bundled files cost nothing until read; and scripts run through bash, so only their output enters context. The description must say what the Skill does and when to use it, because that is what triggering matches on. On the API, Skills need the code execution tool, which this deployment already has. That keeps the baseline small while every guide stays one trigger away.

rationales.A: Caching cuts the price of a repeated prefix, but cached tokens still occupy the window, so 120,000 tokens of mostly irrelevant guidance still dilutes attention on every request.
rationales.C: A lossy digest drops the exact rubric wording and steps teachers rely on, and it still loads all guidance on every request; it is still monolithic, only smaller and less accurate.
rationales.D: Moving the same 120,000 tokens to a different turn does not change how many tokens are in context; it does nothing about cost or context rot.

items.objective: 3.8 Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
items.stem: A private-credit fund's diligence assistant answers analysts' questions about a deal data room of about 600,000 tokens: loan agreements, financial statements and covenant schedules. Because the chosen model has a 1M-token window, a team lead proposes loading the entire data room into every request and caching it. Analysts' questions typically need two to five specific documents and exact figures. Which recommendation is best supported?

options.text: Give the agent a document index and retrieval tools to fetch needed documents just in time, as accuracy and recall degrade as context grows.
Adopt the full load: caching the 600,000-token prefix makes repeat questions cheap and lets Claude cross-reference any document in the room.
Have Claude write a 40,000-token summary of the data room once, and load that summary into every request in place of the source documents.
Adopt the full load but move to the most capable model tier, whose stronger long-context reasoning makes up for the sheer volume of the input.

items.explanation: A window that can hold the data room does not mean it should. Anthropic's context-window documentation warns that as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade (context rot), so curating what is in context matters as much as window size; caching changes the price of repeated tokens, not whether they count. When each question needs a handful of documents and exact figures, the stronger design keeps lightweight references in context and retrieves the specific documents just in time, the same principle tool search applies to tool definitions. Monolithic loading suits small, stable, always-relevant context, which this is not.

rationales.B: Caching lowers the price of the repeated prefix, but all 600,000 tokens still compete for attention on every question. With two to five documents relevant and exact figures required, context rot makes the full load the less accurate design despite the cross-referencing it allows.
rationales.C: A one-off summary loses the exact covenant thresholds and figures analysts need, and it goes stale as the data room changes; it trades precision for size.
rationales.D: A larger model does not remove the degradation that comes with very long inputs, and it raises the cost of every request; it is a model-tier answer to a context-strategy problem.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (CCAR-P Prep Course)

items.objective: 3.8 Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
items.stem: A brokerage's trading-desk assistant uses tool search over about 400 tools from market-data, research, compliance and back-office systems, with almost every tool deferred. Tool names follow internal system codes such as 'mdx_l2snap', and traders phrase requests in desk shorthand. In the eval, the built-in BM25 search misses the right tool on 15% of requests even after descriptions were rewritten with desk keywords; 3,000 logged trader requests, each labelled with the tool used, are available. Order-entry tools are used on nearly every request, and an order-entry latency SLO applies during market hours. Which TWO design decisions should the architect make? (Select TWO)

options.text: Switch to the regex variant, so that Claude can write patterns that match the internal system codes used in tool names exactly.
Keep the order-entry tools non-deferred, so placing, amending and cancelling orders never waits on a search step in market hours.
Build a custom search tool over embeddings of tool descriptions and logged trader requests, returning tool_reference blocks.
Defer the order-entry tools as well and raise the search limit, so that each search loads more candidates and misses fewer tools.
Have the custom search tool return matching tool definitions as JSON text in its result, so Claude can read each schema and call it.
Load all 400 tools up front during market hours, and enable tool search only after the close, when latency matters less.

items.explanation: There are two separate problems. Discovery quality: both built-in variants match against tool names, descriptions and argument text (BM25 by natural-language query, regex by pattern), so when desk shorthand shares few words with system-code names, rewritten descriptions still leave a gap. Anthropic's tool search documentation supports a custom client-side search: your own tool runs any logic, such as embedding-based retrieval, and returns tool_reference blocks in a standard tool_result, which the API expands into full definitions of tools that are still supplied in the tools array, normally deferred. The labelled request log is the data to build and evaluate it. Latency: a tool needed on almost every request should not wait on a search, and the docs advise keeping the 3-5 most frequently used tools non-deferred, which here are the order-entry tools under the SLO.

rationales.A: Regex is still literal matching over the same names and descriptions. Claude would have to guess the system codes, which is exactly what trader shorthand does not reveal.
rationales.D: Deferring order-entry tools puts a search step in front of almost every order, against the SLO, and a larger limit only loads more candidates into context without ranking them better.
rationales.E: A custom search must return tool_reference blocks in a standard tool_result, which the API expands into loaded tools. Schemas pasted as JSON text are only text and do not load the deferred tools.
rationales.F: Loading 400 definitions up front is the case tool search exists to avoid: the docs note selection accuracy degrades past 30-50 tools, so market hours would get the least accurate selection when stakes are highest.

items.objective: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
items.stem: A retail bank is replacing keyword rules with Claude to route incoming card-dispute emails into one of nine dispute categories. The product owner's draft success criterion reads: 'The classifier should be highly accurate.' Before any prompt work begins, the architect must turn this into a criterion the team can test against and that the bank's operations and finance leads will accept. Which criterion best meets that need?

options.text: Reach the highest accuracy that the most capable model can achieve, then decide afterwards whether its latency and cost are acceptable to operations.
Score at least 95% exact-match accuracy on the 60 dispute emails the operations team chose as the clearest examples of each of the nine categories.
Dispute agents rate the routing acceptable or better in a monthly survey, and the prompt is revised whenever that rating drops below target.
On a held-out set of real dispute emails: F1 of at least 0.90, fraud-queue misroutes under 1%, 95% routed in 3 s, cost per email within budget.

items.explanation: Anthropic's success-criteria guidance asks for criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and notes that most use cases need multidimensional evaluation: its own worked example sets an F1 floor, a safety rate, an error-severity split and a latency percentile together on a held-out set. A good criterion therefore names each dimension the sponsors care about (task fidelity, the costly error, latency, price) with a number and a representative test set, so that it can gate later changes.

rationales.A: Not specific or achievable as a target: 'highest possible' has no threshold, and leaving latency and cost to after the fact ignores two documented success criteria the operations and finance leads must sign.
rationales.B: Measurable but one-dimensional, and the set of hand-picked clearest examples does not mirror the real email distribution or its edge cases, so passing it says little about production.
rationales.C: A lagging, subjective signal that cannot gate a change before release; it has no defined threshold per dimension and says nothing about cost, latency or the costly misroute.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
items.stem: A hospital group is launching a patient-portal assistant that answers questions about a patient's own upcoming appointments and bills, reading the patient's record through a read-only tool. The compliance officer wants evidence on HIPAA exposure, the operations director has a 4-second p95 response target, and finance has fixed a monthly budget. Which THREE metric definitions belong in the evaluation scorecard alongside answer accuracy? (Select THREE)

options.text: Mean latency of the model call alone, excluding the record lookup, compared against the operations director's 4-second target
Rate of replies matching a regex for SSNs and phone numbers, reported to the compliance officer as the PHI exposure rate
Rate of replies containing PHI that does not belong to the requesting patient, scored by a binary grader on a held-out set
95th-percentile end-to-end response time, including the record lookup, measured against the 4-second target
Cost per answered conversation, including tool calls and retries, compared with the monthly budget at forecast volume
Cost per API call at list price, excluding tool calls and retries, multiplied by forecast call volume for the budget

items.explanation: Each stakeholder concern needs a metric whose definition actually measures it. For privacy, Anthropic's success-criteria guidance uses a binary LLM classifier asking whether an output contains PHI; here the harm is another patient's PHI, so the grader must judge whose data a reply discloses. Latency must be the percentile the target names, measured end to end as the patient experiences it, and cost must be per answered conversation with every call, tool use and retry counted. Each wrong option names the right dimension but defines it so that it misses the real exposure, delay or spend.

rationales.A: Wrong statistic and wrong scope: a mean hides the slow tail that a p95 target is about, and leaving out the record lookup measures less than the patient waits.
rationales.B: A pattern match catches only a few identifier formats and cannot tell the patient's own data from someone else's; most PHI (names, diagnoses, balances) passes unseen.
rationales.F: Per-call list price leaves out tool calls and retries, which are part of every conversation's real cost, so the forecast undershoots the budget.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
items.stem: An online marketplace uses a Claude agent to answer shopper questions. The agent reads seller-written product listings through a search tool, and any seller can edit their listing text at any time. The current dashboard tracks thumbs-up rate, toxicity rate and p95 latency. The CISO asks for a metric that shows whether the agent is secure against the marketplace's main threat. Which metric should the architect add?

options.text: Jailbreak success rate on a red-team set of hostile shopper chat messages, re-run each release and tracked against a falling target
Toxicity rate of replies on sampled live traffic, measured each week, with the classifier threshold tightened to 0.1% for the CISO
Success rate of instructions planted in seeded test listings, re-run per release, with sampled live replies checked for injection
Weekly count of requests blocked by the web application firewall at the chat endpoint, checked against the security incident log

items.explanation: The threat here is indirect prompt injection: seller-controlled text reaches the agent through a tool result. Anthropic's guidance separates that threat model from jailbreaks and direct injection, where the user is the adversary, and for indirect injection it says to red-team the agent before deployment with documents and tool outputs that contain injection attempts, and to analyze outputs regularly for signs of successful injection. A security metric must therefore measure attack success through the listing channel on a seeded test set at each release, backed by review of sampled live replies, rather than measure the chat channel, toxicity or perimeter activity.

rationales.A: Measures the direct channel, where the shopper is the adversary. The marketplace's main threat is text a seller plants in a listing that the search tool returns; an agent can resist every typed jailbreak and still follow an instruction hidden in a listing.
rationales.B: Toxicity is a safety metric, not a security one. An injected instruction that, say, steers shoppers to a rival seller is not toxic and would pass this check however tight the threshold.
rationales.D: The injection arrives inside listing text fetched by the agent's own tool, not through the chat endpoint, so the firewall count measures the wrong layer, and the incident log records only attacks someone already noticed.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
items.stem: A state benefits agency uses Claude to draft plain-language letters explaining eligibility decisions for a food-assistance program; caseworkers review a sample before mailing. In the pilot, 97% of drafts were judged correct. The legal team notes that a draft wrongly telling an eligible household it is ineligible can deter a valid appeal, while most other errors are awkward wording a caseworker fixes in seconds. How should the architect define the accuracy metric for production sign-off?

options.text: Raise the single accuracy target from 97% to 99.5%, so that the overall error rate becomes low enough to cover the serious errors as well
Keep overall accuracy, but classify every error by severity and set a separate, much tighter threshold on drafts that wrongly deny eligibility
Have caseworkers review every draft before mailing, and replace the accuracy metric with the share of drafts approved without any edits
Track accuracy alongside a reading-level score for each letter, because unclear wording is the most frequent error that the pilot found

items.explanation: A single accuracy number blends errors of very different cost. Anthropic's worked success-criteria example includes an error-severity criterion (a share of errors that cause inconvenience rather than egregious harm) next to the headline score, which is exactly the structure this agency needs: overall accuracy for routine quality, plus a separately measured, much stricter threshold for the error type that harms applicants and creates legal exposure.

rationales.A: A higher blended target still lets a small number of wrongful-denial drafts hide inside the average; the metric never tells legal how often the harmful error occurs.
rationales.C: Full human review is a compensating control, not a metric, and approval-without-edits still lumps a wording fix together with a wrongful denial.
rationales.D: Readability targets the most frequent error, not the most harmful one; the severity problem the legal team raised is left unmeasured.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations
Claude Certified Architect - Professional Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
items.stem: A software company's Claude pull-request reviewer first fetches the diff and related files, then streams its comments into the PR page as they are generated. Engineers say a review feels broken if nothing appears within a few seconds, and team leads need the complete review well before the daily merge window. How should the architect define the latency metric for the eval suite?

options.text: Mean latency of the model call for each review, averaged over the whole eval set and compared with a single target for review time
p95 latency of the model call alone, excluding the diff fetch, since retrieval time belongs to the platform team
p95 time to first streamed token and p95 total completion time, each measured end to end including the diff fetch
Output tokens per review as a proxy for latency, since generation time grows with the number of tokens produced

items.explanation: Anthropic's latency guidance distinguishes overall latency from time to first token (TTFT), which it calls particularly relevant when responses are streamed for a responsive user experience. This reviewer has two latency requirements: engineers judge responsiveness by when the first comment appears, and team leads need the whole review in time. Two percentile metrics, measured end to end as users experience them, cover both; a single average or a model-only timing hides the tail and the time spent fetching the diff.

rationales.A: A mean over the eval set hides the slow tail that makes reviews feel broken, and one total-time figure ignores the first-token wait engineers actually notice.
rationales.B: Excluding the diff fetch measures less than engineers wait; on large PRs the fetch can dominate, and users experience the whole delay whoever owns it.
rationales.D: Token count is a cost and length driver, not a latency measure; it ignores retrieval time, queueing and the first-token wait, and cannot be checked against a time target.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
items.stem: A school district is launching a Claude study assistant for students aged 13 to 18. The safeguarding lead wants a safety metric for launch sign-off. Teachers report the opposite failure from the pilot: the assistant declined to help with set work on the Holocaust, drug-education units and sexual-health lessons. The vendor's draft scorecard has one safety number, the share of outputs a content classifier flags as harmful across 5,000 randomly sampled pilot conversations. Which safety metric definition should the architect require?

options.text: Harmful-output rate on the 5,000 sampled pilot conversations, with the classifier threshold tightened until none of them is flagged
Refusal rate on legitimate sensitive-topic coursework, with a harmful-output measure added once teachers' complaints are resolved
Harmful-reply rate on a red-team set of risky student prompts, paired with a refusal rate on legitimate sensitive coursework
Harmful-reply rate on a red-team set of risky student prompts, with every refusal scored as a pass so that caution is rewarded

items.explanation: Safety fails in two directions here, and the metric must see both. Anthropic's success-criteria guidance states a safety criterion as a flagged-output rate over a stated number of trials, and lists poor or harmful user input among the edge cases an eval must include; random pilot traffic holds few such prompts, so a red-team set is needed to measure the harmful side. The Responsible AI prep course frames the architect's safety question as including the controls that stop Claude from refusing a valid request, so wrongful refusals of set coursework are a safety outcome to measure as well. Reporting the two rates together shows whether tightening one pushes the other out of bounds.

rationales.A: One-sided and on the wrong set: random pilot traffic holds few risky prompts, and tightening the classifier until nothing is flagged pushes the system toward the over-refusal teachers already report.
rationales.B: Measures the teachers' complaint but defers the safeguarding lead's; a launch sign-off with no harmful-reply measure leaves the main child-safety risk unmeasured.
rationales.D: Uses the right risky prompts but scores every refusal as a pass, so an assistant that refused all sensitive topics would score perfectly while failing the curriculum.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations
Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects (CCAR-P Prep Course)

items.objective: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
items.stem: A hospital's clinical-coding team is testing a Claude assistant that reads an inpatient note and returns the single principal diagnosis code as structured output. Coders have labeled 2,000 historical notes with the correct code. Which grading method should the eval use for this criterion?

options.text: An LLM grader that rates each suggested code from 1 to 5 for clinical appropriateness, using a rubric written by the senior coders
ROUGE-L overlap between the code description Claude returns and the description of the labeled code, with a pass mark of 0.8
A code-based exact-match check of the returned code against the labeled code, run automatically on all 2,000 notes at each change
Two certified coders independently review a stratified 200-note sample at each change, since coding errors carry billing and audit risk

items.explanation: Anthropic's eval guidance matches the grader to the criterion. When the output is categorical and a labeled answer exists, code-based grading (exact match) is the documented choice: it is deterministic, fast and cheap, so it can run on the whole labeled set on every change. Model-based and human grading are reserved for criteria that cannot be checked deterministically, such as tone or faithfulness.

rationales.A: An LLM grader adds cost and non-determinism to a question that has one right answer; a Likert score also blurs right and wrong into a scale.
rationales.B: ROUGE-L suits summary relevance; similar code descriptions can score highly even when the code itself is wrong, which is a billing error.
rationales.D: A stratified human sample is slow and costly and covers a tenth of the labeled set; with a labeled answer already available for every note, a deterministic exact-match check covers all 2,000 at each change, and coder time is better spent on criteria code cannot judge.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations
Building with the Claude API (Anthropic Academy)

items.objective: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
items.stem: A wealth-management firm built the eval for its Claude client-letter generator from 40 examples that senior advisers picked as showcases of good letters; each is hand-graded by an adviser. The prompt now scores 39/40, yet compliance keeps finding letters in production that omit required risk disclosures for unusual products. How should the architect redesign the evaluation dataset?

options.text: Keep the 40 showcase cases and have three advisers grade each one independently, so that every score is more reliable and better calibrated
Generate ten paraphrases of each of the 40 showcase cases, giving 400 cases that keep the original adviser grades and the same product coverage
Build several hundred cases that mirror the real mix of client requests, including rare products and messy inputs, graded mostly by automation
Replace the set with only the letters compliance has flagged, so that every case in the suite targets a failure the firm has already seen

items.explanation: Anthropic's eval principles are to be task-specific (mirror the real task distribution, including edge cases), to automate grading where possible, and to prioritize volume over quality: more cases with slightly lower-signal automated grading beat a few hand-graded showcases. Here a code check can confirm that the required disclosure text is present for each product type, and a rubric-based model grader can score the rest, so the larger set stays cheap to run on every change.

rationales.A: More graders per case improves the reliability of each score but not coverage; the rare products that cause the compliance failures are still absent.
rationales.B: Paraphrases inflate the count without adding new products or input types, so the suite still never exercises the unusual products.
rationales.D: A failures-only set is a useful regression slice but no longer reflects the real distribution, so it cannot show whether a fix breaks the common cases.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
items.stem: A national tax agency uses Claude to draft replies to taxpayer correspondence. The team's LLM grader runs on the same model and settings as the drafter and uses the prompt 'Is this reply good? Give a score from 1 to 10, then explain.' It passes 98% of drafts, but when tax officers blind-review 150 of the same drafts they reject 21% for citing the wrong rule. Officers can review about 150 drafts a month, and the eval must run on every prompt change across roughly 600 drafts. What is the most effective fix to the evaluation?

options.text: Use a different grader model with a rubric and examples that check the cited rule, have it reason before scoring, and calibrate it on officers' labels
Grow the eval set from 600 to 6,000 drafts, so that the grader's pass rate becomes statistically tighter and far easier to defend to the agency's auditors
Drop the LLM grader and have tax officers grade every draft by hand, since they are the reviewers who caught the wrong-rule citations
Raise the grader's pass mark from 6 to 9 out of 10, so that only the drafts the grader is highly confident about are counted as passing

items.explanation: The grader disagrees with experts because of how it is built, not because the sample is small. Anthropic's LLM-grader guidance is specific: use a detailed rubric with examples and empirical criteria, have the grader reason before it scores, and use a different model from the one being evaluated. The officers' 150 blind labels are then the calibration set that shows whether the rebuilt grader agrees with experts before it is trusted at scale.

rationales.B: More volume makes a biased measurement more precise, not more accurate; the grader would still miss wrong-rule citations at the same rate.
rationales.C: Officers can review about 150 drafts a month, but the eval must cover 600 drafts on every prompt change; hand grading cannot keep pace, so their labels are better spent calibrating an automated grader.
rationales.D: Rejects more drafts overall without targeting the wrong-rule citations, because the grader still has no criterion for them.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations
Building with the Claude API (Anthropic Academy)

items.objective: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
items.stem: A home-improvement retailer is building the eval dataset for a Claude assistant that answers returns and refunds questions in chat. It already has 1,500 real customer questions sampled from last year's transcripts. Which THREE additions make the dataset a better test of production behavior? (Select THREE)

options.text: Cases where store managers disagree on the right outcome, labeled with the set of acceptable answers rather than with one answer
Very long or abusive messages, including attempts to talk the assistant into approving a refund that falls outside policy
Cases copied from the few-shot examples in the system prompt, so that the suite confirms those examples are being followed
Cases limited to the 100 most frequent questions, since they represent most of the traffic and so most of the business value
Cases whose expected answers were written by the assistant under test, then accepted by the team without any further review
Questions about orders, products or policies that do not exist, and requests that have nothing to do with returns at all

items.explanation: A sampled set mirrors the common distribution, but Anthropic's eval guidance also lists the edge cases that production will send: irrelevant or nonexistent input, overly long input, poor or harmful user input, and ambiguous cases where even humans disagree. Ambiguous cases need labels that allow every acceptable answer, or the grader will punish defensible outputs. Cases that leak from the prompt or the model under test make the suite look better without measuring anything new.

rationales.C: Few-shot examples are already in the prompt, so testing them measures memorization and inflates scores; eval cases should be held out from the prompt.
rationales.D: Narrowing to the most frequent questions removes the tail and the edge cases where real failures occur; the sampled 1,500 already cover the common cases.
rationales.E: Expected answers written by the system under test bake its own mistakes into the key, so the suite can never catch them.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
items.stem: A developer-tools company runs a Claude coding agent in its product. Today the eval suite runs only when the team upgrades to a new model. Last month an engineer added a one-line system-prompt instruction to keep responses brief; support tickets about weaker code fixes rose for three weeks before anyone linked them to the edit. What eval workflow change should the architect make?

options.text: Run the automated suite as a required gate on every change to the prompt, model or effort setting, and block the release on a regression
Keep the model-upgrade gate, and require a second engineer to approve every system prompt edit through code review before it is able to ship
Move the suite to a monthly schedule against production, so that slow regressions from any source are caught within a few weeks
Add a dashboard of support-ticket volume with an alert threshold, and treat a ticket spike as the trigger to run the eval suite

items.explanation: The prep course expects evals to be the gating mechanism for any change to a production system, not only for model swaps. In Anthropic's April 2026 Claude Code postmortem, a length-limit instruction passed the evals that were run before shipping. Later ablations over a broader set of evaluations showed a 3% drop on one of them, and the committed fix was a broad suite of per-model evals for every system-prompt change, plus ablations, soak periods and gradual rollouts. A small wording change is still a change to system behavior, so the full suite should gate it.

rationales.B: Code review checks the edit but not its effect on quality; a reviewer cannot see a 3% drop that only an eval run reveals.
rationales.C: A monthly schedule still lets a regression ship and sit in production for weeks; the gate belongs before release, on each change.
rationales.D: Ticket volume is a lagging signal that fires only after customers are hurt, which is the three-week delay the company has just experienced.

sources.title: An update on recent Claude Code quality reports

items.objective: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
items.stem: A university research office uses Claude to summarize grant proposals for review panels. Each summary must (1) contain six mandatory headed sections, (2) state no fact that is not in the proposal, and (3) read clearly for non-specialists. The office has about 4 hours of reviewer time a week for evaluation and runs 1,200 summaries per eval cycle. Which test framework fits these constraints best?

options.text: Check sections in code, grade faithfulness and clarity with rubric-based LLM graders, and spend reviewer hours calibrating those graders
Have reviewers hand-grade all three criteria on a 60-summary sample each week, since only people can judge faithfulness reliably
Use one LLM grader with a single rubric covering all three criteria on every summary, so the framework stays simple to maintain
Check sections in code, and score faithfulness and clarity by ROUGE-L overlap with reference summaries written by reviewers

items.explanation: A mixed-methodology framework assigns each criterion the cheapest grader that measures it well. Section presence is deterministic, so code grades it at no cost. Faithfulness and clarity are judgments, so rubric-based LLM graders score them at the volume the cycle needs. Scarce human time is spent where it adds most: labeling a sample to calibrate and spot-check the model graders, rather than grading everything or nothing.

rationales.B: Human grading on 60 of 1,200 summaries gives low coverage and slow feedback, and it wastes reviewer time on section checks that code can do exactly.
rationales.C: One grader for everything makes a deterministic check non-deterministic and blurs three separate scores into one, so failures are hard to localize; it also has no human calibration.
rationales.D: ROUGE-L measures word overlap with a reference, not faithfulness to the source; a summary can overlap well and still add facts, and reviewers would have to write 1,200 references.

sources.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

items.objective: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
items.stem: A card issuer is testing a new prompt for the Claude assistant that explains declined transactions to customers. Before the runs, the team set a practical margin of 2 points on its 0-100 explanation-quality score and agreed with finance that a gain beyond that margin is worth up to 1.5 times the current cost per call. On the eval set the new prompt scores 3.4 points higher, with a 95% interval from 2.3 to 4.5 higher, and it costs 1.3 times as much per call. What is the right reading of the result?

options.text: Treat it as inconclusive until a second run on a fresh sample reproduces the gain, since one eval run cannot settle a cost decision
Adopt the new prompt: the whole interval is above the 2-point margin, and 1.3x cost is within the 1.5x ceiling agreed in advance
Route half of traffic to each prompt permanently, which keeps part of the gain while paying only half of the extra running cost
Raise the margin to 4 points and re-run, since a gain that large would make the 30% cost increase much easier to defend to finance

items.explanation: Anthropic's cost-and-intelligence guidance judges a change by its 95% interval against a margin fixed before the runs: a change counts as inside the margin only when its whole interval stays within the limit, and a difference whose interval includes zero is unclear. Here the whole interval, 2.3 to 4.5 points higher, lies above both zero and the 2-point margin, so the gain is real and larger than the margin, and the team agreed the cost trade-off before seeing any data. The pre-set decision rule is met; reading a result without overclaiming also means not underclaiming it by withholding a decision or moving the bar afterwards.

rationales.A: The 95% interval already accounts for sampling noise in this run, and the decision rule was set before the data; demanding a repeat after a clear pass moves the bar and delays a gain the team has already priced.
rationales.C: A permanent split is not a decision; it pays extra on half the traffic for a gain already shown and leaves customers with inconsistent explanations.
rationales.D: Changing the margin after seeing the result is the after-the-fact bar-moving that a pre-set margin exists to prevent, and the cost question was already settled by the agreed ceiling.

items.objective: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
items.stem: A grocery retailer will A/B test a new Claude prompt for its delivery-support chat. The baseline resolution rate is 60% and the team wants to detect an absolute lift of 3 points. The analyst uses the approximation n per arm = 16 x p(1 - p) / d^2 (about 80% power at 5% significance), where p is the baseline rate and d the lift. The chat handles 1,500 conversations a day, split evenly, and the mix of issues and customers differs strongly between weekdays and weekends. How long should the test run?

options.text: About 430 conversations per arm, so under one day of traffic is enough, after which the winning prompt can be rolled out
About 4,270 conversations in total across both arms, so roughly three days at the full 1,500 a day will be enough
Until the dashboard first shows a significant difference at p < 0.05, which usually happens within two or three days
About 4,270 per arm, or about six days at 750 a day per arm, so run one full week to cover the weekday-weekend cycle

items.explanation: Sample size is set before the test from the baseline rate and the smallest lift worth detecting: 16 x 0.6 x 0.4 / 0.03^2 = 3.84 / 0.0009, about 4,270 conversations per arm. At 750 conversations per arm per day that is just under six days, and the run is rounded up to a whole week so the estimate covers the full weekly population, because the effect of the prompt can differ between weekday and weekend customers. The prep course expects the architect to estimate the required sample size and read the result without overclaiming, which also rules out stopping before the planned sample is reached.

rationales.A: Squares d as 0.009 instead of 0.0009 (a decimal slip), understating the sample tenfold; one day also misses the weekly cycle.
rationales.B: The formula gives n per arm, not in total; halving the sample cuts power well below 80%, and three days also misses the weekend.
rationales.C: Stops before the planned sample size, so the 5% error rate no longer holds.

items.objective: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
items.stem: A health system plans an experiment on its Claude tool that summarizes overnight patient messages for triage nurses. The proposed change is a restructured prompt. The draft plan says: 'Hypothesis: the new prompt is better. We will log about 20 metrics and decide afterwards.' What should the architect require before the experiment starts?

options.text: Keep all 20 metrics, and ship the new prompt if any one of them improves significantly, since every metric reflects a real clinical need for nurses
Make all 20 metrics co-primary, and ship the new prompt if the average standardized change across all of them comes out positive
A falsifiable hypothesis, one primary metric, guardrails like missed red-flag symptoms and latency, and a pre-set sample size and decision rule
Fix the primary metric after a one-week pilot shows which metric moved most, then run the formal test on that one metric alone

items.explanation: The prep course expects an experiment plan to set the hypothesis, select metrics and estimate sample size before the run. That means a specific, falsifiable hypothesis (for example, fewer nurse edits per summary), one primary metric chosen in advance from that hypothesis, guardrail metrics that must not get worse (missed urgent or red-flag symptoms, latency, cost), and a sample size and decision rule fixed up front. Choosing metrics after seeing the data, averaging away a clinical loss, or accepting a win on any of many metrics is how experiments overclaim.

rationales.A: With 20 metrics and a ship-if-any rule, at least one will look significant by chance about two times in three at the 5% level if the metrics were independent; correlated metrics lower the figure, but the false-win risk stays high.
rationales.B: An average of standardized changes lets gains on minor metrics mask a loss on the one that matters clinically, such as a missed red-flag symptom, and nothing acts as a guardrail that can block the release.
rationales.D: The primary metric should follow from the hypothesis and the clinical goal, not from whichever of 20 noisy metrics moved most in a pilot; that metric may matter little to triage, and the plan still sets no guardrails.

items.objective: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
items.stem: A data-analytics SaaS vendor's report-writing agent runs on a single model. Offline, on tasks pulled from production logs, a team has shown that an advisor pairing (a smaller executor model that consults a stronger advisor model when it gets stuck) beats the single model's whole score-versus-cost curve across effort levels. Before cutover, how should the architect run the live comparison?

options.text: Cut over all traffic at once; then compare the population's weekly average score and cost for the weeks before and after the switch
Shadow it on a traffic-weighted slice; compare per-task score and cost, watch the consult rate, keep the suite running
Run both setups live and keep the lower blended per-token price; the offline curve has already settled the quality question
Split live traffic evenly between the setups; cut over on the first day the pairing shows a significant score gain, to stop paying sooner

items.explanation: Anthropic's cost-and-intelligence guidance ends its measurement method with a live step: run the winner in shadow on a traffic slice before cutover, then keep the suite running, on tasks weighted like real traffic and scored with cost per task beside the score. It also names the fragile part of an advisor pairing, the consult rate: an executor whose effort changes can stop detecting that it is stuck, fall to consulting on almost none of its tasks, and then score below the executor alone. The live comparison therefore pairs per-task score and cost on representative traffic, watches the consult rate as a guardrail, and cuts over only when both hold.

rationales.A: A before-and-after comparison of weekly averages confounds the change with shifts in the report mix, and it exposes every customer before any live evidence exists.
rationales.C: The guidance compares models on cost per completed task, not per-token price; a pairing can look cheap per token and still cost more per finished report, and offline wins still need live confirmation.
rationales.D: Cutting over on the first significant day is optional stopping: checking daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates the false-positive rate well above 5%, and the plan never checks whether the executor keeps consulting the advisor in production.

items.objective: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
items.stem: A city government's Claude assistant answers residents' questions about permits and parking. The team has a release that revises the system prompt, adds a new tool and changes the effort level, and offline evals pass. Residents depend on the service, and the CIO wants any change that degrades quality to be caught early and reversed quickly. Which TWO practices should the architect require? (Select TWO)

options.text: Grow the offline eval suite tenfold, and ship the release to all residents at once as soon as the larger suite passes
Use the volume of resident complaints to the call center as the main signal that a release has made the assistant worse
Run ablations that test the prompt edit, the new tool and the effort change separately, to see what each does to the eval
Roll out gradually to a small share of traffic with a soak period, guardrail metrics and a tested, fast path to roll back
Release the three changes on consecutive days to all traffic, so each one has a day of production data before the next ships

items.explanation: Anthropic's April 2026 postmortem traced a quality regression to three separate overlapping changes that internal evals did not initially reproduce; its committed fixes included ablations to understand the impact of each line of the system prompt, a broader eval suite, soak periods and gradual rollouts. Ablating each part of a bundled release tells the team which part moved the metric, and a gradual rollout with guardrail metrics catches what offline evals miss while limiting exposure and keeping rollback fast.

rationales.A: A bigger offline suite helps but still cannot reproduce everything production shows; shipping to every resident at once gives no limited exposure and no staged rollback.
rationales.B: Complaint volume is a lagging signal that fires only after residents are affected, which is what the CIO wants to avoid.
rationales.E: Staggering gives some attribution, but each change still reaches every resident at once, a day of traffic is weak evidence, and there is no guardrail or fast rollback path.

sources.title: An update on recent Claude Code quality reports

items.objective: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
items.stem: An online-learning company uses Claude to generate quiz questions from course readings. Its 500-case eval shows that most failures are questions whose answer is not actually stated in the reading. What is the best next step in the improvement loop?

options.text: Study the failures, make one targeted prompt change, then re-run the full suite to confirm the fix and catch regressions
Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch and test the new version only on the failing cases, to confirm those failures are now fixed
Move straight to the most capable model at maximum effort, since a stronger model should stop drawing on its outside knowledge
Copy the failing cases into the prompt as few-shot examples with corrected answers, then re-run the same eval to confirm the gain

items.explanation: Anthropic's eval guidance frames prompt engineering as a cycle of test cases, iterative testing and refinement, then final validation (develop-tests); the API course covers a typical eval workflow. Changing one targeted thing at a time shows which edit caused the improvement, and re-running the full suite, not just the failing slice, confirms the fix without a regression elsewhere. Here a targeted change might require every answer to be supported by a quoted passage from the reading.

rationales.B: A full rewrite changes many things at once, so a gain cannot be attributed, and testing only the failing cases cannot detect new regressions in cases that used to pass.
rationales.C: Jumping to the largest model is costly and skips the cheap prompt fix that the failure pattern points to; the docs advise choosing models on eval evidence against cost.
rationales.D: Putting eval cases into the prompt contaminates the suite: the score rises because the answers were memorized, not because the behavior improved.
