items.objective: 5.1 Implement guardrails and safety controls
items.stem: A university deploys a Claude tutor for a large introductory statistics course. Two output rules must hold. The tutor must never reveal the text of the instructor's answer key for graded weekly problem sets (the key is a known document the tutor uses to give hints), and it must never send a harassing or demeaning reply to a student. The tutor runs around the clock and the screening must fail closed. Which output-screening design fits these rules?

options.text: Match each reply deterministically against the known answer-key text for the leak rule, use a small model classifier for harassment, and hold the reply if either check errors.
Send each reply to one model-based classifier prompted with both rules, and release the reply automatically if the call times out so students are not left waiting.
Use keyword and regex lists for both rules, since deterministic checks are cheap and auditable, and extend the harassment list whenever a new complaint arrives.
Rely on leak-resistant prompt engineering for the answer key and on the model's safety training for tone, avoiding the latency of a separate screening step.

items.explanation: The prep course asks the architect to choose model-based or deterministic checks per rule so the system fails closed. A leak of a known, fixed text is best caught deterministically: exact or fuzzy matching against the answer key is cheap, precise and auditable. Harassment is semantic and needs a model-based classifier, for which Anthropic recommends a lightweight model with a structured verdict. Failing closed means a reply is held, not released, when either check cannot return a verdict.

rationales.B: Fails open, which the requirement forbids, and uses a probabilistic check for a rule that a deterministic match against known text handles more reliably.
rationales.C: Word lists cannot capture demeaning tone or sarcasm, so the harassment rule would leak through while the list grows. Deterministic checks suit known strings, not meaning.
rationales.D: Anthropic advises leak-resistant prompting only when absolutely necessary because it can degrade the task, and training reduces harmful tone without enforcing a rule. Neither fails closed.

sources.title: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects (CCAR-P Prep Course)

items.objective: 5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
items.stem: A contract research organisation uses Claude to draft the patient safety narratives for a clinical study report, working from each participant's case report forms and source records. The prompt already lets Claude say it does not know, has it extract word-for-word quotes from the records before writing, requires a citation for every clinical statement, and retracts any statement without a supporting quote. The head of pharmacovigilance asks whether these controls now make it safe to submit the narratives to the regulator without sign-off by the study's medical monitor. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: No; these techniques reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, so critical clinical content still needs validation by the medical monitor.
Yes, provided each narrative is also generated three times and released only when all three versions agree; consistent answers rule out hallucination.
Yes; a statement verified against a verbatim quote from the records cannot be a hallucination, so the residual risk is now effectively zero.
No, but only for short records; quote extraction is documented for documents over 20k tokens, so long case files can go out without sign-off.

items.explanation: Anthropic's hallucination guidance lists exactly these techniques (permission to say I don't know, quote extraction, per-claim citations, retraction of unsupported claims, best-of-N comparison) and states that they reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, so critical information must still be validated for high-stakes decisions. A safety narrative submitted to a regulator is such a decision, and knowing that residual limitation is what justifies keeping a qualified physician in the loop.

rationales.B: Best-of-N inconsistency is a signal of hallucination, but agreement is not proof of correctness: the same mistake can be reproduced consistently.
rationales.C: Quotes can be misattributed, taken out of context or paired with a wrong inference, and omissions are not caught by citation checks. The docs explicitly say the risk is reduced, not removed.
rationales.D: Misreads the guidance. The 20k-token figure says when quote extraction is most useful for grounding long documents; it is not a length above which hallucination stops. The residual risk applies at any length, and the docs say critical information must still be validated.

items.objective: 5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
items.stem: A retail bank's card-fraud team uses a top-tier Claude model through the Claude API to turn case notes, chargeback narratives and captured card-testing bot scripts into fraud-pattern write-ups for the analysts who maintain the bank's fraud rules. To stop refusals interrupting analysts, the team turned on server-side fallback (beta) with fallbacks set to 'default'. Since then analysts say that some write-ups use a different section order and house style and sometimes omit the required risk-rating field. The HTTP error dashboard is green, and the nightly eval suite, which sends a curated set of past cases to the primary model, still passes. Which diagnosis and fix should the architect pursue first?

options.text: Peak traffic is hitting rate limits and the retried calls return degraded answers; add exponential backoff with jitter and request a higher rate-limit tier.
Refused requests are now answered by a different fallback model; record which model served each response and evaluate that slice on its own.
Longer case files exhaust the output budget and cut the write-up short; raise max_tokens and split each case file into smaller chunks before drafting.
The model alias moved to a newer snapshot after a deprecation; pin the dated model ID in the client and rerun the eval suite against the pinned version.

items.explanation: Server-side fallback retries a refused request inside the same call on the model Anthropic recommends for the refusal category, and returns one successful response that names the model that answered. Write-ups built from attack scripts are the kind of benign security work that can trip the cyber category, so part of the traffic is now silently served by a different model with different formatting habits. An HTTP error dashboard cannot see this, and an eval suite that only exercises the primary model on cases it does not refuse will keep passing. The architect should log the top-level model field and any fallback_message entry in usage.iterations, alert on the fallback share, and evaluate fallback-served traffic as its own slice, prompting and testing the fallback model explicitly.

rationales.A: Rate limiting returns 429 errors, which the HTTP dashboard would show, and it does not change the structure or style of the responses that do succeed.
rationales.C: A max_tokens stop cuts text off with stop_reason max_tokens; it does not change section order or house style, and long cases in the eval set would fail too.
rationales.D: An alias change would affect every call to the primary model, including the eval suite, so the suite would not stay green while only some production write-ups drifted.

items.objective: 5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
items.stem: A state revenue department runs Claude Enterprise with inference hooks pointing at its DLP server, set to fail closed; the DLP policy denies any prompt containing a Social Security number. A quarterly review of Compliance API records finds several chats in which Claude summarized taxpayer returns that included full SSNs. The hook logs show an allow verdict for each of those requests, with no timeouts, errors or circuit-breaker trips. Staff used the web app, not voice mode, and the Compliance API records show that in each of those chats the return was a scanned paper form, uploaded as an image-only PDF or a phone photo rather than pasted as text. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The DLP server received the system prompt and tool definitions with each turn; the extra length pushed the SSNs past the window its matcher scans.
The scans held the SSNs only as pixels; hooks get attachment metadata and extracted text, never image bytes, so that content went uninspected.
Hooks skip ancillary requests; Claude's summaries were produced as ancillary calls like title generation, so they never reached the DLP server.
The circuit breaker opened quietly at peak load and applied a fail-open setting; those requests went through without reaching the DLP server.

items.explanation: Every control on the request path has a blind spot the next control must cover. Inference hooks receive attachments as metadata plus extracted text and never receive raw file or image bytes, so a scanned form uploaded as an image-only PDF or photo gives the hook no text containing the SSN, and the DLP server returns allow. The allow verdicts and clean failure logs point to a coverage gap, not a failure. Compensating controls might restrict image uploads for this group, OCR uploads before they enter the workflow, or screen the conversation record afterwards through the Compliance API.

rationales.A: System prompts and tool definitions are never sent to the hook, so they cannot have padded the payload the DLP server inspected.
rationales.C: Only ancillary requests such as conversation title generation are skipped. A summary Claude writes in the user's conversation is a governed inference request, and the hook log shows it was evaluated.
rationales.D: The organization set failure handling to block, so a tripped breaker would have blocked requests, and the logs show allow verdicts with no failures or breaker trips.

sources.title: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects (CCAR-P Prep Course)

items.objective: 5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
items.stem: A developer-tools company runs a dependency-audit agent on the Claude Agent SDK in its CI pipeline. The parent session runs in bypassPermissions so the job never stalls, and it spawns subagents that fetch and read the READMEs and changelogs of third-party packages. A nightly Message Batches job then expands each finding into a write-up explaining how the vulnerability could be exploited. Which THREE risks or failure modes should the design explicitly account for? (Select THREE)

options.text: Message Batches drop items that a classifier refuses, so the report would silently have fewer write-ups unless the job compares submitted and returned counts.
CI secrets in the job environment are readable by any Bash call the agent makes, so an injection that succeeds through a README could exfiltrate them.
A package README can carry instructions aimed at the agent, which is an indirect prompt injection arriving through content the agent was told to read.
Legitimate vulnerability-analysis requests can trip the cyber safety classifier and be refused, so the pipeline needs explicit refusal handling.
Classifier refusals will surface as HTTP 5xx errors, so the CI retry policy will resubmit them repeatedly and multiply the token cost of every run.
Fetched READMEs are passed to the auto-mode permission classifier, so hostile text in one can talk that classifier into approving a destructive command.

items.explanation: Three documented failure modes meet in this design. Third-party content the agent reads is the classic indirect-injection channel, and some attempts will succeed. With every tool auto-approved, whatever the job can reach, including secrets in its environment, is inside the blast radius, so the guidance is least privilege: do not give Claude secrets it does not need, sandbox tools and scope permissions narrowly. And benign security work can trigger the cyber refusal category, which arrives as a successful response, including in batch results, that the pipeline must detect rather than silently pass on.

rationales.A: False: a refused request in a Message Batch comes back as a succeeded result with stop_reason refusal, not as a missing item. Counts match; the risk is a refusal that looks like a success.
rationales.E: Classifier refusals return HTTP 200 with stop_reason refusal, not 5xx. The real risk is that retries never fire and the gap goes unnoticed.
rationales.F: This agent runs in bypassPermissions, not auto mode, and in Claude Code auto mode tool results are stripped from the classifier's input precisely so hostile content cannot steer it.

items.objective: 5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
items.stem: An online fashion retailer's Claude shopping assistant has a system prompt that includes the internal markdown schedule, margin floors per brand and the rules for when to offer a discount code. Discount eligibility can be computed by the existing promotions service, so the assistant never needs the margin figures themselves. A competitor posted extracts of that prompt online after coaxing the assistant into revealing it. The team proposes adding several paragraphs of anti-leak instructions and refusal scripts to the prompt. Which risk does the team's proposal overlook, and what should come first?

options.text: It underestimates determined extractors; adopt the anti-leak paragraphs and refusal scripts as proposed, and add more each time a new extraction attempt appears.
It ignores model capability; move to the most capable tier, which keeps instructions confidential, and leave the full margin and markdown detail in the prompt.
The data stays in the prompt, so a leak still exposes it; move margins behind a promotions tool that only says if a code is allowed, and screen outputs.
It ignores repeat attackers; ban any shopper who asks about the assistant's instructions, so that an extraction cannot be retried from the same account.

items.explanation: The proposal treats prompt leakage as a wording problem and overlooks that the commercially sensitive data would still sit in the prompt. Anthropic's prompt-leak guidance warns that leak-resistant prompt engineering adds complexity that can degrade performance elsewhere in the task. The first steps are to keep proprietary details out of the prompt when the task does not need them (here a promotions-service tool can answer whether a code is allowed), monitor and post-process outputs with regex, keyword or model-based filters, and audit prompts and outputs periodically. Data that is not in the prompt cannot leak from it.

rationales.A: This is the trade-off the docs warn about: extra prompt complexity costs task quality, and the margin data stays exposed to the next extraction that gets past the scripts.
rationales.B: A bigger model for a data-exposure problem. No tier guarantees confidentiality, and keeping unneeded commercial data in the prompt keeps the exposure in place.
rationales.D: Accounts are cheap to recreate, and the ban also hits curious legitimate shoppers. It does nothing about the data already sitting in the prompt.

items.objective: 5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
items.stem: A school district's family help line runs Claude with retrieval over the district's policy handbook, which is re-indexed whenever the handbook changes, and answers on topics the handbook covers are accurate. Asked about the state's testing exemptions for home-schooled children, which the handbook does not cover, the assistant confidently described an exemption process the state replaced last month. Retrieval logs for those questions show only loosely related handbook passages, none mentioning exemptions, and the prompt simply tells Claude to use the passages to help parents. What limitation does this reveal, and what should the team do first?

options.text: The handbook index is stale; re-index it nightly and add effective-date metadata so that the newest passages always rank first in retrieval.
The retriever returns too few passages; raise top-k from 5 to 20 so that the model sees enough handbook text to locate the exemption rules.
The model's training data is out of date; move to the most capable tier, whose newer training data will cover the state's revised exemption process.
Retrieval does not stop the model filling gaps from its training data; answer only from cited passages and refer parents to staff when none apply.

items.explanation: Grounding puts current facts into the context, but it does not by itself stop the model answering from its training data when the retrieved passages are silent. Retrieval worked as designed here: it returned nothing about exemptions because the handbook contains nothing, and the prompt never told Claude to stay within the passages, so it filled the gap with the older process it had learned, with full confidence. Anthropic's hallucination guidance names the controls: explicitly restrict Claude to information in the provided documents rather than its general knowledge, give it permission to say it does not know, and have it cite a supporting passage for each claim and retract any claim it cannot support. Routing uncovered questions to staff turns 'I don't know' into a useful answer. These controls reduce rather than eliminate hallucination, so answers still need monitoring.

rationales.A: The handbook is already re-indexed on change, and it holds no exemption content to rank. Freshness metadata helps choose between versions of a document; it cannot supply a topic the corpus lacks.
rationales.B: More passages from a handbook that never mentions exemptions add noise, not the missing rule, and the prompt would still let the model fill the gap from memory.
rationales.C: The process changed last month, after any model's training cutoff, and an answer from memory is unverifiable either way. The gap is in how the system grounds answers, not in model capability.

items.objective: 5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
items.stem: A commercial bank's treasury-operations agent proposes three kinds of action, each with a confidence score: (1) matching ledger entries to bank statements, which a journal entry can reverse; (2) placing a temporary hold on a corporate card after suspected fraud, which the client can lift in the app within minutes; and (3) releasing outbound wire transfers, which cannot be recalled once sent. Operations has four reviewers for about 9,000 proposed actions a day: about 250 wires, 1,000 card holds and 7,750 ledger matches. Which review-routing policy should the architect propose?

options.text: Use one rule for all three action types; auto-execute when confidence is at least 0.9 and send everything below it to the reviewer queue.
Send every action of all three types to a reviewer before it runs; four people reading each item is the only way to be sure nothing goes wrong.
Auto-release wires scoring above 0.97 with sampled QA; review every card hold before it is placed; auto-run all ledger matches unqueued.
Review every wire before release whatever its score; auto-run card holds with sampled QA; auto-run ledger matches, queueing low-confidence ones.

items.explanation: The prep course frames review routing on three factors together: the model's confidence, the reversibility of the action and the cost of a wrong answer. An irreversible, high-cost action (a wire) warrants review regardless of confidence, because a confident error is still unrecoverable. Reversible, low-cost actions can run automatically, with confidence used to pull uncertain items into the queue and sampled QA to catch systematic drift. With about 250 wires a day plus a QA sample and the low-confidence matches, the queue is a few hundred items, which four reviewers can read properly.

rationales.A: Confidence alone ignores reversibility and cost. A high-confidence wrong wire still goes out and cannot be recalled, while reviewers spend time on cheap, reversible ledger items.
rationales.B: Roughly 2,250 items per reviewer per day turns review into rubber-stamping. Effort is spread evenly instead of focused on the irreversible decisions.
rationales.C: It differentiates by action type but inverts the risk: it automates the irreversible, high-cost wire on a confidence score and spends review effort on the card hold a client can lift in minutes.

Claude Certified Architect - Professional Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
items.stem: A hospital pharmacy runs an agent on Claude Managed Agents. Its MCP toolset includes submit_formulary_change, and hospital policy says a pharmacist must review every formulary change before it is submitted. Each tool in a toolset can carry its own permission policy: always_allow, always_ask or auto. To cut approval fatigue, an engineer set the toolset's policy to auto, reasoning that the server will still pause anything risky. What should the architect change?

options.text: Nothing; the auto policy pauses any call the server judges risky, which gives the pharmacists the same checkpoint with far fewer interruptions.
Set the toolset to always_allow and write every call to the audit store, so that the pharmacists can review each change the following morning.
Keep auto, and add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to ask a pharmacist in the chat before it calls submit_formulary_change for any drug.
Set submit_formulary_change to always_ask, so every call pauses the session until a pharmacist explicitly allows or denies that change.

items.explanation: Anthropic's documentation states that the Managed Agents auto policy is not a human checkpoint: calls the server judges safe run before anyone sees them, and their effects may be irreversible. Any tool whose every call a person must review needs always_ask, which can be set per tool. The session then goes idle with stop_reason requires_action, and the reviewer replies with user.tool_confirmation (allow, or deny with an optional message). MCP toolsets default to always_ask for this reason.

rationales.A: This is exactly the misconception the docs correct. Under auto, a change the server judges safe is submitted with no pharmacist ever seeing it.
rationales.B: Review after submission is not review before submission. Audit fields are worth keeping, but the policy requires approval before the change takes effect.
rationales.C: A prompt instruction is not an enforced gate, and under auto a call judged safe still executes. Approval must be enforced by the permission policy.

items.objective: 5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
items.stem: A city council in the EU uses Claude to assess housing-benefit applications. Claude produces an eligibility decision, and a caseworker must click confirm before the letter is sent, so the council treats the process as human-reviewed. An internal audit finds that caseworkers see only the verdict, confirm 99.7% of cases, and spend a median of 15 seconds per case. The data protection officer warns that the process may in practice be a decision based solely on automated processing, noting that EU guidance treats human involvement as meaningful only when the reviewer has the information, authority and competence to change the outcome. Which change best addresses the DPO's concern?

options.text: Show caseworkers the evidence and rationale behind each verdict, give them the authority and time to change it, and track override rates to show review is real.
Add a second caseworker who also clicks confirm on every case, so each automated eligibility decision carries two human approvals before the letter goes out.
Add a notice to each decision letter saying AI assisted the assessment, which gives applicants the transparency the regulation requires for such decisions.
Move the assessment to the most capable model tier and publish its accuracy on a held-out set, so caseworkers can trust the verdicts they are confirming.

items.explanation: GDPR Article 22(1) gives a person the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal or similarly significant effects, and where such decisions are permitted the regulation requires suitable safeguards, which in the contract and consent cases include at least the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision. By the criterion the DPO states, a human step counts only if the reviewer has the information, authority and competence to change the outcome. A confirm button on a bare verdict fails that test. Showing the evidence and rationale, giving caseworkers the authority and time to change the result, and tracking override rates makes the human role real and demonstrable.

rationales.B: Two clicks on a bare verdict still give neither reviewer the information to change the outcome, so the involvement fails the criterion the DPO cites.
rationales.C: Disclosure is a separate transparency obligation and worth doing, but it does not change whether the decision itself is solely automated.
rationales.D: Better accuracy makes caseworkers even more inclined to defer. It improves the model, not the human review that the DPO says is missing.

items.objective: 5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
items.stem: A global online marketplace screens about 2 million new product listings and seller messages a day for prohibited items and abusive content. A trust-and-safety team of 40 reviewers can handle about 15,000 items a day. Listings must be decided within an hour; seller messages can wait until the next morning. Which TWO design choices best fit Anthropic's content-moderation guidance at this volume? (Select TWO)

options.text: Return a single allow-or-block verdict per item and tune one threshold, so reviewers are never needed and the queue cannot back up during sales events.
Run every item on the most capable model tier to maximise accuracy, since moderation errors are costly and price per item matters less than recall.
Use graduated risk levels (allow, allow and monitor, human review, block automatically), sized so the review band fits the team's daily capacity.
Ask for structured JSON with a risk level and explanation, batch seller messages overnight, and track precision and recall of each band on labelled data.
Use the prompt to tell Claude which policy categories to ignore, so usage-policy flags on edge content never interfere with the marketplace's rules.
Send every item flagged at any risk level to the 40 reviewers, because human judgement is needed for any content the model has not cleared outright.

items.explanation: Anthropic's content-moderation guide recommends graduated, confidence-based routing rather than a binary verdict: low risk is allowed, slightly higher risk is monitored, a middle band goes to human review and the highest risk is blocked automatically. That lets the human band be sized to reviewer capacity. It also recommends structured output with an explanation field, batching where real-time decisions are not needed, a fast low-cost model for very high volume, and tracking precision and recall.

rationales.A: A binary verdict removes the human band entirely, so borderline cases are either wrongly blocked or wrongly allowed with no one looking.
rationales.B: At millions of items a day the guide points to the fastest, lowest-cost tier; cost per item matters at this scale, and accuracy is managed through routing and measurement.
rationales.E: The guide warns that Anthropic's usage policy may flag content regardless of prompt instructions, so a prompt cannot switch those flags off.
rationales.F: Any non-zero risk would flood a team that handles 15,000 items a day with a share of 2 million. Review effort must be focused on the band that warrants it.

items.objective: 5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
items.stem: A cloud-hosting company's 150 engineers use Claude Code in Manual mode (config value 'default'), which the platform team pinned in managed settings. Telemetry shows each engineer approves around 180 permission prompts a day, at a median of under one second per approval, and last month an engineer approved a command that force-pushed over a shared release branch. The CTO wants far fewer prompts without weakening protection for production. Which approach best focuses human review where it matters?

options.text: Let reversible local work run via auto mode or allow rules, keep ask or deny rules for deploys, force pushes and IAM, and require PR approval to merge.
Keep Manual mode and run mandatory training on reading every prompt carefully, since each approval is a review and more prompts mean more oversight.
Enable auto mode everywhere and rely on its classifier, which blocks force pushes and production deploys by default, as the only gate for those actions.
Run engineers in bypassPermissions inside dev containers and rely on the container boundary to contain any mistakes the agent makes there.

items.explanation: 180 approvals a day at under a second each is approval fatigue: the human step exists but no judgement happens, as the force push showed. Review effort should follow reversibility and the cost of a wrong action. Reversible local edits can proceed without a prompt, while irreversible shared-state actions (deploys, force pushes, IAM changes) stay behind deterministic ask or deny rules, and a human approves the pull request before merge. Auto mode is a useful model-based filter, but the docs say it is not a replacement for review on sensitive operations.

rationales.B: Training does not fix a volume problem. The telemetry shows prompts are already being approved without reading, so more prompts mean less real oversight.
rationales.C: Auto mode does block those actions by default, but it is a classifier, and Anthropic says it does not guarantee safety and is not a replacement for review on sensitive operations, so it should not be the only gate.
rationales.D: A force push or a deploy goes over the network with the engineer's own credentials, which a container does not contain, and bypassPermissions removes every remaining prompt.

items.objective: 5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
items.stem: A university admissions office wants Claude to help review 12,000 undergraduate applications this cycle, with six admissions officers available. The university's admissions regulations require a named admissions officer to make and sign every admit or deny decision. The vice-provost proposes that Claude score each application, that files with very high or very low confidence be admitted or rejected automatically, and that officers review only the borderline middle. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Keep every decision with an officer, as the regulations require, and have Claude prepare evidence-linked summaries pointing to the facts each turns on.
Adopt the plan, but have a second Claude model independently re-score every automatically decided file, so that each final decision has been checked twice over.
Adopt the plan, but have officers spot-check a random 10% sample of automatic decisions each week, and revise the prompt if error rates start to rise.
Have Claude pre-fill a decision on every file and let officers sign high-confidence files in batches unopened, reserving a full read for the borderline middle.

items.explanation: The prep course frames review routing on confidence, reversibility and the cost of a wrong answer. Here a stated rule settles the routing question: every decision must be made and signed by a named officer, and an admissions decision is high-cost and hard to reverse for the applicant, so no confidence band can be finalized automatically. The architect's job is to make mandatory review feasible: 12,000 files is about 2,000 per officer, and structured, evidence-linked summaries let officers check the basis and decide faster without the model deciding for them.

rationales.B: A second model is not a named officer. Model-on-model checking can be a useful QA signal, but every automatic decision would still be made by a model, which the regulations forbid.
rationales.C: Sampling after the fact means 90% of automatic decisions are finalized with no officer involved, which the regulations do not allow.
rationales.D: A signature on a file the officer never opened means Claude made the decision and the officer only signed it. The regulations require the officer to make the decision, not just sign it.

sources.title: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects (CCAR-P Prep Course)
Claude Certified Architect - Professional Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 5.4 Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
items.stem: A children's hospital drafts radiology report impressions from radiologists' dictated findings with the Claude API, in an organization that has HIPAA readiness enabled under Anthropic's BAA. To debug quality problems, the platform team has connected a hosted LLM-observability service that records every full prompt and response, including the dictated findings, so engineers can replay traces. The vendor offers only its standard SaaS terms. The privacy officer asks whether this is compliant. What should the architect decide?

options.text: It is compliant, because Anthropic's BAA covers every service in the request path once HIPAA readiness is enabled.
It is compliant if the vendor deletes each trace within 24 hours, since short-lived copies of PHI need no BAA.
Hash patient names and record numbers in each trace but keep report text, so traces are de-identified under HIPAA.
Sign a BAA with the vendor before PHI reaches it, or send it only IDs, versions and metrics with no report text.

items.explanation: Anthropic's BAA and HIPAA readiness cover eligible Claude API features. The data-retention documentation lists third-party integrations, meaning data processed by external tools or services connected to your application, as not covered. A service that receives and keeps PHI, here full radiology findings, to analyse traces for the hospital is a business associate under 45 CFR 160.103, and 164.502(e) allows the hospital to disclose PHI to it only with satisfactory assurances documented in a written contract that meets 164.504(e): a BAA with that vendor. The alternative is to keep PHI out of the traces: log request IDs, prompt and model versions, token counts, latency and evaluation scores, and replay a case from the PACS and EHR under existing access controls. That also honours the minimum-necessary standard in 164.502(b). Each component in the request path needs its own compliance-boundary check; one vendor's BAA does not extend to another.

rationales.A: HIPAA readiness covers Anthropic's eligible API features in the enabled organization. The documentation states that data processed by external tools or services connected to the application is not covered, so the observability vendor sits outside Anthropic's BAA.
rationales.B: The business-associate definition turns on creating, receiving, maintaining or transmitting PHI on the covered entity's behalf, not on how long it is kept. A vendor that receives full radiology findings for a day still needs a BAA.
rationales.C: Radiology findings routinely carry dates, ages, places and other identifiers, and a hash of a record number is derived from an identifier, so these traces do not meet Safe Harbor de-identification. They remain PHI.

items.objective: 5.4 Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
items.stem: A Dublin-based retail bank runs its complaint-triage assistant on Claude in Amazon Bedrock, calling the global endpoint from eu-west-1 (Ireland). In its outsourcing register and its GDPR records of processing, the bank has now committed that complaint data is processed only in the Ireland Region. The assistant uses a balanced-tier model that the Bedrock documentation lists as available in eu-west-1 on every endpoint type. Which configuration should the architect specify?

options.text: Keep the global endpoint, because every request enters Bedrock in eu-west-1 and AWS is the processor under its own terms.
Switch to the EU geography inference profile, which keeps processing within EU Regions and adds capacity across them.
Keep the global endpoint and deny every Region except eu-west-1 in a service control policy, so routing stays in Ireland.
Use the eu-west-1 in-region endpoint, accepting the regional price premium and no cross-Region capacity for peaks.

items.explanation: Bedrock offers three residency levels, each with a trade-off. The global endpoint routes dynamically across all available Regions for maximum availability at no premium, so it cannot honour a single-Region commitment. A geography inference profile lets Bedrock pick a Region within the geography, which suits an EU-wide requirement but not one tied to Ireland; for any profile, AWS advises checking the model's destination Regions against the requirement. A regional endpoint resolves to the single Region specified, and eu-west-1 is listed for direct in-region routing. The cost is a regional price premium and the loss of cross-Region capacity, so quotas and peak load must be planned. Model availability is part of the decision: Claude Fable 5.1 regional endpoints, for example, are currently in us-east-1 only, so a residency commitment can constrain the model tier. On Bedrock, AWS rather than Anthropic is the processor, which the records of processing must reflect.

rationales.A: Entering Bedrock in eu-west-1 is not the same as processing there: the global endpoint routes requests dynamically across all available Regions. Who the processor is does not change where inference runs.
rationales.B: This is the right choice for an EU-wide requirement, but the commitment names one Region. A geography profile lets Bedrock route each request to any Region in the profile, so processing can happen outside Ireland.
rationales.C: AWS documents that global cross-Region inference needs a service control policy that allows unspecified Regions, and that blocking a destination Region makes requests fail. An SCP can refuse traffic; it cannot steer global routing to Ireland.

items.objective: 5.4 Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
items.stem: A U.S. federal agency's acquisition office is rolling out Claude Code to its developers through Claude for Government Desktop, which runs in a FedRAMP High-authorized environment. The product records every administrative action in a hash-chained audit log that organization administrators can review in the product. For the agency's authority-to-operate (ATO) package, the assessor needs one compliance-matrix row for this control: privileged administrative changes to the AI platform must be attributable to an individual, tamper-evident, and reviewed by the agency. Which row should the architect submit?

options.text: Control: Anthropic's FedRAMP High authorization. Owner: Anthropic. Evidence: the authorization letter, inherited in full by the agency.
Control: tenant hash-chained admin audit log. Owner: the platform admins. Evidence: a screenshot showing that logging is on.
Control: tenant hash-chained admin audit log, reviewed monthly. Owner: agency ISSO. Evidence: dated review records with log extracts.
Control: SCIM group mappings with dollar caps. Owner: agency IT finance. Evidence: a monthly usage export of metering data by group.

items.explanation: The row needs three things to hold up in an assessment: a mechanism that meets the requirement, an owner who can operate it independently, and evidence that it operated. The hash-chained admin log is the mechanism, because each entry is tied to an individual and tampering breaks the chain. The owner must be an agency security role independent of the administrators whose actions are reviewed, such as the information system security officer, which preserves separation of duties. The evidence must show the control operating over the assessment period: dated review records with the log extracts that were reviewed. FedRAMP's rules say an authorization gives agencies reusable security information but does not replace the agency's own continuous monitoring, so the tenant review is the agency's control to run. Anthropic's two-person approval for sensitive operations on its side is a provider control the agency inherits, not one it operates.

rationales.A: Inheritance covers the provider's controls, such as Anthropic's own two-person approval for sensitive operations, not the agency's tenant administration. An authorization letter shows nothing about who made which admin change in this tenant or whether the agency reviewed it.
rationales.B: The right mechanism with the wrong owner and the wrong evidence. Administrators reviewing their own changes breaks separation of duties, and a screenshot shows that logging is switched on, not that anyone reviewed the entries over the assessment period.
rationales.D: This is a real control, but for a different obligation: spend and rate governance. A metering-only usage export carries no record of individual administrative actions, so it cannot show attribution or tamper evidence.

items.objective: 5.4 Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
items.stem: A help-desk software company runs a Claude support assistant for its own product. Answers are grounded in a vector index of about 60 million chunks taken from past support conversations with EU end users. Each chunk stores its text and embedding but no link back to its source ticket or to the people it mentions. The index is updated incrementally, and a full rebuild takes four days of embedding compute. The company's Claude API organization has a Zero Data Retention arrangement, so Anthropic keeps no prompts or outputs after each response. The company receives about 30 GDPR erasure requests a week. Which design should the architect specify so that erasure reaches every copy of a person's data in the pipeline?

options.text: Delete the person's source tickets only, because an embedding is a vector of numbers from which the person cannot be identified.
Tag each chunk with its source and data-subject IDs, so an erasure deletes the sources and every chunk and embedding made from them.
Keep the index as it is, and add the erased person to a blocklist that filters their name out of retrieved chunks and answers.
Rebuild the whole index from the remaining source tickets after each erasure request, so that no copy derived from them survives.

items.explanation: Article 17(1) GDPR obliges the controller to erase personal data without undue delay when a ground applies, and Article 12(3) sets one month to act on the request. In a retrieval pipeline the personal data is not only in the source tickets: each chunk stores the text itself, and its embedding is derived from that text and retrieved with it. Today nothing links a chunk to its source or to the people it mentions, so the company cannot find what to erase. The fix belongs at ingestion: record lineage (the source ID and the data-subject IDs found in the chunk) as metadata, so an erasure becomes a filtered delete of the sources and their derived chunks and embeddings, followed by a check that a search for the person returns nothing. Because the API runs under ZDR, Anthropic holds no copy of the prompts that carried those chunks, so the erasure scope is the company's own stores: sources, index, logs and any caches it keeps.

rationales.A: The chunk text stored beside each embedding is the personal data itself, and with no lineage nothing removes it when the ticket goes. The assistant could still retrieve the person's details into answers.
rationales.C: Suppression is not erasure: the data stays stored and keeps being processed for retrieval. A name filter also misses the email addresses, account numbers and other details that identify the person.
rationales.D: At about 30 requests a week and four days per rebuild, rebuilds could never keep pace, and re-embedding 60 million chunks to remove a handful is disproportionate when lineage metadata allows a targeted delete.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016 (EUR-Lex)

items.objective: 5.4 Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
items.stem: An online fashion retailer has a Zero Data Retention (ZDR) arrangement for its Claude API organization. To meet GDPR storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), its records of processing state that its AI processor keeps no customer data after each request. Teams are building a returns-fraud agent on customer names, addresses and order histories, and an engineer has already proposed the Message Batches API for overnight scoring. Which TWO controls should the architect put in place so that customer data cannot leave ZDR coverage before anyone notices? (Select TWO)

options.text: Rely on the API to reject any request that uses a non-ZDR-eligible feature, and alert the team on those 400 errors
Add a system-prompt rule telling Claude never to use batches, files or code execution when customer data is present
Add a design-review gate that checks each proposed feature against the ZDR eligibility table before it ships
Send every Claude call through an internal gateway that blocks requests to non-eligible endpoints and features
Obtain Anthropic's written confirmation of the ZDR arrangement each year and file it with the records of processing
Audit the application code every quarter for calls to stateful endpoints, and fix any calls that the audit finds

items.explanation: Under ZDR the API does not block features marked No for ZDR. The documentation calls using one a choice to step outside the arrangement for that data, and the feature's own retention then applies: 29 days for Message Batches, until deletion or expiry for the Files API, up to 30 days for code-execution containers. The retailer's storage-limitation commitment therefore has to be enforced on its own side, before the request is sent. A preventive technical control in the request path (a gateway with an allowlist of eligible endpoints and features) stops the silent step at run time, and a preventive process control (design review against the eligibility table) stops it being designed in, as the proposed overnight batch run would be. Under HIPAA readiness the API does return 400 for non-eligible features, which is why relying on the API is tempting; ZDR behaves differently.

rationales.A: That is how HIPAA readiness behaves, not ZDR. Under ZDR nothing blocks the request, so there is no 400 to alert on and the batch simply runs with 29-day retention.
rationales.B: Batches and the Files API are endpoints the application calls, and code execution is available only when the application includes the tool. A prompt rule cannot stop an engineer from calling a stateful endpoint.
rationales.E: Confirmation shows that the arrangement exists. It says nothing about whether the application is using features that fall outside it.
rationales.F: An audit is detective and periodic: by the time a quarterly audit finds the call, the data sent to the stateful feature has already been retained.

items.objective: 5.4 Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
items.stem: An integrated health system signed Anthropic's BAA and enabled HIPAA readiness on its only Claude API organization, which hosts a clinical-note summarizer that handles PHI. Anthropic's documentation states that HIPAA readiness is enforced for the whole organization and cannot be disabled once enabled. An internal analytics team, which handles no PHI, already has its own workspace in the same organization. The next morning that team starts receiving HTTP 400 errors on every request that uses a beta feature it relies on. Leadership wants one fix that keeps the clinical workload protected and unblocks analytics. What should the architect do?

options.text: Ask Anthropic to list the beta feature as HIPAA-eligible under the BAA, and pause the analytics work until it is approved.
Add Zero Data Retention to the organization, so the beta feature is covered by immediate deletion instead of the BAA.
Move the analytics workload to a separate organization without HIPAA readiness, and keep PHI only in the existing one.
Add a redaction step that strips any PHI from analytics requests, so that the API accepts the beta feature on those calls.

items.explanation: The 400s are the control working as designed. Under HIPAA readiness the API rejects any request that uses a non-eligible feature, and beta features are generally not covered unless the eligibility table lists them; the check is on the feature, regardless of what the request contains. Because enforcement is per organization and permanent, Anthropic's documentation says that HIPAA and non-HIPAA workloads need separate organizations. Moving analytics out unblocks it without weakening the clinical boundary, and it keeps the HIPAA organization's feature set small enough to audit. This is the fail-closed behaviour a regulated boundary should have, so the fix is to change the workload's placement, not to weaken the boundary.

rationales.A: Eligibility is set by Anthropic, and beta features are generally outside the BAA until listed, so this gives analytics no date to resume. It would also widen the PHI organization's feature set to serve a workload that handles no PHI.
rationales.B: HIPAA readiness is an alternative to ZDR, not an addition, and ZDR does not make a non-eligible feature eligible. The 400s would continue.
rationales.D: The API rejects the request because of the feature it uses, not because of the data in it. Redaction is good hygiene but does not change the eligibility check, so the requests would still fail.

items.objective: 5.5 Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
items.stem: A consumer lender in Ireland uses Claude to draft credit-limit decisions for EU applicants, and a credit officer reviews each draft before it is sent. Before launch, the architect must define the explanations the system owes to three audiences: applicants, the regulator, and the engineering team that investigates disputed cases. Which design builds transparency in for all three?

options.text: Applicants get the prompt and the model's reasoning; the regulator gets overall accuracy; engineers get each output and the final decision.
Tell every applicant that AI assisted the decision, and keep complete prompts and outputs so engineers can replay any disputed case.
Have Claude return a plain-language explanation field per decision, and give that one field to applicants, regulator and engineers.
Applicants get the main factors and a way to contest; the regulator gets the DPIA and subgroup results; engineers get a per-case trace.

items.explanation: Each audience needs a different artifact, because each uses the explanation for a different job: to understand and contest, to supervise, or to reproduce a case. Applicants need the main factors in plain language and a way to contest. Where a decision is based solely on automated processing and has significant effects, GDPR makes this a legal duty: meaningful information about the logic involved (Art. 15(1)(h)) and the right to human intervention, to express a view and to contest (Art. 22(3)). Here a credit officer reviews each draft; if that review is meaningful the decision may fall outside Art. 22, but a review that only rubber-stamps drafts would not take it out, and contestable, understandable explanations remain best practice that supports transparency under Arts. 13 to 15 either way. The regulator needs system-level evidence: a DPIA, which Art. 35(3)(a) requires for systematic profiling that drives significant decisions, plus outcome results by subgroup. Engineers need a reproducible per-case trace: inputs, retrieved documents, prompt and model versions, output and the reviewer's action.

rationales.A: Each audience gets something, but the wrong thing. Raw prompts and generated reasoning are not a meaningful, verified account of the decision logic; overall accuracy can hide a disparity between subgroups; and outputs without inputs and versions cannot reproduce a disputed case.
rationales.B: Disclosure is necessary but not sufficient: applicants are owed meaningful information about the logic and a way to contest, and the regulator receives nothing. The replay log serves only the debugging team.
rationales.C: A per-decision explanation helps the applicant, but collapsing all audiences onto it leaves the regulator without system-level fairness evidence and engineers without the trace needed to reproduce and fix a disputed case.

items.objective: 5.5 Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
items.stem: A state benefits agency asks an architect to build a Claude pipeline that reads claimants' public social-media activity and gives each claimant a 'reliability rating' used to prioritize fraud investigations. To avoid tipping off suspected fraudsters, the agency wants the rating scheme kept confidential from claimants. What should the architect do?

options.text: Build it, but run a demographic bias audit on the ratings before launch and repeat that audit every quarter.
Build it, but require an investigator to review each high rating before any case is opened against a claimant.
Pause it until counsel completes a privacy impact assessment, then build the rating exactly as it was specified.
Decline it as specified, and propose a lawful alternative such as summarizing evidence already in claim files.

items.explanation: Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits using its models to assign scores or ratings to individuals based on an assessment of their trustworthiness or social behavior without notification or their consent, and this design is built around not notifying. That is a hard limit: no fairness audit, review step or assessment turns a prohibited use into a permitted one. The architect's ethical responsibility is to recognise the boundary at design time and redirect the sponsor to a scope that serves the real goal, here helping investigators work faster from evidence already lawfully in the claim file, which can then be evaluated for fairness and reviewed like any other high-stakes workflow.

rationales.A: A bias audit measures whether a system treats groups unequally. It cannot make an undisclosed social-behaviour rating acceptable, because the prohibition is about the use itself, not its error rates.
rationales.B: Human review is the right control for many high-stakes decisions, but it does not cure a prohibited use. The claimant is still rated on social behaviour without notification or consent.
rationales.C: Pausing for an assessment looks responsible, but it ends by building the same covert rating. An assessment documents risk; it cannot authorise a use that the provider's policy prohibits.

items.objective: 5.5 Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
items.stem: A large urban school district deploys a Claude writing-feedback assistant for students aged 11 to 16; about 30% of the students are English learners. The design has a retrieval index of model essays and rubric exemplars, a rubric prompt that scores 'clarity and conventions', and a confidence threshold below which an essay is queued for a teacher, with a typical 3-day wait. Which THREE are points where unequal outcomes between student groups could arise and should be measured per subgroup? (Select THREE)

options.text: A weekly dashboard that reports English learners' average scores separately from the scores of all other students
A glossary of rubric terms in students' home languages, linked from the feedback page for any student who asks for it
Exemplars in the index drawn only from native-speaker essays, so the grounding suits some students' writing better
Rubric wording on conventions that may penalize dialect or learner phrasing that does not change the meaning
A confidence threshold that may send English learners' essays to the 3-day teacher queue far more often
Logging every request, English learners' included, with prompt and model versions so any dispute can be replayed

items.explanation: Unequal outcomes start where the system treats groups' inputs differently. In this design that happens in three places. The data: an exemplar index built only from native-speaker essays gives weaker, less relevant grounding to English learners. The criteria: a conventions rubric can act as a proxy that penalizes dialect or learner phrasing even when meaning is clear. The routing: if confidence is systematically lower for learners' writing, they wait days for feedback while others get it at once, which is an unequal outcome even if every final score is fair. Anthropic's success-criteria guidance says even 'hazy' topics such as ethics and safety can be quantified; extending that to fairness, the architect should give each of these a per-subgroup criterion. Options that only measure, explain or record outcomes by group are how a disparity is found, not where it starts.

rationales.A: A per-subgroup dashboard is measurement: it is how a disparity would be detected. It does not change what any student's essay is compared with, how it is scored or where it is routed.
rationales.B: An optional glossary adds help without changing the model's input, the rubric or the routing. It may reduce a gap in understanding feedback, but it does not create unequal scores or waits.
rationales.F: Version logging is part of the transparency owed to the debugging team and helps investigate a disparity once found, but it treats every request the same and does not cause unequal outcomes.

items.objective: 5.5 Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
items.stem: A developer-community platform uses a fast, low-cost Claude tier to moderate forum posts. Users report that posts written in non-native English are flagged as 'hostile' more often than similar posts by native speakers. The trust-and-safety lead asks the architect to add a fairness success criterion to the release gate for the next classifier prompt. Which criterion should the architect define?

options.text: Overall precision and recall above 0.9 on a labeled set of 5,000 posts drawn from the platform's current traffic mix.
False-positive flag rate per language group on a labeled set of 5,000 posts, with at most a 1.5x gap between any two groups.
A system-prompt rule telling Claude to judge all posts fairly whatever the author's language, verified through regular spot checks.
Remove the author's language and locale from each request, so the classifier cannot treat any language group differently.

items.explanation: Anthropic's success-criteria guidance says even hazy qualities such as ethics and safety can be quantified, and that a good criterion is specific and measurable rather than an aspiration. The harm reported is a disparity: false positives concentrated in one group. The criterion must therefore measure that disparity directly: the false-positive rate computed separately for each language group on a labeled set, with a maximum allowed gap that the sponsor agrees to. The content-moderation guide already recommends tracking precision and recall; the fairness move is to compute them per subgroup, because an aggregate can look excellent while one minority group bears most of the errors.

rationales.A: An aggregate over the current traffic mix is dominated by the majority group, so it can pass while non-native writers still bear most of the false positives. It measures the wrong thing for the reported harm.
rationales.C: A prompt instruction is a mitigation, not a success criterion, and spot checks are not measurable. Nothing here would detect whether the disparity actually shrank.
rationales.D: Fairness through unawareness fails here: the language signal is in the post text itself, so the model still sees it. Removing the field also removes the group label needed to measure the disparity.

items.objective: 5.5 Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
items.stem: A university admissions office launches an optional Claude assistant that answers applicants' questions about programs. The office also wants the assistant to write a short 'fit summary' of each conversation into the applicant's file for readers to consider. Many international applicants use the assistant in their second language, and many applicants never use it at all. Which design best addresses transparency and fairness?

options.text: Disclose AI use in the privacy policy linked in the site footer, and let readers weigh fit summaries alongside the rest of the file.
Disclose at session start that the assistant is AI, and have a trained reader check each fit summary before it enters the applicant's file.
Disclose at session start that the assistant is AI, and keep conversations out of applicant files so they cannot affect decisions.
Keep the fit summaries but strip names and demographic fields from them, so readers cannot be biased by who the applicant is.

items.explanation: Two problems sit in this design. Transparency: Anthropic's guidance for products built on Claude tells builders to disclose to users of external-facing products that they are interacting with an AI system, and its Usage Policy sets the minimum point for a chatbot as the beginning of each chat session. Fairness: an optional help channel would quietly become an evaluation channel, so applicants who skip it, or who write in their second language, get an extra artifact in their file that measures fluency and willingness to chat rather than fitness for the program, and they were never told the conversation was assessed. Reviewing each summary makes it more accurate but does not remove that unequal, undisclosed input. Keeping the assistant a help tool, with AI disclosure at session start, removes the source of unequal outcomes instead of trying to correct it downstream.

rationales.A: A footer privacy policy is not disclosure at the start of the session, and letting readers weigh the summaries keeps the unequal, undisclosed evaluation channel fully in place.
rationales.B: This is the strongest distractor: disclosure is right and review improves accuracy. But a reviewed summary still evaluates only those who chose to chat, rewards fluency in a second language, and assesses people who were told only that the assistant is AI.
rationales.D: Stripping names does not help, because the disparity comes from who uses the assistant and in which language, which shows in the text itself. The summaries remain an undisclosed input that applies to some applicants and not others.

items.objective: 6.1 Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
items.stem: A national home-goods retailer's VP of Merchandising, who is not technical, asks an architect to "use Claude to fix our product listings." After two discovery sessions, the architect must hand the design team the output of discovery. Which output best meets the standard for structured discovery?

options.text: Requirements each tied to a stated business outcome, plus an assumption log (e.g. catalogue data refreshes nightly) naming who confirms each one.
A recommended stack (top-tier model, agent framework, vector store) drawn from the architect's past builds, with the VP's goals summarised at the end.
A feature list ranked by the VP's stated priorities and validated with her in session two, with open data questions passed to the design team.
A prototype that rewrites fifty listings for the VP to react to, with the requirements confirmed from her reaction and written up afterwards.

items.explanation: The VP has stated a goal, not requirements, so discovery has to translate it. Tying each requirement to a business outcome gives every later design choice a reason a sponsor can check, and an assumption log with named owners turns hidden dependencies (data freshness, catalogue ownership, volume) into items that can be confirmed or falsified before they become defects. That is the standard the Stakeholder Engagement prep course sets for discovery: architectural requirements and documented assumptions, so the design traces to the business case rather than to the architect's own preference.

rationales.B: The design traces to the architect's preference instead of the business case. The goals are an afterthought, so when the sponsor asks why a component exists there is no traceable answer.
rationales.C: Validating a ranked wishlist with the sponsor is capture, not translation: no feature is tied to a business outcome, and the open data questions are exactly the assumptions discovery must log with an owner. Passing them to design leaves the design resting on guesses.
rationales.D: Confirming requirements from reactions to a prototype inverts the order: it anchors the VP on one solution and leaves the business case, boundaries and assumptions undocumented until after build effort is spent.

items.objective: 6.1 Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
items.stem: During discovery for a university admissions-office assistant that answers applicants' questions about deadlines and entry requirements, the Director of Admissions says the tool must be "accurate and safe." The architect needs a success criterion that can later be used to judge go-live and every change after it. Which restatement is best?

options.text: Answers should be accurate and safe as judged by admissions staff who review a sample of conversations each week once the system is live.
At least 90% of applicants rating answers helpful in a post-chat survey, and no complaints escalated to the Director during the first term.
Every answer correct and no unsafe output at all, confirmed by admissions staff reviewing every test conversation before the system goes live.
At least 95% of answers on a 400-question held-out set graded correct against published policy, and under 0.5% flagged by the content filter.

items.explanation: Anthropic's success-criteria guidance asks for criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and shows that even hazy goals such as "safe" can be quantified (for example, a maximum share of outputs flagged by a content filter over a fixed number of trials). A threshold on a named held-out set is what lets the team gate go-live and every later change with evals; a criterion that cannot be measured cannot later decide whether an SLA was met or an iteration helped.

rationales.A: This restates the vague goal and defers judgement until after launch. With no threshold or fixed test set, two reviewers can disagree and no change can be gated against it.
rationales.B: This is measurable but measures the wrong thing. Applicants cannot tell whether an answer matches published policy, and complaints are a lagging, partial signal, so a fluent but wrong deadline can still score well.
rationales.C: A 100% bar is not achievable, so it can never be met and cannot gate anything; a one-off review before launch also says nothing about the changes that follow it.

items.objective: 6.1 Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
items.stem: A regional hospital network's pharmacovigilance unit wants Claude to draft adverse-drug-event reports from clinician notes and patient records. In the first discovery workshop, the engineering lead proposes Claude in Microsoft Foundry, hosted on Azure, because the network already runs on Azure and prompts and completions would stay within Azure, and asks the architect to start comparing latency and cost across delivery routes. What should the architect establish first?

options.text: Whether PHI is in scope and which HIPAA-ready, BAA-backed route that implies, as it rules routes out before cost and latency.
Which route has the lowest p95 latency for a typical adverse-event report, since the unit works to strict regulatory reporting deadlines.
Which features the safety reviewers want most, so the route that offers all of them is shortlisted before the compliance review begins.
Whether Zero Data Retention can be enabled on the Foundry deployment, since ZDR would make that route suitable for PHI.

items.explanation: The prep course asks architects to identify which delivery routes are ruled out by governance or regulated-industry constraints before any other trade-off applies. Clinician notes and patient records contain PHI, and the docs are specific: for PHI, HIPAA readiness under a signed BAA is the arrangement to use, it applies to the Claude API, and it is not available on Claude Platform on AWS or Microsoft Foundry. Keeping prompts inside a cloud tenancy is a data-location property, not a HIPAA arrangement. Settling PHI scope first shrinks the option set; comparing latency and cost on a route that is later disqualified is wasted work.

rationales.B: Reporting deadlines make latency matter, but it is a trade-off to weigh among eligible routes. Benchmarking a route that cannot carry PHI under a HIPAA arrangement wastes the comparison.
rationales.C: Ranking routes on features before compliance inverts the documented order; a route that cannot carry PHI is out however many features it offers.
rationales.D: This rests on a false premise. The API and data retention page says HIPAA readiness, not ZDR, is the arrangement for PHI (an organisation handling PHI does not also need ZDR), and that HIPAA readiness is not available on Claude Platform on AWS or Microsoft Foundry. ZDR is offered on request on some routes, for example Claude Platform on AWS, but it does not make a route suitable for PHI.

items.objective: 6.1 Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
items.stem: A commercial bank wants an assistant that drafts the narrative section of credit memos for relationship managers. Discovery found three inputs: the bank's credit policy manual, revised twice a year; each borrower's debt-service coverage ratio, which the bank's credit risk engine already computes nightly; and the credit decision, which regulation assigns to a named credit officer. Using the four properties of generative AI (next token prediction, knowledge, working memory, steerability) as the decision lens, which split of responsibilities should discovery record?

options.text: Rely on Claude's own knowledge of standard credit policy; take the ratio from the risk engine; Claude drafts; a credit officer decides.
Index the policy manual for retrieval; have Claude compute the ratio from the borrower's statements in context; Claude drafts; an officer decides.
Index the policy manual for retrieval, re-indexed on each revision; take the ratio from the risk engine; Claude drafts; a credit officer decides.
Index the policy manual for retrieval; take the ratio from the risk engine; Claude drafts and decides memos below a materiality threshold.

items.explanation: Each input maps to one owner. The policy manual is this bank's own content and changes twice a year, so it belongs in working memory through retrieval, with the index rebuilt on each revision; slow-changing reference text is the job retrieval does well, unlike live account state. Claude's training knowledge is general and has a cutoff, so it cannot stand in for this bank's policy. The ratio is a deterministic figure the risk engine already produces, and next token prediction should not recompute what a system of record owns. Drafting narrative from supplied facts plays to steerability. The credit decision is regulated and costly to reverse, so it stays with the named officer. The Platform & Solution Design prep course frames discovery exactly this way: what Claude does, what existing systems do and what humans do.

rationales.A: Claude's knowledge is general and fixed at training time; it is not this bank's policy and will not track the twice-yearly revisions. Anthropic's hallucination guidance is to restrict answers to supplied documents for exactly this reason.
rationales.B: The risk engine already computes the ratio. Asking a next-token predictor to recalculate it from statements adds error risk and creates a second, unaudited version of a regulated figure.
rationales.D: The data paths are right, but regulation assigns the decision to a named officer; a materiality threshold does not move that accountability to the model.

items.objective: 6.1 Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
items.stem: A state benefits agency wants Claude to help caseworkers draft replies to applicant correspondence. The architect must turn discovery into a scoped solution architecture with explicit boundary conditions. Which THREE items must discovery capture as inputs to that architecture? (Select THREE)

options.text: Expected letters per day and typical tokens per letter, so call volume, token use and cost can be estimated
The security authorisation baseline the agency's procurement requires, which rules delivery routes in or out
The chunk size and embedding model to use when indexing the agency's policy manual for retrieval
The screen layout caseworkers will use to review, edit and approve each draft before it is sent
The tone instructions and few-shot example letters to place in the reply-drafting system prompt
What the system must not do, such as making eligibility determinations, which stay with a caseworker

items.explanation: The Enterprise Integration & Production course frames use-case creation as estimating call volume, token consumption and cost, assessing feasibility, and translating the business problem into a scoped solution architecture with explicit boundary conditions. Volume and token figures make cost estimable; the security authorisation baseline the agency must procure against is a hard constraint that removes delivery routes before other trade-offs; and an explicit statement of what the system must not decide is the boundary condition that keeps eligibility determinations with an accountable caseworker. The other options are real design work, but they are decisions made from those inputs, not inputs that bound the architecture.

rationales.C: Chunk size and embedding model are retrieval design choices made after requirements are known; they consume discovery outputs rather than bound the architecture.
rationales.D: The review screen is user-interface design for a later phase. Discovery may record that a caseworker approves every draft, but the layout itself is not a volume, constraint or boundary input.
rationales.E: Tone instructions and example letters are prompt-design decisions tuned with evals once the scope is fixed; they do not determine cost, eligible routes or what the system must not do.

items.objective: 6.1 Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
items.stem: A SaaS company wants Claude to summarise support tickets. Discovery confirmed 40,000 tickets a day, about 3,000 input tokens per ticket and 30 days a month, but output length is disputed: the product manager wants 300-token summaries, while support managers want 900-token summaries that include a suggested reply. For estimation only, use illustrative prices of 3 USD per million input tokens and 15 USD per million output tokens. The sponsor's budget is 20,000 USD a month. What should discovery record?

options.text: About 16,200 USD at 300 tokens and 27,000 USD at 900, so output length decides fit; log it as an open assumption for the sponsor to settle.
About 16,200 USD a month at 300 output tokens, inside budget; record 300 tokens as the requirement, confirmed by the product manager who owns it.
About 21,600 USD a month at the 600-token midpoint, just over budget; record that single figure and ask the sponsor for a slightly larger budget.
About 10,800 USD a month either way, since output is small next to 3,000 input tokens; leave the summary length for the design team to settle.

items.explanation: Input is fixed: 40,000 x 3,000 = 120M tokens a day x 3 USD/M = 360 USD, or 10,800 USD a month. Output is where the dispute lives: at 300 tokens, 12M tokens a day x 15 USD/M = 180 USD a day (5,400 USD a month), total 16,200 USD; at 900 tokens, 36M x 15 USD/M = 540 USD a day (16,200 USD a month), total 27,000 USD. One assumption flips the estimate from inside to well over budget, so discovery records both figures and logs output length as an open assumption with the sponsor as the owner who settles it. Estimating volume, tokens and cost and recording the assumptions behind them is what the prep courses ask of discovery; output tokens are priced separately and higher than input, so they cannot be waved away.

rationales.B: The arithmetic is right for one side of the dispute, but recording it as the requirement settles a contested business choice silently and hides that the other option is 7,000 USD over budget.
rationales.C: The midpoint is correct arithmetic (24M output tokens a day, 21,600 USD a month) for a length nobody asked for. Averaging hides the real decision: one option fits the budget and the other does not.
rationales.D: Input-only error. Output tokens cost five times as much per token here, so 300 or 900 output tokens add 5,400 or 16,200 USD a month; the length choice is the biggest cost driver, not a design detail.
