items.objective: 6.2 Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
items.stem: An asset manager's procurement board has twice deferred a decision on how to deploy Claude for drafting research notes. Every note distributed to clients must pass the firm's supervisory review and record-keeping workflow, which compliance has validated for each candidate route's output format and logging. The architect's deck compares three delivery routes on a 30-row feature and benchmark matrix. What change is most likely to let the board reach a decision?

options.text: Add more benchmark rows and a weight for each one, so the matrix produces a single numerical winner that the board can simply approve.
Pair each route with its cost, main risk and reversal effort, including re-validating supervisory review, then recommend one.
Present only the recommended route, noting that reversal can be revisited later if the board's needs change after it goes live.
Propose a longer proof of concept to validate all three routes, so the board can defer until production-grade evidence is available.

items.explanation: The prep course sets the standard directly: present an architectural trade-off in terms a business stakeholder can act on by pairing each choice with a cost, a risk and what a reversal would take, so executive and procurement reviews reach a decision instead of stalling. Here reversal is not just a technical migration: switching routes later means re-validating the supervisory review and record-keeping workflow that client research notes must pass, and the board needs that cost in front of it. A feature or benchmark matrix answers an engineering question; a board needs to know what it pays, what could go wrong, and how expensive it is to change its mind later.

rationales.A: More rows and weights make the matrix more precise but no more decidable; the weights themselves become the next argument, and the cost of re-validating the review workflow on a switch is still missing.
rationales.C: Hiding the alternatives removes the board's ability to judge the trade-off, and deferring reversal to 'later' withholds the one cost the board most needs now: re-validating supervisory review if it changes its mind.
rationales.D: A longer POC is a third deferral. The missing information is decision framing, not more technical validation.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy prep course page)

items.objective: 6.2 Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
items.stem: An architect recommends a balanced-tier model for a hospital system's revenue-cycle service that drafts appeal letters for denied insurance claims. The recommendation came from the team's eval suite on de-identified denial cases, scored against the accuracy bar agreed in discovery. The revenue-cycle director objects, citing a public leaderboard on which a more capable tier scores higher, and asks the architect to justify the recommendation. Which response best defends it?

options.text: Show the team's eval results on de-identified denial cases: the balanced tier met the agreed accuracy bar at lower cost and lower latency.
Point out that leaderboards come from outside labs, and offer the vendor's own published eval comparison across tiers as stronger evidence.
Agree to move to the most capable tier, since a higher benchmark score means fewer errors on any task the appeals service handles.
Offer to route half of live denied claims to each tier for a month and keep whichever tier wins more of its appeals with payers.

items.explanation: Anthropic's model-choice guidance says a good evaluation set built on your actual prompts and data is the most important step, comparing accuracy, quality and edge-case handling and then weighing performance against cost. A defensible recommendation therefore cites the organisation's own eval results against the success criteria agreed in discovery, and states the cost and latency consequence of each tier, which is what lets a non-technical stakeholder accept the trade-off.

rationales.B: A vendor's published comparison is still a different task on different data. Swapping one external eval for another says nothing about denial appeals.
rationales.C: Benchmarks measure other tasks. Conceding without evidence raises cost and latency with no demonstrated quality gain, and it teaches stakeholders that leaderboards override the team's own evals.
rationales.D: An unevaluated production split puts real claims revenue on an untested configuration, and appeal outcomes arrive weeks later and depend on payer behaviour, so they are a slow, noisy measure of draft quality.

sources.title: Claude Platform & Solution Design (Partner Academy prep course page)

items.objective: 6.2 Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
items.stem: A fashion retailer generates product descriptions for 200,000 SKUs each season, with a 2-second latency target in its merchandising tool. The CFO asks, "Why not run everything on the most capable model to be safe?" The team's evals show the fastest tier meets the quality bar on 97% of SKUs; the misses are long technical spec sheets. What should the architect tell the CFO?

options.text: Agree, since the most capable model removes quality risk entirely and the latency target can be renegotiated with merchandising once it ships.
Use an orchestrator model to plan each description and delegate the drafting to workers, giving frontier quality at worker-tier prices.
Keep the fastest tier for everything, since the 3% of misses is within normal variance and does not need its own route or any follow-up.
Stay efficiency-first: keep the fastest tier, which met the bar on our data, and send long spec sheets to a stronger tier, with costs shown.

items.explanation: Anthropic documents an efficiency-first strategy for high-volume, straightforward, latency-sensitive and cost-sensitive work: start on the fastest tier, test thoroughly, and upgrade only where there is a specific capability gap. The evals have located that gap (long spec sheets), so the answer to the CFO is a cost and risk comparison grounded in the team's own data, not a blanket upgrade or a blanket refusal.

rationales.A: Running 200,000 SKUs on the top tier pays for capability the evals show is unnecessary for 97% of items and puts the agreed latency target at risk. No model removes quality risk entirely.
rationales.B: Each description is a small, self-contained task. An orchestrator adds planning, handoff and merge overhead without bulk to hand off, so it costs more, not less.
rationales.C: The misses are not random noise; they cluster on one identifiable input type. Ignoring a known, located gap ships known defects.

sources.title: Optimizing for cost and intelligence (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 6.2 Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
items.stem: A university in Germany is choosing how to deploy Claude for a student-facing study assistant. Its data protection officer requires that model inference run in the EU. A colleague's draft decision brief says this is met by setting inference_geo to an EU value on the Claude API. The steering committee, which holds the budget, will approve whatever the corrected brief recommends. What should the corrected brief tell it?

options.text: inference_geo offers only global or us; recommend a partner route's EU endpoint and leave price and feature differences for engineering after approval.
EU inference is impossible with Claude on any route, so the committee must either waive the requirement or choose another vendor.
inference_geo offers only global or us; a partner route's EU endpoint meets the rule, and moving back to the Claude API later is a one-line endpoint change.
inference_geo offers only global or us; a partner EU endpoint meets it at a regional price premium, with fewer features and re-platforming to reverse.

items.explanation: The residency facts are shared by most options; the discrimination is how the decision is framed for the people who must approve and fund it. On the Claude API, inference_geo currently accepts only "global" and "us". EU-resident inference is available on partner-operated routes: Amazon Bedrock through EU regional endpoints or its EU inference profile, and Claude on Google Cloud (formerly Vertex AI) through its "eu" multi-region endpoint, which is the EU option for current models because Google's specific regional endpoints serve only Claude Sonnet 4.6 and earlier. Regional and multi-region endpoints carry a 10% price premium over global endpoints, and both partner routes lack Claude API features such as Message Batches, the Files API and Agent Skills. A brief the committee can act on states all three consequences: the price premium, the feature loss, and that reversing later means re-platforming rather than a parameter change. Re-verify at each bank release: the data-residency page lists the us/global-only limitation as current, so it may change.

rationales.A: The facts are right, but the brief asks the committee to approve without the price and feature consequences it is being asked to fund; the costs surface after the decision, which is the stall the brief exists to prevent.
rationales.B: EU residency is achievable through Bedrock's EU endpoints or Google Cloud's "eu" multi-region endpoint. Presenting a false impossibility forecloses a viable option.
rationales.C: The route is right, but the reversal cost is understated. The partner routes lack features the Claude API offers and use different endpoints, authentication and billing, so returning later is a re-platforming effort, not a one-line change.

Pricing - cloud platform regional and multi-region endpoints (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 6.2 Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
items.stem: A state transportation department prototyped a public road-works question assistant on the Claude API using Agent Skills, the MCP connector and Message Batches. It handles only published data, and the security office has confirmed that no FedRAMP High, IL or HIPAA requirement applies and that AWS need not be the sole data processor. IT wants production on the department's AWS account with IAM access control and AWS billing, and inference kept in the United States. The architect is writing the route comparison the CIO will approve. Which TWO statements belong in the brief? (Select TWO)

options.text: Amazon Bedrock is required because the customer is a public body, and its gaps in Agent Skills, the MCP connector and batches are an acceptable cost.
Claude on Google Cloud (formerly Vertex AI) on its us multi-region endpoint keeps every prototype feature with no premium over global pricing.
Claude Platform on AWS draws on the Claude API's capacity pool, so it adds no resilience if the department later fails over between the two.
Claude Platform on AWS fits: the prototype's features carry over with IAM access and AWS billing, but Anthropic, not AWS, processes the data.
Pinning inference to the US with inference_geo on Claude Platform on AWS adds a price multiplier over global routing, so the cost line shows it.

items.explanation: The stem removes every condition under which Anthropic's docs point to Amazon Bedrock (FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5, HIPAA-ready compliance, or AWS as sole data processor), so the route with the lowest switching cost wins. Claude Platform on AWS is operated by Anthropic on the Claude API surface, with AWS IAM, AWS Marketplace billing and near-full feature parity, including Agent Skills and batch processing, so the prototype carries over. The brief must still state the trade-off the CIO is accepting: Anthropic, not AWS, is the data processor. It must also show the cost of the US requirement, because US-only inference through inference_geo is priced at a multiplier over global routing. Pairing the recommendation with its cost and its main condition is what lets the CIO approve it.

rationales.A: Being a public body does not trigger the Bedrock guidance; the documented triggers are FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5, HIPAA readiness or AWS as sole processor, and the stem rules them all out. Losing Agent Skills, the MCP connector and Message Batches would be redesign cost bought for no requirement.
rationales.B: Wrong on both counts: Google Cloud does not support Agent Skills, the MCP connector or Message Batches, and its multi-region endpoints carry a 10% premium over global ones. It would also move production off the department's AWS account.
rationales.C: The docs state that Claude Platform on AWS uses a separate capacity pool from both the Claude API and Bedrock and that workloads can fail over between platforms, so the statement understates a resilience option.

items.objective: 6.2 Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
items.stem: A consulting partner is two weeks from a go/no-go decision with a payroll software company that wants Claude to answer its customers' payroll-tax questions inside its product. In discovery, the prospect's CTO raised one objection three times: the assistant must not answer confidently when a question turns on a state rule that the company's knowledge base does not cover. The partner's sales lead plans to reuse a polished general-purpose demo that has won other deals. What should the partner's architect do?

options.text: Rebuild the demo on the prospect's own question types, including one an uncovered state rule decides, and show the assistant flag it and route it.
Reuse the polished demo for consistency, and answer the CTO's objection with the model's published eval results on public accuracy benchmarks.
Reuse the polished demo, and offer a contract clause promising that the assistant will never answer a question outside the knowledge base.
Postpone the demo until Anthropic's Applied AI team can present it, since only Anthropic can speak for how the model treats uncovered questions.

items.explanation: The CTO's objection is about one behaviour, so the demo has to show that behaviour on the prospect's own material. A scenario built from the prospect's question types, including a question an uncovered state rule decides, lets the CTO watch the design do what was asked: Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends explicitly allowing Claude to say it does not know and restricting answers to supplied documents, and the demo shows that choice working along with the route to a human expert. The Stakeholder Engagement prep course names a scenario-based demo and technical objection handling as the architect's part of a partner go-to-market motion, so a deal does not stall on questions only the architect can answer. A generic demo, a benchmark slide or a contractual promise leaves the objection open.

rationales.B: Public benchmarks measure other tasks. They say nothing about how this design behaves when the knowledge base is silent, which is the CTO's actual question, and the generic demo never shows that case.
rationales.C: No design can guarantee 'never', so the clause is a promise the partner cannot keep, and it replaces evidence with a commitment the CTO has no way to check before signing.
rationales.D: Behaviour on uncovered questions is set by the partner's design (grounding, permission to say it does not know, escalation), so the architect must answer it. Joint scoping with Applied AI is for questions only Anthropic can answer, and a delay two weeks before the decision is how deals stall.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy prep course page)

items.objective: 6.3 Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
items.stem: A grocery chain's customer-facing shopping assistant runs on the Claude API's Standard tier. Its marketplace partners now want a 99.9% monthly availability SLA written into their contracts before the holiday peak. The product owner notes that Priority Tier targets 99.5% uptime and proposes buying it to back the commitment. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Priority Tier targets 99.5%, below the promise; base the SLA on failover across separate capacity pools, a degraded mode and stated limits.
Buy Priority Tier and sign the 99.9% SLA; prioritised capacity removes the risk of overload errors for the newest model during the holiday peak.
Sign the 99.9% SLA on the Standard tier; the organisation's rate limits reserve the capacity it needs, and the SDK retries any transient error.
Decline any availability SLA; generative AI cannot be held to uptime targets, so partners should accept best-effort service instead.

items.explanation: The stem carries the discrimination: Priority Tier's own target, 99.5%, is below the 99.9% being promised, so buying it cannot back the commitment. The Standard tier is best-effort, and rate limits are maximums, not guaranteed minimums. A customer-facing SLA therefore has to rest on the architect's own design (for example failover between platforms with separate capacity pools, such as the Claude API and Claude Platform on AWS, plus a degraded mode) and on any negotiated terms, with the upstream limits stated plainly to stakeholders. As context, the service-tiers page currently says new Priority Tier commitments are no longer sold and that the newest models are not covered; re-verify at each bank release, since these are commercial terms.

rationales.B: Even Priority Tier's 99.5% target, given in the stem, is below the 99.9% being promised, and prioritisation reduces overload errors rather than removing them. The arithmetic alone rules it out, whatever the tier's current sales status.
rationales.C: Rate limits cap usage; they do not reserve capacity. SDK retries help with transient errors but cannot turn a best-effort tier into a 99.9% commitment.
rationales.D: Availability is measurable and an SLA can be designed for. Refusing outright fails the expectation-alignment job when a fallback design and honest limits would let the business decide.

sources.title: Claude Platform on AWS - separate capacity pool (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 6.3 Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
items.stem: An insurer's claims-triage assistant has been in production for three months. A prompt change shipped between the quarterly compliance audits, and an SLA breach on triage turnaround went two weeks without a decision on whether to tune the system or rebuild it. Which feedback-loop design addresses both failures?

options.text: Move the compliance audit from quarterly to monthly and add a release checklist, keeping SLA issues in the engineering backlog for sprint planning.
Page the on-call engineer on any SLA breach, and keep compliance on its quarterly audit of the system so that changes are reviewed in a batch.
A single loop where every prompt or model change needs compliance sign-off before release and any SLA breach forces a dated tune-or-rebuild call.
Email all stakeholders a monthly dashboard of token spend and request counts, and make changes whenever someone raises a concern about them.

items.explanation: The prep course asks for a stakeholder feedback loop across the deployment lifecycle that defines what triggers a review, what an SLA breach requires and when to iterate versus re-architect, with governance checkpoints inside the same loop. Both failures in the stem map to a missing part: the prompt change escaped because compliance sat on a calendar outside the release path, and the breach lingered because nothing obliged anyone to decide between tuning and rebuilding by a deadline. Gating every change on compliance sign-off and making a breach force a dated decision closes both.

rationales.A: A more frequent audit still sits outside the release path, so a change can ship between audits, and leaving breaches in the backlog repeats the two-week drift.
rationales.B: Paging detects the breach faster but does not require a tune-or-rebuild decision, and batching changes into a quarterly audit is exactly how the prompt change escaped.
rationales.D: Spend and request counts are activity metrics, not SLA or quality measures, and 'changes when someone raises a concern' is neither a trigger nor a governance gate.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy prep course page)
Claude Certified Architect - Professional Exam Guide v1.0

items.objective: 6.3 Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
items.stem: A health system's clinical coding assistant meets its accuracy target on the eval suite, but p95 latency is 8 seconds against an agreed 4-second SLO, measured from when a coder opens a chart. Over three weeks the team has swept effort, tested a faster tier and trimmed output: every configuration that holds the accuracy target stays above 6 seconds, and the only one under 4 seconds falls below it. Clinicians sign their notes on average a day before coders open the chart. Under the feedback loop's iterate-versus-re-architect rule, what should the architect recommend?

options.text: Keep iterating: run a finer-grained effort sweep and re-run the eval to confirm, since a setting that meets both targets may lie between those tested.
Ship the configuration that meets 4 seconds, since the SLO is what coders feel, and ask coders to check the suggestions more carefully meanwhile.
Re-architect: generate code suggestions when the clinician signs the note, so they are ready when the coder opens the chart; take it to the sponsor.
Turn on streaming so suggestions start appearing sooner, and report the SLO as met by measuring time to first token instead of the full result.

items.explanation: The rule is to iterate while cheap, reversible settings might still meet every target, and to re-architect once they demonstrably cannot. That evidence is already in the stem: Anthropic's documented latency levers (a faster model, effort, shorter output) have been tried and measured, and none meets accuracy and the SLO together. The day between signing and coding means the work need not happen while the coder waits, so generating suggestions when the note is signed takes model latency out of the interactive path entirely, which no setting can do. Because it changes the integration and when cost is incurred, it goes to the sponsor as a re-architecture decision rather than shipping as a tweak.

rationales.A: The stem already holds the evidence the rule asks for. The best accurate setting is 6 seconds against a 4-second target, a gap points between tested settings are unlikely to close, so another sweep only delays the decision that is now due.
rationales.B: This trades the agreed accuracy target for the latency target without the sponsor's decision, and it shifts the cost of errors onto the coders the system was meant to help.
rationales.D: Coders need the complete code set before they can act, so time to first token is not the experience the SLO describes. Redefining the metric to report success misleads stakeholders.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy prep course page)

items.objective: 6.3 Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
items.stem: An online-learning provider runs a tutoring assistant for an advanced microbiology course on the Claude API. Its model can decline a request through a safety classifier; a decline arrives as HTTP 200 with stop_reason refusal and a category, and monitoring now counts these. It shows 6% of lab-protocol questions declined in the bio category, which the docs say beneficial life-sciences work can also trigger. Instructors ask what will change. What should the architect do and tell them?

options.text: Enable fallback to the recommended model for declined requests, track refusal and fallback rates, and say some questions may still be declined.
Add a system-prompt line stating that every user is an enrolled student doing coursework, and tell instructors that this should stop the declines.
Retry each declined request on the same model up to three times, and tell instructors that the declines are transient and will clear on retry.
Move the whole course to the fallback model once a one-week eval passes, and tell instructors every lab-protocol question will then be answered.

items.explanation: Anthropic's refusals page describes fallback for exactly this case: a declined request can be retried on another Claude model, with server-side fallback (in beta on the Claude API) choosing the model Anthropic recommends for the refusal category, and SDK middleware doing the same on other platforms. The response names the model that served it, so refusal and fallback rates can be reported as metrics alongside availability. The page is also clear on the limits: for categories with no recommended fallback the refusal stands, and depending on the category a request may fall back to a less capable model or be declined. Expectation alignment means telling instructors both halves: most declined questions will now be answered, some may not, and the numbers will be visible. Re-verify at each model release: which models run these classifiers and how fallback works are changing quickly.

rationales.B: The decline comes from a safety classifier, not from the model's instructions, and trying to talk past a safeguard is not a fix. Promising that the declines will stop sets an expectation the design cannot meet.
rationales.C: The same request to the same model meets the same classifier, so retries mostly repeat the refusal, and bio refusals before any output are billed. Calling them transient misinforms instructors.
rationales.D: Moving every request gives up the primary model on the 94% it already answers, and the promise ignores that fallback models can also decline. A one-week eval does not make 'every question answered' true.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy prep course page)

items.objective: 6.3 Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
items.stem: A city government's public-information chatbot, which handles only public data on the Claude API, stops answering mid-month. Engineering has confirmed the cause: the organisation reached its usage tier's monthly spend cap. Under Anthropic's documented behaviour, requests, retries included, keep failing until the first day of next month unless the organisation moves to a higher tier, and the budget owner has not yet decided whether to fund that. The communications office is drafting the update for residents and the city council. Which TWO statements belong in it? (Select TWO)

options.text: The AI provider is experiencing an outage affecting its customers, and the city is waiting for the provider to restore the service
The service stopped because the city reached its own monthly usage cap with the AI provider; this is not an outage at the provider
Automatic retries are already running, so residents should expect the chatbot to recover on its own within the next few minutes
The provider returned HTTP 429 rate_limit_error with error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached and no retry-after header on each call
No restore time can be given until the service is back, so this update will only confirm that the team is investigating the problem
Service returns as soon as a higher usage tier is approved, or on the first of next month if it is not; the next update follows that decision

items.explanation: The mechanism is settled in the stem, so the item tests the message. Residents and the council need the real cause in plain words and a restore time they can rely on. The cause is the city's own cap, not a vendor failure. The restore time is known but conditional: Anthropic's rate-limits page says access resumes at the start of the next month, or sooner if the organisation moves to a higher tier, so the honest update ties the date to the pending budget decision and says when the next update will come. That turns an outage notice into a decision the council can see and act on.

rationales.A: Blaming the provider misinforms the council about a limit the city itself reached, and it hides the budget decision that would restore service.
rationales.C: Retries fail until access resumes; promising recovery in minutes sets an expectation that will be broken within the hour.
rationales.D: Accurate, but it belongs in the incident runbook. Residents and councillors need the cause and restore time in plain terms, and this line gives them neither.
rationales.E: The restore path is already known and depends on a business decision; withholding it leaves the council unable to make that decision and invites speculation.

sources.title: Rate limits - reaching your spend cap (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 6.3 Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
items.stem: A developer-tools company built a code-review bot on the model ID claude-sonnet-4-6, which Anthropic's docs describe as a pinned snapshot rather than an alias. Its customer success team told enterprise clients that "pinning the model means its behaviour will never change." After weeks of stable output, with no change to the bot's prompts or settings, review comments shift slightly in style. How should the architect correct the expectation in the stakeholder update?

options.text: The weights behind the ID are fixed, but serving infrastructure can change and shift behaviour slightly, so regression evals stay in the loop.
The snapshot is ageing toward deprecation; move to the newest model once a regression eval passes, and tell clients its behaviour will then stay fixed.
Anthropic retrains the weights behind each model ID monthly, so customers should expect drift and accept it as a normal part of the service.
The shift comes from temperature drift; setting temperature to zero on each request will restore fully deterministic behaviour from now on.

items.explanation: The stem establishes that the ID is a snapshot and that nothing changed on the bot's side, so the question is what explains a small shift and what to promise. Anthropic's versioning docs say weights are fixed per ID, but the serving infrastructure around the model (request routing, safety classifiers, sampling logic) can change, and they name an infrastructure update as the most likely cause of unexpected differences on a stable ID. The honest expectation is 'same model, not byte-identical behaviour', backed by ongoing regression evals as a review trigger.

rationales.B: Deprecation status does not change a snapshot's behaviour, and migrating changes behaviour far more. The new ID carries the same infrastructure caveat, so promising fixed behaviour repeats the original error.
rationales.C: Weights do not change behind an ID; updates ship under a new ID. This statement would alarm clients with a false claim.
rationales.D: Sampling settings do not explain a shift on unchanged settings, and zero temperature does not guarantee determinism; the documented cause is serving-infrastructure change.

items.objective: 6.4 Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
items.stem: A SaaS company's architecture team built a Claude-based pull-request review agent and is handing it to the platform engineering team that will own it from next month. The agent's behaviour depends on a system prompt, two Agent Skills, a CLAUDE.md of repository conventions, and several design decisions, such as why the agent stops at the merge gate and why it can never approve a change it wrote. The platform team will keep extending the agent with Claude Code, and the original architects move to another programme. Which form of implementation guidance gives the new owners the most durable handoff?

options.text: A recorded architecture walkthrough plus a slide deck summarising each component, stored on the shared drive for new joiners to watch.
A design handbook copying the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, the Skills and every design decision into one signed-off PDF at handoff.
An extended support period in which the original architects answer questions until the platform team feels confident.
Versioned repo artifacts: the spec, owned decision records, CLAUDE.md and the Skills, regression-tested on every change.

items.explanation: Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook describes a pipeline in which every stage commits an artifact the next stage can read, so the intent, spec, plan, diff and review findings together form the audit trail. Institutional knowledge is kept as versioned, machine-readable CLAUDE.md files and Skills, and the agent's own configuration is regression-tested like the code it writes. A durable handoff therefore lives with the system: in version control, with named owners for each decision, readable both by the engineers and by the Claude Code sessions they will use to extend it. Point-in-time documents and people-dependent support decay as soon as the system changes or the original team leaves.

rationales.A: A recording and a deck capture the system at one moment, are not readable by the agents the team will use, and silently go stale at the first change; nobody owns keeping them true.
rationales.B: It names the right artifacts but freezes them as a point-in-time copy with no versioning, no owners and no regression tests. It diverges from the system at the first change, and the Claude Code sessions extending the agent never read it.
rationales.C: Extended support keeps the knowledge in the original architects' heads, who are leaving. It postpones the handoff rather than making it durable and builds dependency instead of self-sufficiency.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy course page)

items.objective: 6.4 Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
items.stem: A university's IT architect is writing the rollout plan for Claude Enterprise across its faculties. The CIO, the data protection officer and the faculty deans will walk through it at kickoff, and several settings, including which connectors are enabled, the spend cap for each faculty and which adoption signals are visible to deans, are expected to change during the first term. How should each rollout decision be documented so the plan stays usable as those settings change?

options.text: Record each decision with its rationale and the approving committee, so any later change can be traced to who agreed it.
Keep a change log of each setting's old value, new value, date and approver, reviewed with the deans at each checkpoint.
State the decision, the choices considered, what changing it later would involve and affect, and who owns it.
Record the vendor-recommended value for each setting, and note where and why the university departed from it.

items.explanation: Anthropic Academy's Deploying Claude Enterprise with Confidence course structures every rollout decision in three parts: your decision, the choices you can make, and what happens if you change it later. Its work-along companion records what was decided and who owns it, and becomes the rollout plan walked through at kickoff. The Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM prep course asks architects to present each choice with a cost, a risk and what a reversal would take, so reviews reach a decision. Documenting the reversal path and the owner up front is what keeps a plan usable when settings are expected to change: the next person can see why a value was chosen, who can change it, and what else moves when they do.

rationales.A: Rationale and approver are a good start, but the record omits the choices that were rejected and what changing the setting later would involve or affect. A committee that approved the plan is also not an owner who can act when a setting has to move mid-term.
rationales.B: A change log tracks history, not reasoning. It records what moved, when and who approved it, but gives no rationale for the value and no view of what else a change cascades into, so the next person still cannot judge a proposed change.
rationales.D: Explaining departures from the vendor's guidance records reasoning only where the university deviated. Settings left at the recommended value carry no rationale, and the record names neither an owner nor what changing a setting later would involve.

items.objective: 6.4 Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
items.stem: A hospital's revenue-cycle team runs a Claude agent that corrects denied insurance claims and resubmits them through a submit_claim tool that calls the clearinghouse. During a clearinghouse slowdown, some submit_claim calls timed out after the clearinghouse had in fact accepted the claim. The tool returned an is_error result saying the call timed out, Claude called submit_claim again, and payers denied the second copies as duplicates. The architect is writing the implementation guide for the teams that will build the next side-effecting tools, such as posting payments and writing off balances. Which guidance BEST prevents a repeat?

options.text: Key every write on the tool_use id, and have the backend return the stored result whenever the same id arrives a second time.
Add a circuit breaker that stops submit_claim calls after repeated timeouts and queues claims to resubmit once the clearinghouse recovers.
Key every write on the business action, such as claim and correction version, and have the backend return the first result on a repeat.
Return each timeout as an instructive error telling Claude not to call the tool again, and route the claim to a billing specialist.

items.explanation: A timeout tells the caller nothing about whether the write happened, and here it had. Anything that retries can then repeat the side effect: orchestration code, a queue, a person, or Claude itself, which reads an is_error result and may try the tool again. The guide therefore has to make the write itself safe to repeat. If the tool backend derives an idempotency key from the business action (this claim, this correction) and returns the stored outcome when the same action arrives again, every retry path becomes harmless, and the transient-failure retries that production reliability depends on can stay. Anthropic's tool-use docs give each tool_use block its own unique id, so a second call that Claude decides to make arrives with a new id; only a key tied to the action, not the call, recognises it as the same claim.

rationales.A: Each tool_use block carries its own unique id, so when Claude calls submit_claim again after the error, the new call has a new id. The backend sees two different keys and submits the claim twice, which is exactly the incident.
rationales.B: A circuit breaker protects the clearinghouse and the agent during an outage, but it does not make the write safe to repeat. The queued claims include ones that were already accepted before the timeout, so draining the queue sends duplicates.
rationales.D: This relies on the model honouring an instruction, and it does not solve the underlying uncertainty: the specialist cannot tell whether the first call landed either, so resubmission risk remains, and every transient slowdown becomes manual work.

items.objective: 6.4 Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
items.stem: An online retailer's architect is writing the implementation guide that three internal teams will follow when building Claude-based order-support features on the Claude API. Last quarter one team's integration crashed in production when a response carried a stop_reason value its parser did not recognise, and another team built part of the checkout flow on a feature enabled through a beta header. Which TWO pieces of guidance should the implementation guide contain? (Select TWO)

options.text: Pin anthropic-version and validate responses against the documented schema, rejecting values not in the current reference.
Pin the dated beta header string so the beta feature's contract is frozen the way anthropic-version preserves stable parameters.
Retry a response whose stop_reason is not end_turn, with backoff and a retry cap, so callers receive a finished answer.
Handle unrecognised enum-like values, such as a new stop reason, as a known non-fatal path that is logged rather than a crash.
Flag every beta-header dependency in the design and keep it off SLA-critical paths unless a tested fallback exists.

items.explanation: Anthropic's versioning policy preserves existing input and output parameters within an API version but explicitly allows new optional inputs, new output values, changed error conditions and new variants of enum-like outputs. Pinning anthropic-version therefore does not freeze the enum set, and client code must treat an unknown value as an expected, logged case. Beta features carry a weaker contract: they may have breaking changes with notice, be deprecated or removed, have different rate limits or pricing, or not be available in all regions. The dated beta name identifies the feature; it does not freeze it. Implementation guidance should make beta dependencies visible and keep them off SLA-critical paths unless a tested fallback exists. The two clauses turn one incident and one latent risk into rules the next team can follow.

rationales.A: Pinning the version preserves existing parameters, but within a version Anthropic may add new variants to enum-like outputs. Strict validation against today's reference rejects exactly those values and reproduces the first incident.
rationales.B: The dated name says which beta you call; it does not freeze it. Beta features may have breaking changes with notice, be deprecated or removed, and carry different limits or pricing, so the dependency stays a risk however the header is pinned.
rationales.C: Not every other stop is a failure: tool_use and pause_turn are normal stops that need the loop to continue, max_tokens needs a budget change or continuation, and a refusal belongs on a fallback model, since re-sending it to the same model usually earns another refusal.

items.objective: 6.4 Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
items.stem: A bank runs a credit-memo drafting assistant on Claude Platform on AWS. The architect's handoff guide told the operations team that "all Claude activity is captured in CloudTrail". During a model-risk investigation, the team finds workspace and API-key management events for the period under review but no record of any inference call. The platform's documentation explains why: management operations are logged by default, while inference calls are data events that are logged only when data-event logging is explicitly configured, at additional CloudTrail cost. Which rewrite of the guide's logging section best prevents a repeat?

options.text: Turn on data-event logging for every operation type in every AWS account the bank holds, so that no Claude activity is ever missed.
Correct the guide to say only management events are captured, and reconstruct inference from the assistant's own application logs.
Specify inference data-event logging for this workload, who enables and funds it, how long logs are kept, and a check they arrive.
Enable data-event logging when a model-risk investigation opens, so the extra CloudTrail charges are paid only when needed.

items.explanation: The guide failed because it made an unqualified promise about a control that is off by default and costs money to run. Nobody was named to switch it on or pay for it, and nothing checked that inference events were arriving, so the gap surfaced only when evidence was needed. The rewrite should turn the promise into a specified control: data-event logging for this workload's inference, the owner who enables and funds it, where the logs live and how long they are kept, and a routine check that inference events appear. Anthropic's Claude Platform on AWS docs classify inference as a data event that needs explicit configuration and extra charges, and recommend logging activity on at least a 30-day rolling basis. The guide should also record which request ID to use where: x-amzn-requestid for CloudTrail lookups, request-id for Anthropic support.

rationales.A: Logging every data event in every account buys charges for operations nobody needs and still names no owner or budget. The first cost review is likely to switch it off, which reopens the same gap without anyone noticing.
rationales.B: Being honest about the gap is better than the old promise, but it leaves model-risk evidence in logs the application team writes and can change. CloudTrail in the bank's own account can capture inference once configured, so the guide should close the gap rather than document it.
rationales.D: Logging cannot be switched on retroactively. An investigation always concerns calls that were made before it opened, so those events would never have been recorded, and the bank would be in the same position next time.

items.objective: 6.4 Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
items.stem: A consulting partner has delivered a Claude-based assistant that helps a county building department's plan reviewers draft correction letters for permit applications. The programme director who sponsored it is not technical and must justify next year's funding to the county budget office. The partner also wants to reuse the engagement material with other counties. Which closing deliverable best serves both needs?

options.text: A full architecture specification with component diagrams, API contracts and the eval suite, so the budget office can verify engineering quality.
A comparison of the county's results with public model benchmark scores, showing that the chosen model outranks the alternatives on them.
A marketing case study featuring the county's name and adoption figures, written so it can be published straight away as a public customer story.
A short brief: the problem, results against the pre-launch baseline, and why this route was chosen, with county detail in a separable appendix.

items.explanation: The director has to defend a budget line to people who will not read an architecture, so the deliverable must state value in terms the budget office recognises: the problem solved, results against the baseline measured before launch, and a plain account of why this deployment route was chosen. The partner's second need pulls the same way: if the method, pattern and route decision are kept separate from the county's own data, the next engagement can reuse the structure without disclosing this client's details. The baseline is what makes the results credible, which is why Anthropic's guide to defining success criteria asks for criteria that are specific and measurable from the start. A full specification, vendor benchmarks and a marketing story each serve a different audience.

rationales.A: This is valuable engineering documentation but not legible to a non-technical sponsor or a budget office, and it is tied to this county's system, so it is not reusable as partner IP without heavy rework.
rationales.B: Public benchmarks say nothing about this county's outcomes. Anthropic's model-choice guide says to test with your actual prompts and data, so ranking models on public scores does not justify funding.
rationales.C: Publicity is not decision support for the budget office, naming a government client needs its approval, and adoption figures without a measured baseline do not show value or separate reusable method from client detail.

items.objective: 6.5 Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
items.stem: Six months after handoff, a hospital's Claude-based radiology-report impression drafter has a deterministic monitor tracking the share of draft impressions that radiologists override. The agreed control band is 8 to 12 percent. The monitor has shown 17 percent for two consecutive weeks, concentrated in CT chest studies. The on-call engineer proposes editing the production prompt that afternoon. How should the lifecycle process handle the breach?

options.text: Ship the on-call prompt edit today as an emergency change, spot-checked on a few CT chest studies, with the eval suite run afterwards.
Turn the breach into a structured change record that is diagnosed, specified, and passed through the eval gate before release.
Log the breach for the quarterly architecture review, where accumulated monitoring trends are weighed against the roadmap.
Escalate it to the model vendor as a probable model regression and keep the pipeline unchanged until the vendor confirms a cause.

items.explanation: The breach is real and specific: two weeks outside the agreed 8 to 12 percent band, concentrated in CT chest studies. That calls for a prompt but disciplined iteration, neither an untested same-day edit nor a deferral. Recording it as a structured change lets the team diagnose why CT chest drafts are being overridden, specify the fix, and show on the eval set that it repairs CT chest without regressing other modalities before it reaches radiologists. Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook describes the same loop: deterministic monitors detect control-band breaches, and a breach writes the next intent, so findings re-enter the pipeline as artifacts rather than ad hoc fixes.

rationales.A: Speed is right but the order is wrong. A spot check on a few studies cannot show the edit leaves other modalities intact, and running the eval suite after rollout means radiologists meet any regression first; the change is also undocumented when it ships.
rationales.C: A breach outside the agreed band is itself the review trigger. Parking it for a quarterly meeting leaves radiologists overriding drafts for months and turns monitoring into a report nobody acts on.
rationales.D: The concentration in one modality and study type points first at data or prompt fit, not the model, and nothing is diagnosed yet. Freezing the pipeline while waiting on a vendor leaves the breach unaddressed.

sources.title: Enterprise Integration & Production (Partner Academy course page)

items.objective: 6.5 Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
items.stem: A wealth-management firm's portfolio-commentary service calls a Claude model through the Claude API. Anthropic has just marked that model Deprecated, with a named replacement and a retirement date. Several teams hold API keys, and nobody is sure which services still call the model. What is the appropriate first lifecycle step?

options.text: Export Console usage by API key and model, then schedule replacement evals per service well before retirement.
Keep the current model until nearer the retirement date, since a deprecated model still works and the notice period covers migration.
Switch every service to the named replacement in one coordinated release, gated on the replacement passing the current eval suite.
Ask each team to search its repositories for the model ID string and report the services that reference it.

items.explanation: Anthropic's model deprecation docs say a Deprecated model still works but is not recommended, has a named replacement and a retirement date, and is likely to be less reliable than active models; after retirement, requests fail. Anthropic notifies customers at least 60 days before a public model is retired. To find what still uses a model, the docs point to the Console Usage page export, which breaks usage down by API key and model, and advise testing newer models well before the retirement date. Inventory first, then a per-service migration with an eval gate, because upgrades are not drop-in: newer models reject some parameters the old integration may depend on.

rationales.B: Deprecated models still work but are likely to be less reliable than active ones, and waiting spends the notice period that inventory, evals and migration need. The docs advise testing replacements well before retirement.
rationales.C: Nobody knows which services call the model, so 'every service' cannot yet be listed, and an eval gate cannot cover callers that were never found. Newer models are also not drop-in: they can reject forced tool choice, non-default sampling parameters and prefill with 400 errors, so one release risks a simultaneous failure across services.
rationales.D: A code search misses model IDs held in environment variables, deployment config or secrets, and keys owned by teams nobody remembers. The Console Usage export breaks usage down by API key and model, so it finds callers by what actually ran.

sources.title: Claude API errors - common validation errors (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 6.5 Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
items.stem: An ed-tech company provides essay feedback to secondary schools through the Claude API. Its data-sharing agreements with school districts list the student data it may process: essay text, grade level and the assignment rubric. A prompt iteration that adds each student's special-education accommodation notes to the context lifted rubric agreement by 6 points on the offline eval suite, and the product lead wants it live before the spring term. What should the architect require before the change ships?

options.text: Release it behind a feature flag to 10% of schools as an A/B test, so the offline gain is confirmed on live traffic first.
Re-run the eval suite on a sample of recent production essays to confirm the 6-point gain holds before full release.
Remove student names from the accommodation notes before they reach the prompt, so the change adds no new personal data.
A privacy and governance review of the new data category, with the district agreements amended to cover it before release.

items.explanation: The eval gain shows the change makes feedback better; it does not show the company may process the new data. The district agreements list exactly which student data the service may use, and accommodation notes are a new and sensitive category outside that list. A quality gate cannot catch this, because it measures output, not permission. The change therefore needs a governance checkpoint that asks whether the data flow is allowed, and the agreements must be amended, before any student's notes enter a prompt; the review may also choose controls such as minimisation. The Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM prep course's objectives place governance checkpoints in the same lifecycle feedback loop as the eval gate for this reason.

rationales.A: A 10% rollout still sends those schools' accommodation notes into prompts the agreements do not cover. An experiment measures quality; it does not authorise a data flow the contracts exclude.
rationales.B: More eval evidence answers whether the change is better, not whether it is permitted. The eval gate checks quality, so the uncovered data category would ship unnoticed.
rationales.C: Accommodation notes still describe an identifiable student once they sit beside that student's essay and account, so dropping names does not bring them inside the agreements. Minimisation is a control the review may choose, not a substitute for it.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy course page)
Enterprise Integration & Production (Partner Academy course page)

items.objective: 6.5 Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
items.stem: A grocery chain is launching a Claude-powered recipe and substitution assistant, built on the Claude API, in its mobile app. Marketing plans to switch it on for all 4 million app users at once on a holiday weekend. The go-live section of the handoff plan assumes the organisation's published rate limits guarantee that the capacity will be there on launch day. What should the architect change in the go-live plan?

options.text: Request a limit increase sized to projected peak before launch, since an approved higher limit reserves that capacity for launch day.
Raise the SDK retry count to absorb launch-day 429 errors, since retries with backoff will clear temporary throttling.
Route launch traffic through the default workspace, since it carries the organisation's full limits, not a smaller share of them.
Ramp traffic up in stages over the weekend and run the launch in its own workspace with its own spend and rate limits.

items.explanation: Anthropic's rate-limit docs say all limits represent maximum allowed usage, not guaranteed minimums. They are enforced with a token bucket, so they can bite over short intervals, and a sharp increase in usage can trigger acceleration limits that return 429 errors; both the rate-limit and errors pages advise ramping traffic up gradually and keeping usage patterns consistent. On the Claude API, spend and rate limits can be set on any workspace except the default one, so isolating the launch in its own capped workspace protects other workloads and the budget. A go-live plan for a big-bang consumer launch should therefore stage the rollout rather than flip a switch.

rationales.A: Limits are ceilings, not reservations. An approved increase raises the maximum the organisation may use but sets no capacity aside, and a sudden jump to all users can still trigger acceleration limits.
rationales.B: Retries treat the symptom. A sudden all-users launch keeps triggering acceleration limits, and extra retries add load to the same bucket, so users still see failures and latency.
rationales.C: The default workspace is the one workspace that cannot carry its own spend or rate limits, and it shares the organisation's limits with everything else, so it removes isolation rather than adding capacity.

items.objective: 6.5 Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
items.stem: A Claude partner is pursuing an opportunity with a B2B software company that wants Claude to triage incoming bug reports against its 12-year-old monorepo and draft candidate fixes. Discovery is complete, but the deal has stalled for six weeks after a generic chatbot demo: the VP of Engineering doubts Claude will cope with the company's own code, and the security lead has open questions about how source code is handled. The partner's architect must move the engagement from discovery into a scoped design. Which THREE actions should the architect take? (Select THREE)

options.text: Pass the security questions to the account executive to settle commercially, so the architect can stay focused on the build.
Re-run the original demo on the most capable model tier with a larger context, to show raw headroom on a codebase this size.
Rebuild the demo around a bug class found in discovery, run on a repository sample the customer chooses to share, end to end.
Answer each open objection with evidence specific to this buyer, such as the data-handling terms and the sample results.
Propose joint scoping with the Anthropic Applied AI team, using the discovery findings, to agree pilot scope and success criteria.
Offer a fixed-price pilot across every bug category now, letting scope and success criteria emerge from what the pilot finds.

items.explanation: The deal stalled on two questions a generic demo cannot answer: will Claude work on this company's code, and how is that code handled. A scenario-based demo built on a bug class from discovery, run on a sample the customer chose to share, answers the first in the buyer's own terms. Evidence-based objection handling answers the second and records what is still open, rather than leaving technical questions to someone who cannot resolve them. Joint scoping with the Anthropic Applied AI team then turns the discovery findings and the resolved objections into an agreed pilot scope with measurable success criteria, which is what moves the engagement into design. These are the steps the Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM prep course names for the architect's role in a partner go-to-market motion, so that an opportunity does not stall on questions only the architect can answer.

rationales.A: How source code is handled is a technical question, and a commercial concession does not answer it. Handing it off leaves the objection open and the deal stalled on exactly the kind of question the architect is there to resolve.
rationales.B: The VP's doubt is about relevance to this codebase, not raw capability. A bigger model on the same generic demo still shows nothing about the company's own code, and it raises the cost picture before any scope exists.
rationales.F: An unscoped pilot has no agreed definition of success, so it cannot show value and invites scope creep. Success criteria need to be specific and measurable before the build starts, not discovered afterwards.

sources.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM (Partner Academy course page)
Define success criteria and build evaluations (Claude Docs)

items.objective: 7.1 Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
items.stem: A retail bank is rolling Claude Code out to 400 engineers on MDM-enrolled laptops under Claude for Enterprise. Internal audit requires two controls that an engineer without local admin rights cannot switch off: bypassPermissions mode and auto mode must both be unavailable. Engineers can set their own shell environment variables, including the API base URL and the cloud-provider switch. Squads still want to tune their own lint and format hooks per repository. Which configuration best meets the audit requirement without centralising the squads' conventions?

options.text: Set both disable keys in server-managed settings, which Claude Code fetches from the admin console at startup, and keep each squad's hooks in its committed project settings.
Commit both disable keys to every repository's .claude/settings.json under branch protection, and let each squad keep its own hooks in that same committed file.
Publish a managed CLAUDE.md stating that bypass mode and auto mode are prohibited, and let each squad keep its lint and format hooks in its repository settings.
Deliver both disable keys as endpoint-managed settings through the MDM profile or HKLM policy, and keep each squad's hooks in its committed project settings.

items.explanation: The deciding constraint is tamper resistance by a non-admin user. Endpoint-managed settings delivered through an MDM plist or the Windows HKLM registry resist tampering because writing them requires admin privileges, and managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order, so no CLI flag, local file or project file can override them. The stem's detail that engineers control their own environment variables is what rules out the server channel: server-managed settings arrive through a fetch, and Claude Code skips that fetch when a user exports a cloud-provider variable or a non-default API base URL, which is why Anthropic documents them as a client-side control rather than a security boundary and recommends endpoint-managed settings on MDM-enrolled devices. Team conventions that should stay flexible belong one layer down, in the committed project .claude/settings.json.

rationales.A: An engineer who exports CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK or a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL makes Claude Code skip the server fetch entirely, so the controls vanish without admin rights. Anthropic documents server-managed settings as a client-side control, not a security boundary, and points MDM-enrolled fleets to the endpoint-managed channel.
rationales.B: Project settings live in the engineer's own checkout: they can edit or delete .claude/settings.json locally without committing, and the keys apply only when Claude Code runs inside those repositories. Branch protection controls the remote, not the laptop.
rationales.C: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration. A managed CLAUDE.md is the right place for behavioural guidance and compliance reminders, but it cannot make a permission mode unavailable; only managed settings keys do that.

sources.title: Set up Claude Code for your organization

items.objective: 7.1 Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
items.stem: A hospital group's integration team maintains the repository for its radiology-order interface engine, which moves HL7 orders between the imaging system and the EHR. The lead wants every engineer who clones the repo to get the same guardrails and automation automatically. One engineer needs a personal allow rule for a local script that replays synthetic orders in this repository; the same laptop holds clones of repositories with live PHI extracts, where the privacy office forbids that exception. Where should each piece of configuration live?

options.text: Team rules, hooks and plugins in the committed .claude/settings.json; the personal allow rule in that engineer's own ~/.claude/settings.json.
Team rules, hooks and plugins in the committed .claude/settings.json; the personal allow rule in that engineer's .claude/settings.local.json.
Each engineer copies the team rules into their own ~/.claude/settings.json, and the personal allow rule goes in that same user file.
Team rules in organisation-wide managed settings for every hospital repository, and the personal allow rule in the engineer's ~/.claude.json.

items.explanation: Claude Code's documented team-sharing convention is to commit .claude/settings.json so everyone who clones the repository receives the same permissions, hooks and plugins, and to put personal exceptions in .claude/settings.local.json, which Claude Code keeps out of git when it creates it and which applies only in this repository. The privacy office's rule is the deciding constraint: the exception must not follow the engineer into the PHI-bearing repositories, which rules out user-level settings. Shared configuration travels with the code, and personal exceptions never reach colleagues or other projects.

rationales.A: User settings apply that allow rule in every repository on the engineer's laptop, including the PHI-bearing ones where the privacy office forbids it. The local settings file scopes it to this repository only.
rationales.C: User-level settings apply to every project on that laptop and are not versioned with the repository, so the team copies drift apart and new joiners start without them.
rationales.D: Managed settings are for organisation policy, not one team's conventions, and centralising them removes per-team flexibility. ~/.claude.json holds app state, not settings, so a rule placed there is ignored.

items.objective: 7.1 Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
items.stem: A grocery chain's platform team has written 35 Claude Code skills covering store-system deploy checklists, point-of-sale schema conventions and incident templates. Because the point-of-sale code is in PCI DSS scope, the chain's assessor requires developer tooling that touches it to come only from a versioned, change-controlled source. All 500 developers across 40 repositories must receive the same set, updates must roll out centrally, and developers must not be able to load plugins from any other source. Which distribution strategy fits best?

options.text: Copy the 35 skill folders into every repository's .claude/skills directory and ask each repo owner to pull a fresh copy whenever the platform team announces a change.
Paste the content of all 35 skills into the organisation's managed CLAUDE.md so that every session loads them at startup and nothing depends on installation.
Ship them as plugins from an internal versioned marketplace that managed settings register and force-enable, allowlisting that source and blocking sideload flags.
Deploy the 35 skills into the managed skills directory on every laptop through MDM, and leave plugin sources open so that teams can still add their own.

items.explanation: Claude Code documents several fleet channels (a plugin marketplace, the Enterprise skills directory under managed settings, and organisation skills provisioned on claude.ai that sync to users who sign in with a claude.ai account). The marketplace fits here because it versions the set, rolls updates out centrally, and pairs with managed source controls, which is what the PCI assessor's change-controlled-source requirement needs. Managed settings register the marketplace with extraKnownMarketplaces and force-enable its plugins with enabledPlugins; strictKnownMarketplaces allowlists the approved source and disableSideloadFlags rejects --plugin-dir and similar flags. Skills stay progressively disclosed: only names and descriptions sit in context until one is invoked.

rationales.A: Forty copies drift as soon as one owner misses an announcement, there is no central rollout, and nothing stops a developer adding unvetted plugins.
rationales.B: Inlining every skill into CLAUDE.md throws away progressive disclosure: all 35 procedures load into every session, consuming context and reducing adherence. CLAUDE.md is guidance, not a distribution or enforcement channel.
rationales.D: This does distribute the skills centrally to every machine, but leaving plugin sources open fails the assessor's single-source requirement: without a managed source allowlist (strictKnownMarketplaces) and blocked sideload flags (disableSideloadFlags), any developer can still load plugins from an unvetted source.
