items.objective: 7.1 Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
items.stem: A state transportation department runs Claude Code only through Amazon Bedrock, so usage stays inside its existing AWS authorization boundary and billing. Finance wants a monthly spending ceiling for each developer, set differently for each of four program offices, and the ceiling must stop that developer's very next request once reached; the department's AWS cost data refreshes only a few times a day. It also wants a near-real-time view of token spend per office. Which approach fits this deployment route?

options.text: Set group-level usage-credit spend limits for each office in the claude.ai admin console, and read per-office spend from the Claude Code analytics dashboard.
Set a workspace spend limit on the Claude Console's auto-created Claude Code workspace, and give each office its own Console API key for attribution.
Set an AWS budget with budget actions for each office's spend, and enforce OpenTelemetry export in managed settings with an office tag in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.
Run a Claude apps gateway in front of Bedrock with a monthly cap for each office's IdP group, and keep OpenTelemetry export for near-real-time attribution.

items.explanation: Spend controls depend on the access route. On Bedrock the cloud provider bills the usage, and Anthropic's analytics and usage-credit limits do not see it. A self-hosted Claude apps gateway adds per-developer spend limits on these providers: a cap set on an IdP group becomes the default ceiling each member inherits, the gateway checks it live on every inference request, and a developer over the cap gets a 429 on the next request until the period resets or an admin raises it. OpenTelemetry export works on every provider and gives the near-real-time per-office view, tagged through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. The deciding constraints are a per-developer ceiling and stopping the very next request, which billing-driven controls cannot do when cost data lags by hours.

rationales.A: Usage-credit spend limits and the analytics dashboard belong to the Teams and Enterprise route. Bedrock usage never passes through them, so neither the limit nor the view would see the department's spend.
rationales.B: The Console workspace limit governs Console API usage, which this department does not use. Keys cannot be created for the auto-created Claude Code workspace, and a Console key would bypass the AWS boundary the department chose.
rationales.C: AWS budget actions can attach a deny IAM policy, so they can stop usage, but only once billed cost data catches up, which here lags by hours, and they act on an office's role or account rather than checking each developer's ceiling on every request. They miss the stop-the-next-request requirement.

items.objective: 7.1 Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
items.stem: A public university's central IT group is rolling Claude Code out to roughly 300 staff developers who build the student-records and timetabling systems. Leadership has said it must be able to forecast spend before the autumn term starts, must not lose control of which integrations touch student records, and wants staff to build confidence before Claude works more autonomously. Which THREE practices should the rollout plan include? (Select THREE)

options.text: Launch to all 300 developers on day one with bypassPermissions enabled in dev containers, so early friction does not slow adoption.
Start with a small pilot group and establish a usage and cost baseline with tracking tools before widening access to other staff.
Have one central team configure the shared MCP servers and check a .mcp.json into the codebase so every developer benefits.
Begin with guided usage such as codebase Q&A, small bug fixes and plans for review, before moving users on to more agentic work.
Let each developer find and connect their own MCP servers, so that the central team never becomes a bottleneck for integrations.
Give every developer usage credits with no spend limit during the first quarter, so that early experimentation is never blocked by a usage ceiling.

items.explanation: Each constraint maps to documented guidance. Forecasting needs a small pilot group and a measured baseline before wider rollout. Control over integrations comes from one central team configuring MCP servers and committing a .mcp.json so every user benefits. Building confidence before autonomy is the guided-usage step: codebase Q&A, smaller bug fixes and plans for review before users move on to more agentic work. Together they build evidence and shared configuration before scale.

rationales.A: Bypass in dev containers is acceptable isolation, but a day-one launch to all 300 skips the pilot baseline the costs guidance requires before wider rollout, which is the cost-surprise risk the stem names.
rationales.E: Uncoordinated MCP connections multiply unvetted integrations and duplicate effort; the documented pattern is central configuration shared through the codebase.
rationales.F: Uncapped credits remove the very ceiling that makes spend forecastable. The costs guidance pairs usage credits with spend limits at organisation, group or member level, and a forecast needs a measured pilot baseline first.

sources.title: Team Enablement & Operational Productivity (CCAR-P prep course)

items.objective: 7.2 Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
items.stem: An online fashion retailer's checkout team uses Claude Code to implement discount-stacking rules. Several generated changes looked complete and passed visual review but missed edge cases such as rounding on split-tender orders. The team has a thorough test suite, and wants a deterministic gate that sends Claude back to fix failures rather than relying on the model's judgement. Which control fits?

options.text: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to always run the full test suite and fix every failure before it reports that the work is done.
Configure a Stop hook that runs the suite and exits with code 2 on failure, which blocks the turn from ending and feeds failures back to Claude.
Move the checkout team to the most capable model tier, so that generated code handles edge cases like split-tender rounding without extra checks.
Add a PostToolUse hook that records test results to a team dashboard after each edit, so reviewers can see failures in the weekly review.

items.explanation: Anthropic's best practices name this the trust-then-verify gap: Claude stops when the work looks done, so give it a check it can run. Gating options rise in strength from asking in the prompt, to a goal condition, to a Stop hook that deterministically blocks the turn from ending and returns the failures. Hooks give deterministic control where CLAUDE.md is advisory, and exit code 2 on a Stop hook prevents Claude from stopping and returns stderr so it can fix the failures. The requirement for a deterministic gate rather than the model's judgement is what rules out every advisory option. Claude Code caps consecutive Stop-hook continuations (eight by default, configurable with CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP), so pair the gate with CI for a hard merge block.

rationales.A: This is the weakest gate on the documented ladder. CLAUDE.md is context the model may or may not act on, so it cannot guarantee the turn will not end with failing tests.
rationales.C: A larger model is a capability fix for a verification problem. Plausible code that misses edge cases is exactly the failure a runnable check catches, whichever model writes it.
rationales.D: PostToolUse runs after the action and cannot undo it, and logging to a dashboard gates nothing; failures surface a week later, after the work is already merged.

items.objective: 7.2 Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
items.stem: A health-tech company enabled Anthropic's managed Code Review on the repository that handles patient-record exports. Its engineering policy says no pull request with an Important finding may merge. A month later an audit finds three PRs that merged with open Important findings, even though branch protection requires all status checks to pass. On each of them the Code Review check run completed with a neutral conclusion, its Important findings listed in the Details summary. What change actually enforces the policy?

options.text: Add a rule to REVIEW.md stating that any Important finding must block the merge, so the reviewer marks its check run as failed from now on.
Add a required CI job that reads the machine-readable severity counts from the Code Review check run and fails if the Important count exceeds zero.
Change the review trigger from Manual to After every push, so that each new commit is re-reviewed and no finding is missed before merge.
Make the Claude GitHub app a required approver in branch protection, so an open Important finding withholds its approval of the PR.

items.explanation: Managed Code Review findings never approve or block a pull request: the check run always completes with a neutral conclusion, which is why branch protection let the PRs through. To gate merges on severity, the documented approach is to parse the machine-readable severity counts from the check run in your own CI and fail a required job. The general lesson for review discipline is to put the gate in a deterministic control you own rather than assuming an advisory reviewer enforces policy.

rationales.A: REVIEW.md shapes what the reviewer looks for, not how its check run concludes. The check still completes neutral, so the merge path is unchanged.
rationales.C: Reviewing every push multiplies cost by the number of pushes and still produces only neutral checks. More reviews do not create a gate.
rationales.D: Code Review does not act as an approver; its findings neither approve nor block. A required-approver rule cannot be satisfied or withheld by it.

sources.title: Team Enablement & Operational Productivity (CCAR-P prep course)

items.objective: 7.2 Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
items.stem: A B2B SaaS company first had Claude review code in the same session that wrote it, and reviews almost always passed. It then added a reviewer subagent prompted to 'find every gap'. PRs now collect 20 to 30 findings each, developers chase all of them, and velocity has dropped with no fall in escaped defects. What review design should the architect recommend?

options.text: Keep a fresh-context reviewer that sees only the diff, and rewrite its brief to flag only gaps affecting correctness or stated requirements.
Return to same-session review with a longer checklist, since the writing session already holds the full context of why each change was made.
Keep the gap-finding reviewer and require developers to resolve every finding before merge, since each one may be a production defect.
Swap the reviewer subagent onto the most capable model tier so its findings become fewer and more accurate, keeping the same prompt.

items.explanation: Both failures are documented. A reviewer in the writing session is biased toward code it just wrote, so independent review uses a fresh context that sees only the diff and the criteria. But a reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound, and chasing every finding leads to over-engineering. The fix here is a more precise instruction: keep the independence and replace the open-ended 'find every gap' brief with one that flags only gaps affecting correctness or stated requirements. That balances trustworthiness before production against delivery speed.

rationales.B: The shared context is the problem, not an asset: the writer is biased toward its own work, which is why same-session reviews almost always passed.
rationales.C: Treating every finding as mandatory is the over-engineering trap the docs warn about, and the data already shows it slowed delivery without reducing escaped defects.
rationales.D: The volume comes from the instruction to find every gap, not from model capability. A stronger model given the same brief will still report gaps on sound work.

items.objective: 7.2 Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
items.stem: A federal agency's platform team plans to migrate 1,800 Java source files off a deprecated logging library by running claude -p once per file from a CI job. The runs will be unattended, on build agents that also hold deployment credentials. Which practices should the team adopt? (Select TWO)

options.text: Trial the prompt on two or three representative files and refine it until the output is right before launching the full fan-out run.
Run the jobs with --dangerously-skip-permissions on the build agents so the fan-out never stalls on a permission prompt part-way through.
Feed all 1,800 files into a single interactive session so that Claude keeps one consistent view of the migration across the codebase.
Skip per-file test runs to save build minutes, since the same prompt applied to every file will produce consistent, correct results.
Pass --allowedTools on each claude -p call so the unattended runs can use only the tools that the migration actually requires.

items.explanation: Anthropic's documented fan-out pattern calls claude -p per file with --allowedTools to scope what unattended runs may do, and tests on two or three files first so the prompt is refined before it is multiplied 1,800 times. Scoping tools matters doubly here because the build agents hold deployment credentials; trialling first is cheap insurance against a systematic error repeated across the whole codebase.

rationales.B: Skipping permissions on agents that hold deployment credentials removes every guard from unattended runs; bypass is documented for isolated environments only.
rationales.C: One session for 1,800 files exhausts context and degrades quality; per-file fan-out exists precisely so each run gets a clean, focused context.
rationales.D: Identical prompts do not guarantee correct output on every file. Without a runnable check per file, the trust-then-verify gap scales with the batch.

items.objective: 7.2 Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
items.stem: A school district's software team adopted Claude Code on a Team plan with the Claude GitHub app installed. The CIO wants to show the school board that the tooling has improved delivery, and proposes reporting 'lines accepted' and 'suggestion accept rate' as the headline measures. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Report lines of code with Claude Code from the contribution metrics as the headline, since they count every AI-written line that reaches merged PRs.
Report suggestion accept rate as a quality measure, since a suggestion a developer accepts was judged correct before merge.
Report PRs with Claude Code (%) alone, since a rising share of assisted PRs shows that delivery has improved.
Treat contribution metrics as a conservative undercount and pair them with delivery measures such as DORA metrics.

items.explanation: Claude Code's contribution metrics are deliberately conservative and represent an underestimate: code rewritten by more than 20 percent, lock files and generated code are not attributed, and lines-accepted counts do not track later deletions. Anthropic recommends reading them alongside DORA metrics or sprint velocity rather than alone. A board needs evidence that delivery improved, which an activity count cannot show on its own.

rationales.A: Attribution is intentionally partial: only lines with high confidence of Claude Code involvement are counted, so the figure is an undercount, and a line count measures activity rather than delivery outcomes.
rationales.B: Acceptance is not correctness: accept rate counts approvals of an edit at the moment it is proposed, not whether the code survives review or production.
rationales.C: The share of assisted PRs measures adoption, not delivery. It can rise while lead time, failure rate or throughput stay flat, so it needs pairing with delivery measures such as DORA metrics.

items.objective: 7.3 Support debugging and operational issue resolution
items.stem: At a regional clinic network, the rule 'never put realistic patient identifiers in test fixtures' has been in services/patient-export/CLAUDE.md for a month. Developers who launch Claude Code at the repository root report that it still creates new fixture files under services/patient-export/tests/ with realistic identifiers, usually without reading any existing file there first. In an affected session, /context lists the root CLAUDE.md but not the subdirectory file. What should the team's first-line runbook entry say?

options.text: Move the rule to the root CLAUDE.md; a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads when Claude reads a file there, not when it creates one.
Add the rule to ~/.claude.json on each developer's laptop; that file is read in every session, wherever Claude Code is launched.
Rewrite the rule in capitals with IMPORTANT in front; emphasis makes the subdirectory CLAUDE.md carry more weight when it is read.
Have developers run /clear or restart Claude Code when it happens; CLAUDE.md edits take effect only after the session reloads.

items.explanation: Anthropic's configuration-debugging workflow starts with /context to see what actually loaded, and a memory file missing from it means checking its location against the load rules. CLAUDE.md files at and above the launch directory load at session start, but a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads on demand only when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool, not at launch and not when it writes or creates files there. Moving the rule to the root file makes it load in every session. Path-scoped rules also trigger on reads, so they would leave the same gap, and a must-never rule can additionally be backed by a hook.

rationales.B: ~/.claude.json holds app state and UI toggles, not instructions or settings; the debugging guide lists configuration placed there as ignored, so the rule would never load.
rationales.C: Emphasis cannot help a file that never enters context. /context already shows the subdirectory file is absent, so the wording is not the problem.
rationales.D: The rule has been in place for a month, so a stale session is not the cause; a fresh session launched at the root still omits the subdirectory file until Claude reads a file there.

sources.title: Team Enablement & Operational Productivity (CCAR-P prep course)

items.objective: 7.3 Support debugging and operational issue resolution
items.stem: A commercial insurer now routes all Claude Code traffic through a new internal LLM gateway that logs requests for compliance. Since the cutover, developers on API-key billing report that every turn in long sessions is slow and costly, including turns sent seconds apart. /usage shows the main prompt cache hit ratio near zero; models, plugins and MCP servers are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Developers editing CLAUDE.md mid-session, which changes the cached prefix and forces the whole conversation to be recomputed every turn.
The five-minute cache lifetime on API-key billing, which expires between turns and should be raised to the one-hour cache option.
Rate limiting from higher traffic since cutover, which throttles cached requests first and makes the remaining turns slower and more costly.
The gateway stripping cache_control markers from requests, so the whole conversation history is billed and processed uncached every turn.

items.explanation: The symptom is a near-zero hit ratio on every turn, starting at the gateway cutover, with nothing else changed. Prompt caching is an exact prefix match driven by cache_control markers, and Anthropic documents that a gateway which silently strips those markers bills the whole history uncached on every turn. Connecting the symptom to the architecture change, rather than to developer behaviour, is the diagnostic step; the fix is to make the gateway pass the markers through.

rationales.A: Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session does not break the cache; the change simply does not apply until /clear, /compact or a restart.
rationales.B: A five-minute TTL causes a miss only after an idle gap longer than five minutes, not on turns sent seconds apart; a longer TTL cannot help if nothing is being cached.
rationales.C: Rate limits produce 429 errors and delays, not cache misses; and because cache reads do not count toward input limits on most models, caching would ease throttling rather than suffer from it.

sources.title: How Claude Code uses prompt caching

items.objective: 7.3 Support debugging and operational issue resolution
items.stem: A state revenue department's tax-modernisation repository commits a .claude/settings.json that registers the department's dor-tools marketplace and enables several of its plugins. Those listed in the marketplace by relative path install automatically for every contributor who trusts the folder. Only fiscal-review fails, with 'Plugin "fiscal-review" is enabled in project settings but isn't installed'; the marketplace lists it by its own GitHub repository because the change-control board requires it to stay in that separately audited repository. Central IT owns managed settings and will not change them this quarter. What should the team's runbook direct?

options.text: Have each contributor re-accept the workspace trust dialog for the folder, since repository plugin entries apply only after trust.
Copy fiscal-review into the dor-tools repository and list it by relative path, so that it installs automatically like the other plugins.
Have each contributor install fiscal-review from dor-tools once at project scope, and add that one-time install step to the onboarding notes.
Add the fiscal-review GitHub repository to the committed project settings as an approved marketplace source, so its external source is trusted.

items.explanation: Committing enabledPlugins turns a plugin on for collaborators but does not download it. A plugin listed by a relative path loads from the marketplace copy, which is why the other dor-tools plugins work, but one whose marketplace entry points at an external source is fetched only when user settings, an untracked settings.local.json, the --settings flag or managed settings enable it. The documented fix is for each contributor to run claude plugin install fiscal-review@dor-tools --scope project once, which belongs in the onboarding runbook. Copying the plugin would also work technically, but the change-control board's audited-repository rule rules it out. If central IT later agrees, managed extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins install the plugin on every machine with no per-contributor step.

rationales.A: Trust governs whether the repository's extraKnownMarketplaces entries register, and these contributors have already trusted the folder. The message is about a missing install, which trust does not trigger.
rationales.B: A relative-path copy would install automatically, but it forks fiscal-review out of the separately audited repository the change-control board requires, leaving an unaudited copy that drifts from the one the other team maintains.
rationales.D: Approving a source is an allowlist (strictKnownMarketplaces), which is managed-only, so a project file cannot set it; and an allowlist never registers or installs anything, it only limits which sources may be added.

sources.title: Manage Claude Code plugins for your organization
Plugin loading: enabled in project settings but not installed

items.objective: 7.3 Support debugging and operational issue resolution
items.stem: A developer on a school district's student-information-system team, on the district's Claude Team plan, sees 'You've hit your weekly limit' in Claude Code while finishing the grade-posting fix that must ship before report cards publish tomorrow morning; the message says the limit resets in three days. Switching to the smallest model with /model gives the same message. The district admin has enabled usage credits that members can request from inside Claude Code, and district policy keeps all work on student-records code inside the district's contracted plan. What should the team's self-service troubleshooting guide tell them?

options.text: Run /compact to shrink the conversation, since the weekly limit message appears when the session's context window fills up.
Sign in with a personal Claude Pro account to finish tonight's fix, then switch back to the district Team seat once the limit resets.
Request usage credits from the admin now inside Claude Code, since weekly limits span every model and switching cannot help.
Switch to a model from a different family with /model, since each model family keeps its own separate weekly allowance.

items.explanation: Session and weekly limits on Team and Enterprise seats are shared across all models, so the failed /model switch is expected; only a model-family limit, such as an Opus limit, is escaped by switching family. With the reset three days away and a deadline tomorrow, waiting is the wrong move: the developer should request usage credits now (on Team and Enterprise, /usage-credits sends the request to the admin), and raise it early so the admin can act before the deadline. A personal account would breach the district's policy for student-records code. Encoding this triage in a self-service guide keeps a common, predictable message from becoming a support ticket.

rationales.A: A context or auto-compact warning is a different message from a usage limit; compacting changes context size, not the seat allowance already consumed.
rationales.B: A personal consumer account sits outside the district's contracted plan and its data terms, which the district's policy for student-records code forbids; the deadline does not change that.
rationales.D: Only a model-family-specific limit, such as an Opus limit, is worked around by switching family. A weekly seat limit applies to every model.

items.objective: 7.3 Support debugging and operational issue resolution
items.stem: A cloud-security vendor's developer-experience team pushed a batch of new plugins last week. Some engineers now see tool calls rejected unexpectedly and odd behaviour that colleagues cannot reproduce. The architect wants one diagnostic step in the team runbook that separates a customization problem from a policy or install problem, so these cases stop reaching the architect. Claude Code's safe mode starts a session with CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, MCP servers and non-managed hooks turned off, while organisation-managed policy and permissions still apply. Which runbook step fits?

options.text: Have every engineer run in safe mode until the plugin authors ship fixes; that stops the rejected tool calls while the batch is investigated.
Relaunch the session in safe mode: if the issue goes away a customization is the cause, and if not, check managed settings with /status.
Run /doctor on each affected laptop and remove any extension it flags as unused; unused extensions are what cause rejected tool calls.
Roll last week's plugin batch back for every engineer, then re-release the plugins one at a time while watching for the errors to return.

items.explanation: claude --safe-mode disables CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers and custom agents while keeping auth, model, built-in tools and permissions. Organisation-managed settings policy and managed hooks still apply, while managed plugins, skills, CLAUDE.md and MCP servers are turned off. If the problem disappears, a customization is the cause; if it persists, the next places to look are managed settings, environment variables or the install, which /status and claude doctor expose. One branching step lets each engineer localise the fault in minutes without waiting on the architect or disturbing colleagues.

rationales.A: This is a workaround, not a diagnostic: it switches off every customization for everyone, including those that work, and never tells an engineer whether the cause is a customization or policy, so policy cases persist and still reach the architect.
rationales.C: /doctor checks install health, invalid settings files and unused extensions, but an unused extension costs context rather than rejecting tool calls, and the step does not separate a customization cause from a policy cause.
rationales.D: A fleet-wide rollback disrupts every engineer to chase a problem only some see, takes days of staged re-releases, and still cannot tell a policy or install cause from a customization one, because it leaves managed settings and the install untouched.
